abstract: A design for a fully analog version of a self-organizing feature map neural network has been completed. Several parts of this design are in fabrication. The feature map algorithm was modified to accommodate circuit solutions to the various computations required. Performance effects were measured by simulating the design as part of a frontend for a speech recognition system. Circuits are included to implement both activation computations and weight adaption 'or learning. External access to the analog weight values is provided to facilitate weight initialization, testing and static storage. This fully analog implementation requires an order of magnitude less area than a comparable digital/analog hybrid version developed earlier.

The feature map algorithm was modified to accommodate circuit solutions to the various computations required. Performance effects were measured by simulating the design as part of a frontend for a speech recognition system. Circuits are included to implement both activation computations and weight adaption 'or learning. paragraphs: This paper presents a completed design for a fully analog self-organizing feature-map network. Implementing the network requires circuits for both computing activity and adapting connection weights. The authors modify the feature-map algorithm to suit the circuit solutions available for its computations, treating algorithm and hardware design together.

They assess the effects of these modifications by simulating the design as a front end for speech recognition. The design also allows external access to analog weights. That access supports initialization, testing, and static storage, making the learned parameters accessible beyond the circuitry that updates and uses them.

The fully analog implementation requires about one-tenth the area of an earlier comparable digital/analog hybrid version. This makes physical size a major stated advantage of the design. At the reported stage, several components are in fabrication, while the performance assessment comes from simulation. The contribution combines a hardware-adapted learning algorithm, circuits for learning and activation, and a substantial reduction in the area needed for the implementation.
summary.tldr: A fully analog feature-map design implements learning and activation in about one-tenth the area of an earlier hybrid version.

title: An Analog Self-Organizing Neural Network Chip

abstract: While the network loading problem for 2-layer threshold nets is NP-hard when learning from examples alone (as with backpropaga(cid:173) tion), (Baum, 91) has now proved that a learner can employ queries to evade the hidden unit credit assignment problem and PAC-load nets with up to four hidden units in polynomial time. Empirical tests show that the method can also learn far more complicated functions such as randomly generated networks with 200 hidden units. The algorithm easily approximates Wieland's 2-spirals func(cid:173) tion using a single layer of 50 hidden units, and requires only 30 minutes of CPU time to learn 200-bit parity to 99.7% accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper investigates learning threshold networks when the learner can use queries as well as examples. The motivating difficulty is hidden-unit credit assignment: determining how internal units should contribute to the desired output. Learning two-layer threshold networks from examples alone is described as an NP-hard problem.

Access to queries changes the learning setting. The abstract cites a proof that a query-based learner can avoid this credit-assignment obstacle and learn networks with up to four hidden units in polynomial time under the PAC framework. That theoretical guarantee has a specific scope, while the reported empirical tests investigate substantially larger problems.

Those tests include randomly generated networks with 200 hidden units. The algorithm also approximates the two-spirals function using one layer of 50 hidden units and learns 200-bit parity to 99.7% accuracy in 30 minutes of CPU time. Together, these results distinguish the proven small-network guarantee from broader experimental capability and illustrate why allowing a learner to ask queries can materially change the difficulty of constructing hidden units.
summary.tldr: Learning with queries enables a polynomial-time guarantee for small threshold networks and strong reported results on larger problems.

title: Constructing Hidden Units using Examples and Queries

abstract: The primate brain must solve two important problems in grasping move(cid:173) ments. The first problem concerns the recognition of grasped objects: specifically, how does the brain integrate visual and motor information on a grasped object? The second problem concerns hand shape planning: specifically, how does the brain design the hand configuration suited to the shape of the object and the manipulation task? A neural network model that solves these problems has been developed. The operations of the net(cid:173) work are divided into a learning phase and an optimization phase. In the learning phase, internal representations, which depend on the grasped ob(cid:173) jects and the task, are acquired by integrating visual and somatosensory information. In the optimization phase, the most suitable hand shape for grasping an object is determined by using a relaxation computation of the network. Present Address: Parallel Distributed Processing Research Dept., Sony Corporation, 6-7-35 Kitashinagawa, Shinagawa-ku, Tokyo 141, Japan

paragraphs: This paper models two connected problems in grasping: integrating information about an object and choosing a hand configuration suited to using it. The required hand shape depends on both the object's shape and the manipulation task. The authors develop a neural network that combines visual information with somatosensory information, linking perception to hand-shape planning.

The network operates in two phases. During learning, it acquires internal representations by integrating the sensory inputs. These representations depend on the objects being grasped and on the task. Learning therefore establishes a shared representation of information that will later be used to determine an appropriate grasp.

During optimization, the network uses a relaxation computation to determine the most suitable hand shape. Relaxation lets the network settle toward a configuration that serves the grasping problem. The contribution is a unified model in which sensory integration supplies the representations used for action planning. This connects recognizing a grasped object with preparing the hand for a particular manipulation, within the same computational system.
summary.tldr: A neural network learns joint visual and somatosensory representations, then uses relaxation to select task-appropriate hand shapes.

title: Integration of Visual and Somatosensory Information for Preshaping Hand in Grasping Movements

abstract: Channel equalization problem is an important problem in high-speed communications. The sequences of symbols transmitted are distorted by neighboring symbols. Traditionally, the channel equalization problem is considered as a channel-inversion operation. One problem of this approach is that there is no direct correspondence between error proba(cid:173) bility and residual error produced by the channel inversion operation. In this paper, the optimal equalizer design is formulated as a classification problem. The optimal classifier can be constructed by Bayes decision rule. In general it is nonlinear. An efficient hybrid linear/nonlinear equalizer approach has been proposed to train the equalizer. The error probability of new linear/nonlinear equalizer has been shown to be bet(cid:173) ter than a linear equalizer in an experimental channel.

Traditionally, the channel equalization problem is considered as a channel-inversion operation. One problem of this approach is that there is no direct correspondence between error proba(cid:173) bility and residual error produced by the channel inversion operation. In this paper, the optimal equalizer design is formulated as a classification problem. The optimal classifier can be constructed by Bayes decision rule. In general it is nonlinear. An efficient hybrid linear/nonlinear equalizer approach has been proposed to train the equalizer. The error probability of new linear/nonlinear equalizer has been shown to be bet(cid:173) ter than a linear equalizer in an experimental channel.

paragraphs: In high-speed communication, neighboring transmitted symbols can interfere with one another, making the received signal difficult to interpret. Channel equalization addresses this distortion. The paper questions the usual framing of equalization as reversing the channel, because a smaller residual error after inversion does not directly establish a lower probability of choosing the wrong symbol.

The authors instead formulate equalization as classification: the equalizer must decide which symbol produced the observation. They describe the optimal classifier through the Bayes decision rule. This changes the focus from how accurately a transformation reverses distortion to how accurately the resulting system distinguishes the possible transmitted symbols.

Because the optimal decision rule is generally nonlinear, the paper proposes an efficient training approach combining linear and nonlinear components. On an experimental channel, this hybrid equalizer has a lower error probability than a linear equalizer. The result supports the classification formulation in that setting and shows why nonlinear decision making can help with the actual communication objective.
summary.tldr: Treating channel equalization as symbol classification motivates a hybrid equalizer that beats a linear equalizer on an experimental channel.

title: A Hybrid Linear/Nonlinear Approach to Channel Equalization Problems

abstract: Linear threshold elements are the basic building blocks of artificial neural networks. A linear threshold element computes a function that is a sign of a weighted sum of the input variables. The weights are arbitrary integers; actually, they can be very big integers-(cid:173) exponential in the number of the input variables. However, in practice, it is difficult to implement big weights. In the present literature a distinction is made between the two extreme cases: linear threshold functions with polynomial-size weights as opposed to those with exponential-size weights. The main contribution of this paper is to fill up the gap by further refining that separation. Namely, we prove that the class of linear threshold functions with polynomial-size weights can be divided into subclasses according to the degree of the polynomial. In fact, we prove a more general that there exists a minimal weight linear threshold function result- for any arbitrary number of inputs and any weight size. To prove those results we have developed a novel technique for constructing linear threshold functions with minimal weights.

paragraphs: A linear threshold element makes a decision from the sign of a weighted sum of its inputs. Although this rule is simple, representing some functions can require very large integer weights. The paper studies the minimum weight sizes needed for such representations, motivated by the practical difficulty of implementing large weights.

Earlier distinctions separated functions requiring polynomial-size weights from those requiring exponential-size weights. The authors refine the polynomial side of that division, proving that it contains distinct subclasses according to the degree of the polynomial. Thus, functions whose weights are all described as polynomially bounded can still differ meaningfully in their minimum requirements.

The paper also states a more general existence result for minimal-weight threshold functions across input counts and weight sizes. Its proofs use a new technique for constructing functions with minimal weights. The contribution is a finer description of representational demands: knowing that a function admits polynomial-size weights does not fully characterize how large those weights must be to implement it.
summary.tldr: The paper proves a finer hierarchy of threshold functions based on the minimum integer weight sizes needed to represent them.

title: On Neural Networks with Minimal Weights

abstract: Gaussian Processes provide good prior models for spatial data, but can be too smooth. In many physical situations there are discontinuities along bounding surfaces, for example fronts in near-surface wind fields. We describe a modelling method for such a constrained discontinuity and demonstrate how to infer the model parameters in wind fields with MCMC sampling.
originalAbstract: Gaussian Processes provide good prior models for spatial data, but can be too smooth. In many physical situations there are discontinuities along bounding surfaces, for example fronts in near-surface wind fields. We describe a modelling method for such a constrained discontinuity and demonstrate how to infer the model parameters in wind fields with MCMC sampling.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a mismatch between smooth spatial models and physical fields that contain abrupt changes. Gaussian processes provide useful prior models for spatial data, but their smoothness can be excessive for some applications. Near-surface wind fields illustrate the issue: a front can form a boundary across which the field changes discontinuously.

The proposed method adds a constrained discontinuity to a Gaussian process model. The central modeling idea is to accommodate an abrupt change along a bounding surface within the spatial description. This matters because the boundary is part of the physical structure being represented. A model that smooths across it can fail to express the kind of change the authors want to capture.

The paper also demonstrates inference of the model parameters for wind fields using Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. This connects the proposed representation to a method for estimating it from data. The contribution is thus both a way to express constrained spatial discontinuities and a demonstrated sampling-based approach to parameter inference in the motivating wind-field setting.
summary.tldr: The paper adds constrained discontinuities to Gaussian process wind-field models and demonstrates parameter inference using MCMC.

title: Adding Constrained Discontinuities to Gaussian Process Models of Wind Fields

abstract: We introduce stagewise processing in error-correcting codes and image restoration, by extracting information from the former stage and using it selectively to improve the performance of the latter one. Both mean-field analysis using the cavity method and sim(cid:173) ulations show that it has the advantage of being robust against uncertainties in hyperparameter estimation.
originalAbstract: We introduce stagewise processing in error-correcting codes and image restoration, by extracting information from the former stage and using it selectively to improve the performance of the latter one. Both mean-field analysis using the cavity method and sim(cid:173) ulations show that it has the advantage of being robust against uncertainties in hyperparameter estimation.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a staged approach to error-correcting codes and image restoration. Its central idea is to extract information from an earlier processing stage and pass selected information to a later stage. The later stage uses that information to improve its result, making the relationship between stages part of the processing method.

Selectivity is an explicit feature of the proposal. The information obtained earlier is used selectively to help the subsequent stage, rather than simply treating the first result as the final answer. In both application areas, this creates a mechanism for an intermediate result to contribute to further recovery or correction.

The authors study the approach using mean-field analysis based on the cavity method and through simulations. Both support an advantage in robustness when hyperparameter estimates are uncertain. That finding matters because the stated benefit concerns sensitivity to parameter estimation, alongside performance improvement across stages. The contribution is a shared processing strategy for the two tasks, supported by both theoretical analysis and simulation evidence.
summary.tldr: Selectively reusing information across processing stages improves robustness to uncertain hyperparameter estimates in coding and image restoration.

title: Stagewise Processing in Error-correcting Codes and Image Restoration

abstract: Using methods of Statistical Physics, we investigate the rOle of model complexity in learning with support vector machines (SVMs). We show the advantages of using SVMs with kernels of infinite complexity on noisy target rules, which, in contrast to common theoretical beliefs, are found to achieve optimal general(cid:173) ization error although the training error does not converge to the generalization error. Moreover, we find a universal asymptotics of the learning curves which only depend on the target rule but not on the SVM kernel.
originalAbstract: Using methods of Statistical Physics, we investigate the rOle of model complexity in learning with support vector machines (SVMs). We show the advantages of using SVMs with kernels of infinite complexity on noisy target rules, which, in contrast to common theoretical beliefs, are found to achieve optimal general(cid:173) ization error although the training error does not converge to the generalization error. Moreover, we find a universal asymptotics of the learning curves which only depend on the target rule but not on the SVM kernel.

paragraphs: A highly complex model is often expected to generalize poorly when its training error differs from its test error. This paper examines that intuition for support vector machines using statistical-physics methods. It focuses on how kernel complexity affects learning noisy target rules.

The analysis finds advantages for kernels with infinite complexity. In the studied setting, they achieve optimal generalization even though training error does not approach generalization error. This separates successful prediction from the assumption that the two error measures must converge to one another.

The authors also identify universal asymptotic learning curves whose behavior depends on the target rule rather than the particular SVM kernel. The contribution is a theoretical account of when model complexity and kernel choice become less decisive than the task itself. These conclusions concern the analyzed asymptotic regime, providing a counterpoint to simple complexity-based explanations rather than an unrestricted endorsement of every infinite-dimensional kernel.
summary.tldr: Statistical-physics analysis finds optimal SVM generalization with infinite-complexity kernels and target-dependent universal learning-curve asymptotics.

title: Asymptotic Universality for Learning Curves of Support Vector Machines

abstract: To classify a large number of unlabeled examples we combine a lim- ited number of labeled examples with a Markov random walk represen- tation over the unlabeled examples. The random walk representation ex- ploits any low dimensional structure in the data in a robust, probabilistic manner. We develop and compare several estimation criteria/algorithms suited to this representation. This includes in particular multi-way clas- siﬁcation with an average margin criterion which permits a closed form solution. The time scale of the random walk regularizes the representa- tion and can be set through a margin-based criterion favoring unambigu- ous classiﬁcation. We also extend this basic regularization by adapting time scales for individual examples. We demonstrate the approach on synthetic examples and on text classiﬁcation problems.
originalAbstract: To classify a large number of unlabeled examples we combine a lim- ited number of labeled examples with a Markov random walk represen- tation over the unlabeled examples. The random walk representation ex- ploits any low dimensional structure in the data in a robust, probabilistic manner. We develop and compare several estimation criteria/algorithms suited to this representation. This includes in particular multi-way clas- siﬁcation with an average margin criterion which permits a closed form solution. The time scale of the random walk regularizes the representa- tion and can be set through a margin-based criterion favoring unambigu- ous classiﬁcation. We also extend this basic regularization by adapting time scales for individual examples. We demonstrate the approach on synthetic examples and on text classiﬁcation problems.

paragraphs: The paper studies classification when only a limited number of examples have labels. It combines those labels with a Markov random walk representation over the unlabeled examples. The representation is designed to exploit low-dimensional structure in the data probabilistically, giving the unlabeled observations a role in how classification is performed.

The authors develop and compare several estimation criteria and algorithms for this representation. One is a multiclass method based on an average-margin criterion that admits a closed-form solution. The random walk’s time scale controls regularization of the representation, and a margin-based criterion selects that scale to favor less ambiguous classification.

They also allow individual examples to have different time scales, extending the flexibility of this regularization mechanism. This makes the scale of the representation an adjustable part of learning, rather than a single fixed choice shared by all observations. Demonstrations on synthetic data and text-classification problems illustrate the approach in both constructed examples and an applied classification setting.
summary.tldr: Markov random walks use unlabeled data structure for classification, with walk time scales controlling regularization.

title: Partially labeled classification with Markov random walks

abstract: We show that two important properties of the primary visual cortex emerge when the principle of temporal coherence is applied to natural image sequences. The properties are simple-cell-like receptive ﬁelds and complex-cell-like pooling of simple cell outputs, which emerge when we apply two different approaches to temporal coherence. In the ﬁrst approach we extract receptive ﬁelds whose outputs are as temporally co- herent as possible. This approach yields simple-cell-like receptive ﬁelds (oriented, localized, multiscale). Thus, temporal coherence is an alterna- tive to sparse coding in modeling the emergence of simple cell receptive ﬁelds. The second approach is based on a two-layer statistical generative model of natural image sequences. In addition to modeling the temporal coherence of individual simple cells, this model includes inter-cell tem- poral dependencies. Estimation of this model from natural data yields both simple-cell-like receptive ﬁelds, and complex-cell-like pooling of simple cell outputs. In this completely unsupervised learning, both lay- ers of the generative model are estimated simultaneously from scratch. This is a signiﬁcant improvement on earlier statistical models of early vision, where only one layer has been learned, and others have been ﬁxed a priori.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether temporal coherence in natural image sequences can explain two properties associated with primary visual cortex. Temporal coherence favors outputs that remain consistent over time. The authors investigate two approaches and obtain receptive fields resembling those of simple cells, as well as pooling behavior resembling that of complex cells.

The first approach extracts receptive fields whose outputs are as temporally coherent as possible. The resulting fields are oriented, localized, and multiscale. This provides temporal coherence as an alternative to sparse coding for modeling the emergence of simple-cell-like receptive fields, showing that the reported structures can arise from a different learning principle.

The second approach uses a two-layer statistical generative model that includes both individual-cell temporal coherence and temporal dependencies between cells. Learning from natural data produces simple-cell-like fields and complex-cell-like pooling. Both layers are learned together from scratch without supervision. This is the stated advance over earlier statistical models that learned one layer while fixing others in advance: the model learns both kinds of organization within a single procedure.
summary.tldr: Temporal-coherence learning from natural image sequences produces simple-cell-like receptive fields and, in a jointly learned two-layer model, complex-cell-like pooling.

title: Temporal Coherence, Natural Image Sequences, and the Visual Cortex

paragraphs: The paper asks what determines the thickness of axon branches. Its starting hypothesis is that axonal dimensions have evolved to balance two demands: transmitting signals with little delay and keeping the total volume of the branching structure small. The question becomes whether this tradeoff predicts a relationship between the thicknesses of connected branches.

The authors derive a branching law for optimal diameters under a general cost function. At a split, the parent diameter raised to the power v + 2 equals the sum of the two daughter diameters raised to that same power. Here, v describes the assumed relationship between axon diameter and signal conduction speed. The predicted geometry therefore depends on how diameter affects propagation.

The authors compare the law with available experimental measurements and report reasonable agreement. That agreement supports the proposed optimization account without establishing that the tradeoff is the sole determinant of axonal shape. The contribution is a quantitative connection between a functional hypothesis about neural wiring and the geometry of individual branch points.
summary.tldr: Balancing signal delay against axon volume yields a branching law that agrees reasonably with available measurements.

title: Branching Law for Axons

abstract: In this work, we consider the problem of learning a positive semidefinite matrix. The critical issue is how to preserve positive semidefiniteness during the course of learning. Our algorithm is mainly inspired by LPBoost [1] and the general greedy convex optimization framework of Zhang [2]. We demonstrate the essence of the algorithm, termed PSDBoost (positive semidefinite Boosting), by focusing on a few different applications in machine learning. The proposed PSDBoost algorithm extends traditional Boosting algorithms in that its parameter is a positive semidefinite matrix with trace being one instead of a classifier. PSDBoost is based on the observation that any trace-one positive semidefinitematrix can be decomposed into linear convex combinations of trace-one rank-one matrices, which serve as base learners of PSDBoost. Numerical experiments are presented.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning a positive semidefinite matrix while preserving that property throughout learning. Its algorithm, PSDBoost, adapts ideas from boosting and greedy convex optimization to a matrix-valued parameter. The learned object is constrained to have trace one, so maintaining both matrix structure and normalization is central to the formulation.

The key observation is that any trace-one positive semidefinite matrix can be expressed as a convex combination of trace-one rank-one matrices. PSDBoost uses these simpler matrices as its base learners. Building the parameter through such combinations provides a direct structural way to preserve the required properties during the learning process.

This extends the boosting viewpoint beyond combining classifiers: here, the pieces collectively form a constrained matrix. The authors illustrate the algorithm through several machine-learning applications and present numerical experiments. The main contribution is the construction principle and its algorithmic use, showing how a demanding matrix constraint can be respected through the choice of building blocks.
summary.tldr: PSDBoost learns trace-one positive semidefinite matrices by combining rank-one matrix base learners.

title: PSDBoost: Matrix-Generation Linear Programming for Positive Semidefinite Matrices Learning

abstract: The odor transduction process has a large time constant and is susceptible to various types of noise. Therefore, the olfactory code at the sensor/receptor level is in general a slow and highly variable indicator of the input odor in both natural and artificial situations. Insects overcome this problem by using a neuronal device in their Antennal Lobe (AL), which transforms the identity code of olfactory receptors to a spatio-temporal code. This transformation improves the decision of the Mushroom Bodies (MBs), the subsequent classifier, in both speed and accuracy.Here we propose a rate model based on two intrinsic mechanisms in the insect AL, namely integration and inhibition. Then we present a MB classifier model that resembles the sparse and random structure of insect MB. A local Hebbian learning procedure governs the plasticity in the model. These formulations not only help to understand the signal conditioning and classification methods of insect olfactory systems, but also can be leveraged in synthetic problems. Among them, we consider here the discrimination of odor mixtures from pure odors. We show on a set of records from metal-oxide gas sensors that the cascade of these two new models facilitates fast and accurate discrimination of even highly imbalanced mixtures from pure odors.

paragraphs: Odor sensors respond slowly and are vulnerable to noise, so their raw readings can be unreliable indicators of an odor's identity. The paper takes inspiration from insect olfaction, where the antennal lobe transforms receptor responses into patterns distributed across neurons and time before a subsequent structure classifies them.

The authors build two connected models. The first is a rate model of the antennal lobe based on integration and inhibition, providing a stage for conditioning sensor signals. The second resembles the sparse, random organization of insect mushroom bodies and serves as the classifier. Its connections adapt through a local Hebbian learning procedure.

The combined system is evaluated on recordings from metal-oxide gas sensors, with the task of distinguishing mixtures from pure odors. It enables fast and accurate discrimination even for highly imbalanced mixtures. The result supports the usefulness of this biological processing sequence for the tested artificial sensing problem, while the models also offer an account of how insect-inspired signal conditioning and classification can work together.
summary.tldr: An insect-inspired signal processor and sparse classifier distinguish odor mixtures from pure odors quickly and accurately in gas-sensor recordings.

title: Artificial Olfactory Brain for Mixture Identification

abstract: We propose a novel bound on single-variable marginal probability distributions in factor graphs with discrete variables. The bound is obtained by propagating bounds (convex sets of probability distributions) over a subtree of the factor graph, rooted in the variable of interest. By construction, the method not only bounds the exact marginal probability distribution of a variable, but also its approximate Belief Propagation marginal (``belief''). Thus, apart from providing a practical means to calculate bounds on marginals, our contribution also lies in providing a better understanding of the error made by Belief Propagation. We show that our bound outperforms the state-of-the-art on some inference problems arising in medical diagnosis.

The bound is obtained by propagating bounds (convex sets of probability distributions) over a subtree of the factor graph, rooted in the variable of interest. By construction, the method not only bounds the exact marginal probability distribution of a variable, but also its approximate Belief Propagation marginal (``belief''). Thus, apart from providing a practical means to calculate bounds on marginals, our contribution also lies in providing a better understanding of the error made by Belief Propagation. We show that our bound outperforms the state-of-the-art on some inference problems arising in medical diagnosis.

paragraphs: The paper studies uncertainty about a single variable in a factor graph whose variables take discrete values. Its goal is to bound that variable’s marginal probability distribution, rather than merely return one estimated distribution. Such bounds describe a set of possible probability assignments within which the exact answer is guaranteed to lie.

The method propagates convex sets of probability distributions along a subtree rooted at the variable of interest. These sets carry bounds through the graph. A distinctive feature is that the resulting bound contains both the exact marginal and the approximate marginal produced by Belief Propagation, often called that algorithm’s belief.

Containing both distributions connects the method to understanding approximation error: the bound constrains where the exact answer and the Belief Propagation answer can be. It therefore contributes a practical bounding procedure and a way to reason about that approximation. On some medical diagnosis inference problems, the authors report that their bound outperforms the state of the art, with the claim restricted to those evaluated problems.
summary.tldr: Propagating sets of distributions produces bounds that contain both exact marginals and Belief Propagation estimates in discrete factor graphs.

title: Bounds on marginal probability distributions

abstract: Representing distributions over permutations can be a daunting task due to the fact that the number of permutations of n objects scales factorially in n. One recent way that has been used to reduce storage complexity has been to exploit probabilistic independence, but as we argue, full independence assumptions impose strong sparsity constraints on distributions and are unsuitable for modeling rankings. We identify a novel class of independence structures, called riffled independence, which encompasses a more expressive family of distributions while retaining many of the properties necessary for performing efficient inference and reducing sample complexity. In riffled independence, one draws two permutations independently, then performs the riffle shuffle, common in card games, to combine the two permutations to form a single permutation. In ranking, riffled independence corresponds to ranking disjoint sets of objects independently, then interleaving those rankings. We provide a formal introduction and present algorithms for using riffled independence within Fourier-theoretic frameworks which have been explored by a number of recent papers.

paragraphs: A probability distribution over rankings can become enormous because the number of possible orderings grows factorially with the number of objects. Independence assumptions can reduce that burden, but the paper argues that full independence imposes overly restrictive sparsity on ranking distributions. It introduces riffled independence as a more expressive alternative.

The construction resembles shuffling two separately ordered groups of cards. Each disjoint group of objects receives an independently drawn ranking, and the two rankings are then interleaved to form a complete ordering. This distinguishes the order within each group from the way the groups are mixed in the final ranking.

The resulting family retains many properties useful for efficient inference and reduced sample complexity while representing more distributions than the full-independence approach discussed in the paper. The authors formalize the structure and provide algorithms within Fourier-theoretic frameworks for ranked data. The contribution is a form of factorization tailored to permutations: it exploits separable parts of ranking generation while allowing those parts to be interwoven in the observed order.
summary.tldr: Riffled independence models rankings by independently ordering disjoint groups and then interleaving them, balancing expressiveness with computational structure.

title: Riffled Independence for Ranked Data

abstract: Metric learning has become a very active research field. The most popular representative--Mahalanobis metric learning--can be seen as learning a linear transformation and then computing the Euclidean metric in the transformed space. Since a linear transformation might not always be appropriate for a given learning problem, kernelized versions of various metric learning algorithms exist. However, the problem then becomes finding the appropriate kernel function. Multiple kernel learning addresses this limitation by learning a linear combination of a number of predefined kernels; this approach can be also readily used in the context of multiple-source learning to fuse different data sources. Surprisingly, and despite the extensive work on multiple kernel learning for SVMs, there has been no work in the area of metric learning with multiple kernel learning. In this paper we fill this gap and present a general approach for metric learning with multiple kernel learning. Our approach can be instantiated with different metric learning algorithms provided that they satisfy some constraints. Experimental evidence suggests that our approach outperforms metric learning with an unweighted kernel combination and metric learning with cross-validation based kernel selection.

paragraphs: Metric learning adjusts how distances between examples are measured. A common approach learns a linear transformation and then measures Euclidean distance in the transformed space. Kernelized methods allow a richer representation, but they introduce another choice: which kernel should define that representation for the learning problem?

This paper addresses that choice by combining metric learning with multiple kernel learning. Instead of selecting a single predefined kernel, the approach learns a linear combination of several. The same construction can combine information from different data sources. The authors present a general framework that can accommodate different metric-learning algorithms when those algorithms satisfy the required constraints.

Experimental evidence suggests that learned kernel combinations outperform both unweighted combinations and kernel selection through cross-validation. The contribution is therefore a way to make the representation choice part of learning the distance itself. The reported advantage is empirical, while the framework's applicability remains conditional on the constraints placed on the underlying metric-learning algorithm.
summary.tldr: A general framework learns kernel combinations for metric learning, with empirical advantages over unweighted combinations and kernel selection.

title: Metric Learning with Multiple Kernels

abstract: Motivated by the spread of on-line information in general and on-line petitions in particular, recent research has raised the following combinatorial estimation problem. There is a tree T that we cannot observe directly (representing the structure along which the information has spread), and certain nodes randomly decide to make their copy of the information public. In the case of a petition, the list of names on each public copy of the petition also reveals a path leading back to the root of the tree. What can we conclude about the properties of the tree we observe from these revealed paths, and can we use the structure of the observed tree to estimate the size of the full unobserved tree T? Here we provide the first algorithm for this size estimation task, together with provable guarantees on its performance. We also establish structural properties of the observed tree, providing the first rigorous explanation for some of the unusual structural phenomena present in the spread of real chain-letter petitions on the Internet.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate the spread of information when only some copies become public. It represents the full spread as an unobserved tree, with nodes randomly revealing their copies. For chain-letter petitions, the names recorded on a public copy disclose a path back to the tree’s root, exposing part of its history.

These revealed paths form an observed tree, but that tree is only a partial view of the underlying spread. The authors ask both what structural properties this visible portion has and whether it contains enough information to estimate the size of the full tree. Their analysis explicitly connects the observation mechanism to the structure researchers can see.

The paper provides the first algorithm for this size-estimation task, together with provable performance guarantees. It also establishes properties of the observed tree that give a rigorous explanation for some unusual structures found in real online chain-letter petitions. The contribution shows how incomplete public traces can support inference about a larger diffusion process under the stated tree-based observation model.
summary.tldr: An algorithm with provable guarantees estimates the size of a hidden information-diffusion tree from randomly revealed paths.

title: Reconstructing Patterns of Information Diffusion from Incomplete Observations
An Integer Optimization Approach to Associative Classification

abstract: We provide a detailed study of the estimation of probability distributions---discrete and continuous---in a stringent setting in which data is kept private even from the statistician. We give sharp minimax rates of convergence for estimation in these locally private settings, exhibiting fundamental tradeoffs between privacy and convergence rate, as well as providing tools to allow movement along the privacy-statistical efficiency continuum. One of the consequences of our results is that Warner's classical work on randomized response is an optimal way to perform survey sampling while maintaining privacy of the respondents.
originalAbstract: We provide a detailed study of the estimation of probability distributions---discrete and continuous---in a stringent setting in which data is kept private even from the statistician. One of the consequences of our results is that Warner's classical work on randomized response is an optimal way to perform survey sampling while maintaining privacy of the respondents.

paragraphs: The paper studies probability estimation when individual data must remain private even from the statistician carrying out the analysis. It considers both discrete and continuous distributions. This places privacy inside the estimation problem itself, because the analyst cannot simply work with unrestricted observations.

The authors establish sharp minimax convergence rates for this setting. These rates characterize the best worst-case estimation performance under the privacy constraints. They expose a fundamental relationship between privacy and statistical efficiency: the privacy requirement affects how quickly an estimated distribution can approach the underlying one as evidence accumulates.

The work also supplies tools for choosing positions along that privacy-efficiency tradeoff. A concrete consequence concerns Warner's randomized response method for surveys, which the analysis identifies as optimal for maintaining respondent privacy in the studied setting. This connects an established survey technique to a broader theory of private probability estimation. The significance is both a performance benchmark for locally private procedures and a principled account of how privacy choices relate to the accuracy those procedures can attain.
summary.tldr: Sharp minimax bounds characterize privacy–accuracy tradeoffs in locally private distribution estimation and establish optimality of randomized response in the studied survey setting.

title: Local Privacy and Minimax Bounds: Sharp Rates for Probability Estimation

abstract: We propose to train an ensemble with the help of a reservoir in which the learning algorithm can store a limited number of samples. This novel approach lies in the area between offline and online ensemble approaches and can be seen either as a restriction of the former or an enhancement of the latter. We identify some basic strategies that can be used to populate this reservoir and present our main contribution, dubbed Greedy Edge Expectation Maximization (GEEM), that maintains the reservoir content in the case of Boosting by viewing the samples through their projections into the weak classifier response space. We propose an efficient algorithmic implementation which makes it tractable in practice, and demonstrate its efficiency experimentally on several compute-vision data-sets, on which it outperforms both online and offline methods in a memory constrained setting.

paragraphs: Ensemble training can face a memory constraint that prevents retaining all available examples. This paper introduces a reservoir that stores a limited number of samples for learning. The approach occupies a middle ground between offline and online training: the learner keeps a restricted collection of examples available for use while operating within a bounded storage budget.

The authors examine basic strategies for filling the reservoir and introduce Greedy Edge Expectation Maximization, or GEEM, for boosting. GEEM maintains reservoir contents by viewing examples through their projections into the response space of weak classifiers. This makes the classifiers' responses to examples central to the selection of what remains stored.

An efficient implementation makes the approach tractable in practice. Experiments on several computer vision datasets show that it outperforms both online and offline methods in a memory-constrained setting. The findings support reservoir management as an important part of ensemble learning when storage is limited, with the reported advantage specifically established under that resource constraint.
summary.tldr: GEEM manages a limited training reservoir for boosting and outperforms compared online and offline methods under memory constraints.

title: Reservoir Boosting : Between Online and Offline Ensemble Learning

abstract: Suppose $k$ centers are fit to $m$ points by heuristically minimizing the $k$-means cost; what is the corresponding fit over the source distribution? This question is resolved here for distributions with $p\geq 4$ bounded moments; in particular, the difference between the sample cost and distribution cost decays with $m$ and $p$ as $m^{\min\{-1/4, -1/2+2/p\}}$. The essential technical contribution is a mechanism to uniformly control deviations in the face of unbounded parameter sets, cost functions, and source distributions. To further demonstrate this mechanism, a soft clustering variant of $k$-means cost is also considered, namely the log likelihood of a Gaussian mixture, subject to the constraint that all covariance matrices have bounded spectrum. Lastly, a rate with refined constants is provided for $k$-means instances possessing some cluster structure.

paragraphs: A set of k-means centers can fit a finite dataset well without immediately revealing how well it fits the distribution that produced the data. This paper bounds the gap between those two costs when the source distribution has bounded moments of order p, with p at least four. The question applies even when the centers were obtained through heuristic optimization.

For m observations, the stated dependence of the gap is m raised to min{-1/4, -1/2 + 2/p}. The central technical contribution is a mechanism for controlling deviations uniformly despite unbounded parameter sets, costs, and source distributions. This matters because the analysis must cover the fitted choice of centers, not just one choice fixed beforehand.

The authors also apply the mechanism to Gaussian-mixture log likelihood, viewed as a soft-clustering counterpart, under a bounded-spectrum condition on covariance matrices. They provide refined constants for k-means problems with cluster structure. Together, these results connect finite-sample clustering quality to distribution-level fit under explicit moment and structural conditions.
summary.tldr: Moment-based uniform bounds relate observed k-means cost to population cost and extend to constrained Gaussian-mixture clustering.

title: Moment-based Uniform Deviation Bounds for $k$-means and Friends

abstract: We develop an accelerated randomized proximal coordinate gradient (APCG) method, for solving a broad class of composite convex optimization problems. In particular, our method achieves faster linear convergence rates for minimizing strongly convex functions than existing randomized proximal coordinate gradient methods. We show how to apply the APCG method to solve the dual of the regularized empirical risk minimization (ERM) problem, and devise efficient implementations that can avoid full-dimensional vector operations. For ill-conditioned ERM problems, our method obtains improved convergence rates than the state-of-the-art stochastic dual coordinate ascent (SDCA) method.

We show how to apply the APCG method to solve the dual of the regularized empirical risk minimization (ERM) problem, and devise efficient implementations that can avoid full-dimensional vector operations. For ill-conditioned ERM problems, our method obtains improved convergence rates than the state-of-the-art stochastic dual coordinate ascent (SDCA) method.

paragraphs: The paper develops an accelerated randomized proximal coordinate gradient method for composite convex optimization. This setting combines parts of an objective that can be handled through gradient and proximal updates. Coordinate methods work with selected portions of the variables, making the cost of individual updates an important consideration alongside the number of updates required.

The main theoretical result concerns strongly convex objectives: the proposed method achieves faster linear convergence rates than existing randomized proximal coordinate gradient methods. Linear convergence describes a recurring proportional reduction in optimization error. The improvement therefore concerns how quickly repeated updates reduce that error under the stated strong convexity condition.

The authors also apply the method to the dual formulation of regularized empirical risk minimization. They develop implementations that avoid operations on full-dimensional vectors, connecting the convergence analysis to computational efficiency. For ill-conditioned empirical risk minimization problems, they establish improved convergence rates over stochastic dual coordinate ascent. This identifies a specific setting where the acceleration offers a theoretical advantage.
summary.tldr: An accelerated coordinate optimization method improves convergence guarantees for strongly convex objectives and ill-conditioned empirical risk minimization.

title: An Accelerated Proximal Coordinate Gradient Method

abstract: We present data-dependent learning bounds for the general scenario of non-stationary non-mixing stochastic processes. Our learning guarantees are expressed in terms of a data-dependent measure of sequential complexity and a discrepancy measure that can be estimated from data under some mild assumptions. We use our learning bounds to devise new algorithms for non-stationary time series forecasting for which we report some preliminary experimental results.
originalAbstract: We present data-dependent learning bounds for the general scenario of non-stationary non-mixing stochastic processes. Our learning guarantees are expressed in terms of a data-dependent measure of sequential complexity and a discrepancy measure that can be estimated from data under some mild assumptions. We use our learning bounds to devise new algorithms for non-stationary time series forecasting for which we report some preliminary experimental results.

paragraphs: This paper develops learning guarantees for forecasting time series whose statistical behavior can change over time. It considers non-stationary, non-mixing stochastic processes, a general setting that allows both distributional change and dependence that need not satisfy a mixing condition. The aim is to ground forecasting algorithms in theory suited to that setting.

The bounds depend on a data-dependent measure of sequential complexity and a discrepancy measure. These quantities organize the guarantee around the complexity of sequential prediction and the discrepancy relevant to learning from changing data. The authors state that the discrepancy can be estimated from observations under mild assumptions, making that part of the guarantee accessible from data.

The authors then use the bounds to design forecasting algorithms for non-stationary time series. They report preliminary experimental results for these algorithms. The contribution therefore connects a general theoretical formulation to algorithm design, while the empirical evidence is explicitly early-stage. The stated estimability of discrepancy also remains conditional on the assumptions identified by the authors.
summary.tldr: Data-dependent learning bounds guide forecasting algorithms for time series that may be non-stationary and non-mixing.

title: Learning Theory and Algorithms for Forecasting Non-stationary Time Series

abstract: Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) is a distance on the space of probability measures which has found numerous applications in machine learning and nonparametric testing. This distance is based on the notion of embedding probabilities in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. In this paper, we present the first known lower bounds for the estimation of MMD based on finite samples. Our lower bounds hold for any radial universal kernel on $\R^d$ and match the existing upper bounds up to constants that depend only on the properties of the kernel. Using these lower bounds, we establish the minimax rate optimality of the empirical estimator and its $U$-statistic variant, which are usually employed in applications.

paragraphs: Maximum Mean Discrepancy, or MMD, measures distance between probability distributions by representing them in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Applications generally have finite samples rather than direct access to the distributions. This paper asks how accurately MMD can be estimated from those samples and whether commonly used estimators already achieve the best possible rate.

The authors derive lower bounds on estimation error for any radial universal kernel on Euclidean space. Lower bounds describe a fundamental limit on estimation accuracy. Their bounds match existing upper bounds apart from constants that depend only on properties of the kernel, connecting achievable performance with the difficulty inherent in the estimation problem.

This establishes minimax rate optimality for the empirical estimator and its U-statistic variant. In plain terms, these familiar estimators achieve the best worst-case rate under the setting studied. Rate optimality concerns how estimation accuracy scales with sample size; the remaining kernel-dependent constants are still part of the comparison. The result provides theoretical support for estimators already used in applications.
summary.tldr: Matching lower and upper bounds establish minimax rate optimality of common MMD estimators for radial universal kernels.

title: Minimax Estimation of Maximum Mean Discrepancy with Radial Kernels

abstract: In this paper, we propose to adopt the diffusion approximation tools to study the dynamics of Oja's iteration which is an online stochastic gradient method for the principal component analysis. Oja's iteration maintains a running estimate of the true principal component from streaming data and enjoys less temporal and spatial complexities. We show that the Oja's iteration for the top eigenvector generates a continuous-state discrete-time Markov chain over the unit sphere. We characterize the Oja's iteration in three phases using diffusion approximation and weak convergence tools. Our three-phase analysis further provides a finite-sample error bound for the running estimate, which matches the minimax information lower bound for PCA under the additional assumption of bounded samples.

paragraphs: Oja’s iteration estimates a leading principal component while data arrive as a stream. It updates a running estimate instead of repeatedly solving the full principal component analysis problem, offering lower time and memory demands. This paper examines how that stochastic update evolves, with the aim of explaining its convergence and the accuracy obtainable from a finite amount of data.

The authors describe the normalized estimate as a Markov chain on the unit sphere: its location is continuous, but updates occur at discrete steps. They then use diffusion approximations and weak convergence tools to characterize the iteration through three phases. This gives a mathematical description of the learning dynamics across different stages.

The three-phase analysis leads to a finite-sample error bound for the running estimate. Under the additional assumption that samples are bounded, this bound matches the minimax information lower bound for PCA. The finding connects a computationally economical streaming procedure with statistically optimal error behavior in the stated setting, while retaining the bounded-sample qualification.
summary.tldr: A three-phase diffusion analysis of Oja’s streaming PCA update yields an error bound matching the minimax lower bound under bounded samples.

title: Diffusion Approximations for Online Principal Component Estimation and Global Convergence

abstract: Deep learning requires data. A useful approach to obtain data is to be creative and mine data from various sources, that were created for different purposes. Unfortunately, this approach often leads to noisy labels. In this paper, we propose a meta algorithm for tackling the noisy labels problem. The key idea is to decouple when to update'' from how to update''. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm by mining data for gender classification by combining the Labeled Faces in the Wild (LFW) face recognition dataset with a textual genderizing service, which leads to a noisy dataset. While our approach is very simple to implement, it leads to state-of-the-art results. We analyze some convergence properties of the proposed algorithm.

The key idea is to decouple when to update'' from how to update''. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm by mining data for gender classification by combining the Labeled Faces in the Wild (LFW) face recognition dataset with a textual genderizing service, which leads to a noisy dataset. While our approach is very simple to implement, it leads to state-of-the-art results. We analyze some convergence properties of the proposed algorithm.

paragraphs: Combining data sources can produce training examples for a new task, but the labels obtained this way may be unreliable. This paper addresses that problem with a meta-algorithm for learning from noisy labels. Its central idea separates the decision to perform an update from the procedure used to calculate that update.

This separation makes update timing an explicit part of the learning method. A training rule determines how parameters change, while a distinct decision determines when that rule should act. The authors describe the resulting approach as simple to implement and analyze some of its convergence properties, connecting the practical learning procedure with theoretical questions about its behavior.

For an empirical demonstration, the authors construct a gender-classification dataset by combining faces from Labeled Faces in the Wild with a text-based gender-labeling service. This combination produces noisy labels, providing a direct test of the proposed approach. They report state-of-the-art results in this demonstration, supporting the value of controlling when learning updates occur in the presence of label noise.
summary.tldr: A simple meta-algorithm separates update timing from update computation to improve learning with noisy labels.

title: Decoupling "when to update" from "how to update"

abstract: We present a new approach to modeling sequential data: the deep equilibrium model (DEQ). Motivated by an observation that the hidden layers of many existing deep sequence models converge towards some fixed point, we propose the DEQ approach that directly finds these equilibrium points via root-finding. Such a method is equivalent to running an infinite depth (weight-tied) feedforward network, but has the notable advantage that we can analytically backpropagate through the equilibrium point using implicit differentiation. Using this approach, training and prediction in these networks require only constant memory, regardless of the effective “depth” of the network. We demonstrate how DEQs can be applied to two state-of-the-art deep sequence models: self-attention transformers and trellis networks. On large-scale language modeling tasks, such as the WikiText-103 benchmark, we show that DEQs 1) often improve performance over these state-of-the-art models (for similar parameter counts); 2) have similar computational requirements to existing models; and 3) vastly reduce memory consumption (often the bottleneck for training large sequence models), demonstrating an up-to 88% memory reduction in our experiments. The code is available at https://github.com/locuslab/deq.

paragraphs: Deep Equilibrium Models approach sequence modeling by solving directly for a stable hidden representation. The motivation is the observation that hidden layers in many deep sequence models tend toward a fixed point. A root-finding procedure locates that equilibrium, corresponding to an infinitely deep feedforward network whose layers share weights.

Training differentiates through the equilibrium using implicit differentiation. This allows training and prediction to use constant memory with respect to the network’s effective depth. That qualification matters: the memory claim concerns depth, and the method’s central advantage is obtaining the equilibrium representation without retaining a growing sequence of layer states.

The authors apply the approach to self-attention transformers and trellis networks. On large-scale language-modeling tasks, including WikiText-103, DEQs often improve performance at similar parameter counts while requiring comparable computation. The reported experiments reduce memory consumption by as much as 88%. The findings position equilibrium computation as a way to retain the modeling benefits of effective depth while substantially reducing its memory demands.
summary.tldr: Deep Equilibrium Models solve for fixed-point representations and differentiate implicitly, enabling constant memory with respect to effective depth.

title: Deep Equilibrium Models

abstract: Least-mean squares (LMS) solvers such as Linear / Ridge / Lasso-Regression, SVD and Elastic-Net not only solve fundamental machine learning problems, but are also the building blocks in a variety of other methods, such as decision trees and matrix factorizations. We suggest an algorithm that gets a finite set of $n$ $d$-dimensional real vectors and returns a weighted subset of $d+1$ vectors whose sum is \emph{exactly} the same. The proof in Caratheodory's Theorem (1907) computes such a subset in $O(n^2d^2)$ time and thus not used in practice. Our algorithm computes this subset in $O(nd)$ time, using $O(\log n)$ calls to Caratheodory's construction on small but "smart" subsets. This is based on a novel paradigm of fusion between different data summarization techniques, known as sketches and coresets. As an example application, we show how it can be used to boost the performance of existing LMS solvers, such as those in scikit-learn library, up to x100. Generalization for streaming and distributed (big) data is trivial. Extensive experimental results and complete open source code are also provided.

The proof in Caratheodory's Theorem (1907) computes such a subset in $O(n^2d^2)$ time and thus not used in practice. Our algorithm computes this subset in $O(nd)$ time, using $O(\log n)$ calls to Caratheodory's construction on small but "smart" subsets. This is based on a novel paradigm of fusion between different data summarization techniques, known as sketches and coresets. As an example application, we show how it can be used to boost the performance of existing LMS solvers, such as those in scikit-learn library, up to x100. Generalization for streaming and distributed (big) data is trivial. Extensive experimental results and complete open source code are also provided.

paragraphs: Least-mean-squares solvers support regression and serve as components in other learning methods. This paper accelerates such computation through a compact, exact summary of vectors. Given n vectors of dimension d, its algorithm returns a weighted subset of d+1 vectors whose weighted sum exactly matches the original sum.

A construction based on Caratheodory's theorem already provides such a subset, but its O(n^2d^2) runtime makes it impractical for this purpose. The new algorithm takes O(nd) time by making O(log n) calls to that construction on carefully selected small subsets. Its design combines two approaches to summarizing data: sketches and coresets.

As an application, the authors use these summaries to improve existing least-mean-squares solvers, including implementations in scikit-learn, reporting speedups of up to 100 times. They also describe straightforward extensions to streaming and distributed data. The exactness claim concerns the preserved vector sum, while the application results demonstrate how that mathematical summary can support faster solver computation.
summary.tldr: An exact vector-summarization algorithm runs in O(nd) time and supports reported least-mean-squares solver speedups of up to 100 times.

title: Fast and Accurate Least-Mean-Squares Solvers

abstract: We propose a constraint-based causal feature selection method for identifying causes of a given target variable, selecting from a set of candidate variables, while there can also be hidden variables acting as common causes with the target. We prove that if we observe a cause for each candidate cause, then a single conditional independence test with one conditioning variable is sufficient to decide whether a candidate associated with the target is indeed causing it. We thus improve upon existing methods by significantly simplifying statistical testing and requiring a weaker version of causal faithfulness. Our main assumption is inspired by neuroscience paradigms where the activity of a single neuron is considered to be also caused by its own previous state. We demonstrate successful application of our method to simulated, as well as encephalographic data of twenty-one participants, recorded in Max Planck Institute for intelligent Systems. The detected causes of motor performance are in accordance with the latest consensus about the neurophysiological pathways, and can provide new insights into personalised brain stimulation.

paragraphs: A brain feature associated with an outcome need not cause it, particularly when hidden variables influence both. This paper proposes a constraint-based method for selecting genuine causes of a target from candidate variables while allowing such hidden common causes. Its main contribution is a condition under which the required statistical testing becomes much simpler.

The key assumption is that a cause of each candidate cause is observed. Under that condition and the method's causal assumptions, the authors prove that one conditional independence test with a single conditioning variable suffices to decide whether an associated candidate causes the target. The method also requires a weaker version of causal faithfulness than existing approaches. Neuroscience motivates the observed-cause assumption because a neuron's previous state can influence its current activity.

The authors demonstrate the approach on simulated data and encephalographic recordings from twenty-one participants. The identified causes of motor performance agree with established neurophysiological pathways. They suggest these findings could inform personalized brain stimulation, presenting that as a possible application rather than a demonstrated intervention outcome.
summary.tldr: With an observed cause for each candidate and the stated causal assumptions, one conditional independence test can identify whether an associated feature causes the target.

title: Selecting causal brain features with a single conditional independence test per feature

abstract: Hyperbolic embeddings have recently gained attention in machine learning due to their ability to represent hierarchical data more accurately and succinctly than their Euclidean analogues. However, multi-relational knowledge graphs often exhibit multiple simultaneous hierarchies, which current hyperbolic models do not capture. To address this, we propose a model that embeds multi-relational graph data in the Poincaré ball model of hyperbolic space. Our Multi-Relational Poincaré model (MuRP) learns relation-specific parameters to transform entity embeddings by Möbius matrix-vector multiplication and Möbius addition. Experiments on the hierarchical WN18RR knowledge graph show that our Poincaré embeddings outperform their Euclidean counterpart and existing embedding methods on the link prediction task, particularly at lower dimensionality.

paragraphs: Hyperbolic embeddings can represent hierarchical data accurately using compact representations. Knowledge graphs present an additional challenge because different relationships can impose different hierarchies on the same entities. The paper addresses this multiplicity, which the existing hyperbolic models discussed in the abstract do not capture.

MuRP places entities in the Poincaré ball, a model of hyperbolic space, and learns parameters specific to each relationship. It uses Möbius matrix-vector multiplication and Möbius addition to transform entity embeddings. These relation-dependent transformations give the model a way to account for multiple hierarchies while keeping its representations in hyperbolic geometry.

The authors evaluate link prediction on WN18RR, a hierarchical knowledge graph. Their Poincaré embeddings outperform both a Euclidean counterpart and existing embedding methods, especially when the embedding dimension is small. The finding supports the combination of hyperbolic geometry and relation-specific transformations for this task. The emphasis on lower dimensionality matters because the model obtains strong reported results with relatively compact entity representations.
summary.tldr: MuRP uses relation-specific transformations in hyperbolic space to represent multiple hierarchies and improve compact knowledge-graph embeddings.

title: Multi-relational Poincaré Graph Embeddings

abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) has demonstrated impressive performance in automatically designing high-performance neural networks. The power of deep neural networks is to be unleashed for analyzing a large volume of data (e.g. ImageNet), but the architecture search is often executed on another smaller dataset (e.g. CIFAR-10) to finish it in a feasible time. However, it is hard to guarantee that the optimal architecture derived on the proxy task could maintain its advantages on another more challenging dataset. This paper aims to improve the generalization of neural architectures via domain adaptation. We analyze the generalization bounds of the derived architecture and suggest its close relations with the validation error and the data distribution distance on both domains. These theoretical analyses lead to AdaptNAS, a novel and principled approach to adapt neural architectures between domains in NAS. Our experimental evaluation shows that only a small part of ImageNet will be sufficient for AdaptNAS to extend its architecture success to the entire ImageNet and outperform state-of-the-art comparison algorithms.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search often designs a network on a smaller dataset because searching directly on a large dataset is expensive. The difficulty is that a design that works well on the smaller task may lose its advantage when transferred. This paper treats that transfer as a domain adaptation problem involving the architecture itself.

The authors analyze bounds on how well a selected architecture generalizes between domains. Their analysis connects generalization with validation error and the distance between the two data distributions. This makes the mismatch between the search dataset and the destination dataset part of the architecture-selection problem, rather than assuming that success on the smaller task will carry over.

These theoretical observations lead to AdaptNAS, a method for adapting neural architectures across domains. In the reported evaluation, using only a small portion of ImageNet was sufficient for AdaptNAS to achieve success on the full dataset and outperform the comparison algorithms. The finding supports incorporating information from the destination domain while retaining the practical motivation for avoiding a full-scale architecture search.
summary.tldr: AdaptNAS uses domain adaptation to help architectures found on smaller datasets transfer successfully to larger target datasets.

title: Adapting Neural Architectures Between Domains

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) rely on graph convolutions to extract local features from network data. These graph convolutions combine information from adjacent nodes using coefficients that are shared across all nodes. Since these coefficients are shared and do not depend on the graph, one can envision using the same coefficients to define a GNN on another graph. This motivates analyzing the transferability of GNNs across graphs. In this paper we introduce graphon NNs as limit objects of GNNs and prove a bound on the difference between the output of a GNN and its limit graphon-NN. This bound vanishes with growing number of nodes if the graph convolutional filters are bandlimited in the graph spectral domain. This result establishes a tradeoff between discriminability and transferability of GNNs.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks combine information from neighboring nodes using coefficients shared throughout a graph. Because those coefficients do not depend on a particular graph, the same learned parameters can potentially be used on another graph. This paper investigates the mathematical basis for that possibility by studying how network outputs relate across graph representations.

The authors introduce graphon neural networks as limiting objects for graph neural networks. They then bound the difference between a finite graph network's output and the output of its graphon limit. This supplies a way to analyze transfer through a common limiting representation, rather than relying solely on the fact that the same coefficients can be reused.

The bound approaches zero as the number of nodes grows when the convolutional filters are bandlimited in the graph spectral domain. That filter condition is central to the stated result. The analysis establishes a tradeoff between transferability and discriminability: restricting spectral behavior supports transfer, while the ability to distinguish graph information is also affected. Parameter sharing alone therefore does not describe the full transferability question.
summary.tldr: Graphon limits yield a conditional transferability bound for graph neural networks and expose a tradeoff with discriminability.

title: Graphon Neural Networks and the Transferability of Graph Neural Networks

abstract: We propose to jointly analyze experts' eye movements and verbal narrations to discover important and interpretable knowledge patterns to better understand their decision-making processes. The discovered patterns can further enhance data-driven statistical models by fusing experts' domain knowledge to support complex human-machine collaborative decision-making. Our key contribution is a novel dynamic Bayesian nonparametric model that assigns latent knowledge patterns into key phases involved in complex decision-making. Each phase is characterized by a unique distribution of word topics discovered from verbal narrations and their dynamic interactions with eye movement patterns, indicating experts' special perceptual behavior within a given decision-making stage. A new split-merge-switch sampler is developed to efficiently explore the posterior state space with an improved mixing rate. Case studies on diagnostic error prediction and disease morphology categorization help demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model and discovered knowledge patterns.
