paragraphs: Experts reveal aspects of their reasoning through both where they look and what they say. This paper jointly analyzes eye movements and verbal narration to discover interpretable patterns in complex decisions. The aim is to make expert knowledge usable within statistical models that support collaborative decision-making between people and machines.

The proposed dynamic Bayesian nonparametric model organizes hidden knowledge patterns into phases of a decision process. Each phase has its own distribution of topics in the spoken narration, together with changing relationships between those topics and eye movements. This organization links verbal content to perceptual behavior within a particular stage, rather than treating all observations as interchangeable evidence.

To fit the model, the authors develop a split-merge-switch sampler that explores possible posterior configurations with improved mixing. Case studies address diagnostic error prediction and disease morphology categorization, demonstrating the usefulness of the model and its discovered patterns. The contribution is both an analysis method for expert behavior and a way to connect that behavior to downstream predictive tasks.
summary.tldr: A dynamic Bayesian model combines expert gaze and narration to identify interpretable phases and knowledge patterns in decision-making.

title: Dynamic Fusion of Eye Movement Data and Verbal Narrations in Knowledge-rich Domains

abstract: Graph-based neural network models are producing strong results in a number of domains, in part because graphs provide flexibility to encode domain knowledge in the form of relational structure (edges) between nodes in the graph. In practice, edges are used both to represent intrinsic structure (e.g., abstract syntax trees of programs) and more abstract relations that aid reasoning for a downstream task (e.g., results of relevant program analyses). In this work, we study the problem of learning to derive abstract relations from the intrinsic graph structure. Motivated by their power in program analyses, we consider relations defined by paths on the base graph accepted by a finite-state automaton. We show how to learn these relations end-to-end by relaxing the problem into learning finite-state automata policies on a graph-based POMDP and then training these policies using implicit differentiation. The result is a differentiable Graph Finite-State Automaton (GFSA) layer that adds a new edge type (expressed as a weighted adjacency matrix) to a base graph. We demonstrate that this layer can find shortcuts in grid-world graphs and reproduce simple static analyses on Python programs. Additionally, we combine the GFSA layer with a larger graph-based model trained end-to-end on the variable misuse program understanding task, and find that using the GFSA layer leads to better performance than using hand-engineered semantic edges or other baseline methods for adding learned edge types.

paragraphs: Graph models can encode both an object’s intrinsic structure and additional relationships useful for reasoning. For a program, these might be its syntax structure and relations obtained through program analysis. This paper asks how a neural model can learn those more abstract relationships from the original graph rather than relying on manually supplied edges.

The authors consider relationships defined by graph paths accepted by a finite-state automaton. They make these relationships learnable by relaxing the problem into automaton policies in a graph-based partially observable decision process, trained through implicit differentiation. The resulting Graph Finite-State Automaton layer produces a weighted adjacency matrix that adds a learned edge type to the base graph.

These results connect structured path-following behavior with useful learned relations, showing how a differentiable layer can derive task-relevant graph structure during end-to-end training.
summary.tldr: A differentiable finite-state automaton layer learns useful graph edges from paths, improving variable-misuse detection in the reported experiments.

title: Learning Graph Structure With A Finite-State Automaton Layer

abstract: The state-of-the art machine learning approach to training deep neural networks, backpropagation, is implausible for real neural networks: neurons need to know their outgoing weights; training alternates between a bottom-up forward pass (computation) and a top-down backward pass (learning); and the algorithm often needs precise labels of many data points. Biologically plausible approximations to backpropagation, such as feedback alignment, solve the weight transport problem, but not the other two. Thus, fully biologically plausible learning rules have so far remained elusive. Here we present a family of learning rules that does not suffer from any of these problems. It is motivated by the information bottleneck principle (extended with kernel methods), in which networks learn to compress the input as much as possible without sacrificing prediction of the output. The resulting rules have a 3-factor Hebbian structure: they require pre- and post-synaptic firing rates and an error signal - the third factor - consisting of a global teaching signal and a layer-specific term, both available without a top-down pass. They do not require precise labels; instead, they rely on the similarity between pairs of desired outputs. Moreover, to obtain good performance on hard problems and retain biological plausibility, our rules need divisive normalization - a known feature of biological networks. Finally, simulations show that our rules perform nearly as well as backpropagation on image classification tasks.

paragraphs: Backpropagation poses several difficulties as a model of biological learning: neurons would need information about outgoing weights, learning requires a separate backward pass, and training often depends on precise labels. This paper proposes a family of learning rules designed to avoid these requirements, motivated by a kernel-based extension of the information bottleneck principle.

The objective is to compress input information while preserving what is useful for predicting outputs. The derived updates have three factors: activity before a synapse, activity after it, and an error signal. That error signal combines global teaching information with a layer-specific term, both available without a top-down pass. Supervision comes from similarities between pairs of desired outputs rather than precise labels.

In image-classification simulations, the rules perform nearly as well as backpropagation. These findings show how an information-based objective can yield biologically motivated learning updates with competitive performance in the studied tasks.
summary.tldr: A kernelized information bottleneck yields three-factor Hebbian rules that avoid backward passes and precise labels while approaching backpropagation performance in simulations.

title: Kernelized information bottleneck leads to biologically plausible 3-factor Hebbian learning in deep networks

abstract: To handle vast amounts of data, it is natural and popular to compress vectors and matrices. When we compress a vector from size N down to size n << N, it certainly makes it easier to store and transmit efficiently, but does it also make it easier to process? In this paper we consider lossless compression schemes, and ask if we can run our computations on the compressed data as efficiently as if the original data was that small. That is, if an operation has time complexity T(input-size), can we perform it on the compressed representation in time T(n) rather than T(N)? We consider the most basic linear algebra operations: inner product, matrix-vector multiplication, and matrix multiplication. In particular, given two compressed vectors, can we compute their inner product in time O(n)? Or perhaps we must decompress first and then multiply, spending Omega(N) time? The answer depends on the compression scheme. While for simple ones such as Run-Length-Encoding (RLE) the inner product can be done in O(n) time, we prove that this is impossible for compressions from a richer class: essentially n^2 or even larger runtimes are needed in the worst case (under complexity assumptions). This is the class of \emph{grammar-compressions} containing most popular methods such as the Lempel-Ziv family. These schemes are more compressing than the simple RLE, but alas, we prove that performing computations on them is much harder.

paragraphs: Compressing a large vector or matrix clearly reduces storage, but it does not automatically make computations equally cheap. This paper asks whether basic linear algebra can operate at a cost determined by the compressed size. It studies lossless representations and operations including inner products, matrix-vector products, and matrix multiplication.

The answer depends on the compression scheme. For run-length encoding, an inner product can be computed in time linear in the compressed representation's size. The authors show that richer grammar-based compression behaves differently. Under complexity assumptions, worst-case computations can require essentially quadratic or even larger runtimes in the compressed size, ruling out the hoped-for linear-time behavior.

The grammar-compression class includes popular methods such as the Lempel-Ziv family, which can compress more effectively than run-length encoding. The results therefore identify a tradeoff between obtaining a compact representation and making that representation convenient for computation. They do not say that every compressed input is hard; the lower bounds concern worst-case instances under stated complexity assumptions. Stronger compression alone cannot guarantee proportionally faster linear algebra.
summary.tldr: Under complexity assumptions, grammar-based compression cannot generally make basic linear algebra run as cheaply as its compressed size might suggest.

title: Impossibility Results for Grammar-Compressed Linear Algebra

abstract: Recent breakthroughs in deep neural networks (DNNs) have fueled a tremendous demand for intelligent edge devices featuring on-site learning, while the practical realization of such systems remains a challenge due to the limited resources available at the edge and the required massive training costs for state-of-the-art (SOTA) DNNs. As reducing precision is one of the most effective knobs for boosting training time/energy efficiency, there has been a growing interest in low-precision DNN training. In this paper, we explore from an orthogonal direction: how to fractionally squeeze out more training cost savings from the most redundant bit level, progressively along the training trajectory and dynamically per input. Specifically, we propose FracTrain that integrates (i) progressive fractional quantization which gradually increases the precision of activations, weights, and gradients that will not reach the precision of SOTA static quantized DNN training until the final training stage, and (ii) dynamic fractional quantization which assigns precisions to both the activations and gradients of each layer in an input-adaptive manner, for only "fractionally" updating layer parameters. Extensive simulations and ablation studies (six models, four datasets, and three training settings including standard, adaptation, and fine-tuning) validate the effectiveness of FracTrain in reducing computational cost and hardware-quantified energy/latency of DNN training while achieving a comparable or better (-0.12%~+1.87%) accuracy. For example, when training ResNet-74 on CIFAR-10, FracTrain achieves 77.6% and 53.5% computational cost and training latency savings, respectively, compared with the best SOTA baseline, while achieving a comparable (-0.07%) accuracy. Our codes are available at: https://github.com/RICE-EIC/FracTrain.

paragraphs: Training deep networks on resource-limited edge devices is expensive in computation, energy, and time. Lower numerical precision can reduce those costs. FracTrain explores how to save more by changing precision throughout training and across individual inputs, instead of assigning a fixed precision for the entire process.

Its progressive component gradually increases the precision of weights, activations, and gradients. It reaches the precision used by leading static quantized training methods only at the final training stage. Its dynamic component assigns activation and gradient precision separately for each layer according to the input. Together, these mechanisms adjust how much numerical precision is used to update parameters.

Simulations and ablations across six models, four datasets, and three training settings report lower computational cost and hardware-quantified energy and latency, with comparable or better accuracy. For ResNet-74 on CIFAR-10, the reported computational and training-latency savings are 77.6% and 53.5% against the best stated baseline, with a 0.07% accuracy decrease. The findings support adapting precision as a practical training-efficiency mechanism.
summary.tldr: FracTrain varies numerical precision over training and across inputs to reduce training costs while maintaining comparable accuracy.

title: FracTrain: Fractionally Squeezing Bit Savings Both Temporally and Spatially for Efficient DNN Training

abstract: Conditional estimation given specific covariate values (i.e., local conditional estimation or functional estimation) is ubiquitously useful with applications in engineering, social and natural sciences. Existing data-driven non-parametric estimators mostly focus on structured homogeneous data (e.g., weakly independently and stationary data), thus they are sensitive to adversarial noise and may perform poorly under a low sample size. To alleviate these issues, we propose a new distributionally robust estimator that generates non-parametric local estimates by minimizing the worst-case conditional expected loss over all adversarial distributions in a Wasserstein ambiguity set. We show that despite being generally intractable, the local estimator can be efficiently found via convex optimization under broadly applicable settings, and it is robust to the corruption and heterogeneity of the data. Various experiments show the competitive performance of this new class of estimator.

Existing data-driven non-parametric estimators mostly focus on structured homogeneous data (e.g., weakly independently and stationary data), thus they are sensitive to adversarial noise and may perform poorly under a low sample size. To alleviate these issues, we propose a new distributionally robust estimator that generates non-parametric local estimates by minimizing the worst-case conditional expected loss over all adversarial distributions in a Wasserstein ambiguity set. We show that despite being generally intractable, the local estimator can be efficiently found via convex optimization under broadly applicable settings, and it is robust to the corruption and heterogeneity of the data. Various experiments show the competitive performance of this new class of estimator.

paragraphs: Local conditional estimation asks what to predict when particular input variables take specified values. The paper targets nonparametric estimators, which avoid committing to a fixed parametric form. Many existing methods emphasize relatively homogeneous data, leaving them sensitive to adversarial corruption and potentially unreliable when only a small number of observations is available.

The proposed estimator chooses a local estimate by minimizing the worst conditional expected loss across a collection of possible data distributions. This collection is a Wasserstein ambiguity set. Considering the worst case within that set makes uncertainty about the distribution part of the estimation problem itself, rather than relying entirely on the observed distribution.

Although this optimization is generally intractable, the authors identify broadly applicable settings where convex optimization can solve it efficiently. They establish robustness to corrupted and heterogeneous data and report competitive experimental performance. The practical significance is the combination of a protective estimation objective with tractable computation under the stated settings; the abstract does not claim that every version of the general problem becomes easy.
summary.tldr: A worst-case distributional objective produces robust local estimates and admits efficient convex solutions in broadly applicable settings.

title: Distributionally Robust Local Non-parametric Conditional Estimation

abstract: Federated learning usually employs a client-server architecture where an orchestrator iteratively aggregates model updates from remote clients and pushes them back a refined model. This approach may be inefficient in cross-silo settings, as close-by data silos with high-speed access links may exchange information faster than with the orchestrator, and the orchestrator may become a communication bottleneck. In this paper we define the problem of topology design for cross-silo federated learning using the theory of max-plus linear systems to compute the system throughput---number of communication rounds per time unit. We also propose practical algorithms that, under the knowledge of measurable network characteristics, find a topology with the largest throughput or with provable throughput guarantees. In realistic Internet networks with 10~Gbps access links for silos, our algorithms speed up training by a factor 9 and 1.5 in comparison to the master-slave architecture and to state-of-the-art MATCHA, respectively. Speedups are even larger with slower access links.

title: Throughput-Optimal Topology Design for Cross-Silo Federated Learning

abstract: We study the problem of online learning with primary and secondary losses. For example, a recruiter making decisions of which job applicants to hire might weigh false positives and false negatives equally (the primary loss) but the applicants might weigh false negatives much higher (the secondary loss). We consider the following question: Can we combine ``expert advice'' to achieve low regret with respect to the primary loss, while at the same time performing {\em not much worse than the worst expert} with respect to the secondary loss? Unfortunately, we show that this goal is unachievable without any bounded variance assumption on the secondary loss. More generally, we consider the goal of minimizing the regret with respect to the primary loss and bounding the secondary loss by a linear threshold. On the positive side, we show that running any switching-limited algorithm can achieve this goal if all experts satisfy the assumption that the secondary loss does not exceed the linear threshold by $o(T)$ for any time interval. If not all experts satisfy this assumption, our algorithms can achieve this goal given access to some external oracles which determine when to deactivate and reactivate experts.

paragraphs: An online learner may face two ways of judging the same decisions. The paper's hiring example distinguishes a recruiter's treatment of errors from applicants' greater concern about false negatives. It asks whether combining expert advice can achieve low regret on a primary loss while performing little worse than even the worst expert on a secondary loss.

The authors show that this goal is impossible without a bounded-variance assumption on the secondary loss. They then study the more general goal of controlling primary regret while keeping secondary loss within a linear threshold. This separates the desired performance on the main objective from a bound on the additional cost.

The findings identify conditions and additional information that make simultaneous loss control possible.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes when online learners can control a secondary loss while maintaining low primary regret, and when that goal is impossible.

title: Online Learning with Primary and Secondary Losses

abstract: Lifelong learning and adaptability are two defining aspects of biological agents. Modern reinforcement learning (RL) approaches have shown significant progress in solving complex tasks, however once training is concluded, the found solutions are typically static and incapable of adapting to new information or perturbations. While it is still not completely understood how biological brains learn and adapt so efficiently from experience, it is believed that synaptic plasticity plays a prominent role in this process. Inspired by this biological mechanism, we propose a search method that, instead of optimizing the weight parameters of neural networks directly, only searches for synapse-specific Hebbian learning rules that allow the network to continuously self-organize its weights during the lifetime of the agent. We demonstrate our approach on several reinforcement learning tasks with different sensory modalities and more than 450K trainable plasticity parameters. We find that starting from completely random weights, the discovered Hebbian rules enable an agent to navigate a dynamical 2D-pixel environment; likewise they allow a simulated 3D quadrupedal robot to learn how to walk while adapting to morphological damage not seen during training and in the absence of any explicit reward or error signal in less than 100 timesteps.

This paper draws inspiration from synaptic plasticity, the biological capacity for connections to change with experience. It investigates whether learning rules can equip a network to keep organizing its own weights during an agent's lifetime.

The search optimizes synapse-specific Hebbian rules rather than directly optimizing network weights. Networks then begin with random weights and use the discovered rules to modify their connections through experience. The authors demonstrate this approach across reinforcement-learning tasks with different sensory modalities and more than 450,000 trainable plasticity parameters.

title: Meta-Learning through Hebbian Plasticity in Random Networks

abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) aims to build autonomous visual agents that follow instructions and navigate in real scenes. To remember previously visited locations and actions taken, most approaches to VLN implement memory using recurrent states. Instead, we introduce a History Aware Multimodal Transformer (HAMT) to incorporate a long-horizon history into multimodal decision making. HAMT efficiently encodes all the past panoramic observations via a hierarchical vision transformer (ViT), which first encodes individual images with ViT, then models spatial relation between images in a panoramic observation and finally takes into account temporal relation between panoramas in the history. It, then, jointly combines text, history and current observation to predict the next action. We first train HAMT end-to-end using several proxy tasks including single step action prediction and spatial relation prediction, and then use reinforcement learning to further improve the navigation policy. HAMT achieves new state of the art on a broad range of VLN tasks, including VLN with fine-grained instructions (R2R, RxR), high-level instructions (R2R-Last, REVERIE), dialogs (CVDN) as well as long-horizon VLN (R4R, R2R-Back). We demonstrate HAMT to be particularly effective for navigation tasks with longer trajectories.

paragraphs: Vision-and-language navigation requires an agent to follow instructions while moving through a visual environment. Choosing the next action can depend on locations and actions far back in its history. HAMT addresses this memory requirement by incorporating a long history of panoramic observations into a transformer-based decision process.

The history encoder operates hierarchically. It first encodes individual images, then models spatial relationships among images within each panorama, and finally models temporal relationships across past panoramas. The action predictor combines this history with the instruction text and current observation. Training starts with end-to-end proxy tasks, including action and spatial-relation prediction, followed by reinforcement learning to improve the navigation policy.

The authors report state-of-the-art results across tasks involving detailed instructions, high-level instructions, dialogue, and long routes. They find the method particularly effective when trajectories are longer. These results support the usefulness of explicitly organizing visual memory at several scales, so that information from earlier observations can participate in the current navigation decision.
summary.tldr: HAMT combines hierarchically encoded visual history with instructions and current observations to improve navigation, especially on longer routes.

title: History Aware Multimodal Transformer for Vision-and-Language Navigation

abstract: Missing data are prevalent and present daunting challenges in real data analysis. While there is a growing body of literature on fairness in analysis of fully observed data, there has been little theoretical work on investigating fairness in analysis of incomplete data. In practice, a popular analytical approach for dealing with missing data is to use only the set of complete cases, i.e., observations with all features fully observed to train a prediction algorithm. However, depending on the missing data mechanism, the distribution of complete cases and the distribution of the complete data may be substantially different. When the goal is to develop a fair algorithm in the complete data domain where there are no missing values, an algorithm that is fair in the complete case domain may show disproportionate bias towards some marginalized groups in the complete data domain. To fill this significant gap, we study the problem of estimating fairness in the complete data domain for an arbitrary model evaluated merely using complete cases. We provide upper and lower bounds on the fairness estimation error and conduct numerical experiments to assess our theoretical results. Our work provides the first known theoretical results on fairness guarantee in analysis of incomplete data.

paragraphs: A common response to missing data is to keep only observations with every feature recorded. This paper examines what that choice means for assessing fairness. Depending on how values become missing, the retained observations can have a substantially different distribution from the full population that would be available if all values were observed.

That difference matters because a model can appear fair among complete cases while showing disproportionate bias toward marginalized groups in the full-data setting. The authors study how to estimate fairness in that target setting when an arbitrary model can be evaluated only on complete cases. The central issue is whether fairness measured on the available subset accurately describes fairness in the population of interest.

The paper derives upper and lower bounds on fairness estimation error and uses numerical experiments to assess the theoretical findings. These bounds characterize the uncertainty created by evaluating on a potentially unrepresentative subset. The contribution is a theoretical treatment of fairness assessment with incomplete data, clarifying why apparent fairness among retained observations may not transfer to the intended population.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds how much fairness estimates based only on complete records can differ from fairness in the full-data population.

title: Assessing Fairness in the Presence of Missing Data

abstract: Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) is a recently proposed framework for out-of-distribution (o.o.d) generalization. Most of the studies on IRM so far have focused on theoretical results, toy problems, and simple models. In this work, we investigate the applicability of IRM to bias mitigation-a special case of o.o.d generalization-in increasingly naturalistic settings and deep models. Using natural language inference (NLI) as a test case, we start with a setting where both the dataset and the bias are synthetic, continue with a natural dataset and synthetic bias, and end with a fully realistic setting with natural datasets and bias. Our results show that in naturalistic settings, learning complex features in place of the bias proves to be difficult, leading to a rather small improvement over empirical risk minimization. Moreover, we find that in addition to being sensitive to random seeds, the performance of IRM also depends on several critical factors, notably dataset size, bias prevalence, and bias strength, thus limiting IRM's advantage in practical scenarios. Our results highlight key challenges in applying IRM to real-world scenarios, calling for a more naturalistic characterization of the problem setup for o.o.d generalization.

paragraphs: Invariant Risk Minimization, or IRM, aims to help models generalize beyond their training distribution. This paper examines whether that promise carries over to mitigating dataset biases in deep natural language inference models. Its focus is the move from simplified demonstrations toward settings that more closely resemble practical language learning.

The investigation proceeds through three levels of realism: synthetic data with synthetic bias, natural data with synthetic bias, and natural data with naturally occurring bias. This progression lets the authors examine how IRM behaves as both the learning problem and the bias become less artificial. The central challenge is learning complex useful features in place of an available biased shortcut.

In the more naturalistic settings, IRM produces only a small improvement over empirical risk minimization. Its performance also varies with random seeds, dataset size, bias prevalence, and bias strength. These findings identify concrete factors that constrain its practical advantage in the studied setting. The paper argues that understanding out-of-distribution generalization requires problem setups that capture these naturalistic difficulties, alongside theoretical analyses and simplified examples.
summary.tldr: Tests on increasingly realistic natural language inference show that IRM’s bias-mitigation gains can be small and sensitive to data and training conditions.

title: IRM—when it works and when it doesn't: A test case of natural language inference

abstract: Finding a good way to model probability densities is key to probabilistic inference. An ideal model should be able to concisely approximate any probability while being also compatible with two main operations: multiplications of two models (product rule) and marginalization with respect to a subset of the random variables (sum rule). In this work, we show that a recently proposed class of positive semi-definite (PSD) models for non-negative functions is particularly suited to this end. In particular, we characterize both approximation and generalization capabilities of PSD models, showing that they enjoy strong theoretical guarantees. Moreover, we show that we can perform efficiently both sum and product rule in closed form via matrix operations, enjoying the same versatility of mixture models. Our results open the way to applications of PSD models to density estimation, decision theory, and inference.

paragraphs: A useful probability-density model needs more than the ability to fit data. Probabilistic inference also requires combining models through multiplication and removing variables through marginalization. This paper studies positive semi-definite, or PSD, models for non-negative functions as a representation that can support these operations while also providing strong approximation and learning properties.

The authors characterize both approximation capability and generalization capability. These address related but distinct questions: how well the model class can represent a target density, and how well learned models can extend beyond their training data. The paper establishes theoretical guarantees for these properties, supporting PSD models as a principled representation for probability modeling.

The same representation permits products and marginalization to be computed efficiently in closed form using matrix operations. This gives PSD models the operational versatility associated with mixture models. The contribution brings representational guarantees and tractable probability operations into one framework, opening possible applications in density estimation, decision theory, and inference rather than presenting those applications as already demonstrated outcomes.
summary.tldr: PSD probability models combine theoretical approximation and generalization guarantees with efficient closed-form multiplication and marginalization.

title: PSD Representations for Effective Probability Models

abstract: Training-time safety violations have been a major concern when we deploy reinforcement learning algorithms in the real world.This paper explores the possibility of safe RL algorithms with zero training-time safety violations in the challenging setting where we are only given a safe but trivial-reward initial policy without any prior knowledge of the dynamics and additional offline data.We propose an algorithm, Co-trained Barrier Certificate for Safe RL (CRABS), which iteratively learns barrier certificates, dynamics models, and policies. The barrier certificates are learned via adversarial training and ensure the policy's safety assuming calibrated learned dynamics. We also add a regularization term to encourage larger certified regions to enable better exploration. Empirical simulations show that zero safety violations are already challenging for a suite of simple environments with only 2-4 dimensional state space, especially if high-reward policies have to visit regions near the safety boundary. Prior methods require hundreds of violations to achieve decent rewards on these tasks, whereas our proposed algorithms incur zero violations.

paragraphs: Safe reinforcement learning must consider the actions taken during learning, as well as the final policy. This paper explores avoiding every training-time safety violation when starting with only a safe policy that earns trivial reward. The setting provides neither prior knowledge of the system dynamics nor additional offline data, making safe improvement particularly challenging.

The proposed CRABS algorithm repeatedly learns three connected components: a dynamics model, a policy, and barrier certificates that certify safety. It learns the certificates through adversarial training and adds regularization that encourages larger certified regions, creating room for exploration. The certificates ensure policy safety under the explicit assumption that the learned dynamics are calibrated.

Simulations show that avoiding violations is challenging even in environments with only two to four state dimensions, especially when rewarding behavior approaches the safety boundary. Prior methods require hundreds of violations to obtain decent rewards on these tasks, whereas the proposed algorithms incur none. These results support the feasibility of the approach in the tested settings, with the stated safety guarantee depending on dynamics calibration.
summary.tldr: CRABS jointly learns safety certificates, dynamics, and policies, achieving zero violations in reported simulations with safety guarantees conditional on calibrated dynamics.

title: Learning Barrier Certificates: Towards Safe Reinforcement Learning with Zero Training-time Violations

abstract: Large scale distributed optimization has become the default tool for the training of supervised machine learning models with a large number of parameters and training data. Recent advancements in the field provide several mechanisms for speeding up the training, including {\em compressed communication}, {\em variance reduction} and {\em acceleration}. However, none of these methods is capable of exploiting the inherently rich data-dependent smoothness structure of the local losses beyond standard smoothness constants. In this paper, we argue that when training supervised models, {\em smoothness matrices}---information-rich generalizations of the ubiquitous smoothness constants---can and should be exploited for further dramatic gains, both in theory and practice. In order to further alleviate the communication burden inherent in distributed optimization, we propose a novel communication sparsification strategy that can take full advantage of the smoothness matrices associated with local losses. To showcase the power of this tool, we describe how our sparsification technique can be adapted to three distributed optimization algorithms---DCGD, DIANA and ADIANA---yielding significant savings in terms of communication complexity. The new methods always outperform the baselines, often dramatically so.

paragraphs: Distributed training must exchange information between machines, making communication a major part of optimization cost. Existing techniques include compression, variance reduction, and acceleration. This paper argues that further improvements are possible by exploiting the detailed smoothness structure of each local loss, rather than summarizing that structure with a single smoothness constant.

The authors use smoothness matrices, which retain richer information about how local losses vary. They propose a communication sparsification strategy designed to take advantage of these matrices. The approach connects the information sent during distributed optimization to the structure of the losses being optimized, providing a more informative basis for compression.

To demonstrate the method, the paper adapts it to DCGD, DIANA, and ADIANA. The resulting algorithms achieve significant communication-complexity savings, and the authors report that the new methods consistently outperform their baselines, often by large margins. The stated contribution spans theory and practice: richer descriptions of local smoothness support better communication strategies across three distributed optimization algorithms, rather than only a single specialized procedure.
summary.tldr: Matrix-valued smoothness information guides communication sparsification that reduces communication complexity for three distributed optimization algorithms.

title: Smoothness Matrices Beat Smoothness Constants: Better Communication Compression Techniques for Distributed Optimization

abstract: Latent dynamics models have emerged as powerful tools for modeling and interpreting neural population activity. Recently, there has been a focus on incorporating simultaneously measured behaviour into these models to further disentangle sources of neural variability in their latent space. These approaches, however, are limited in their ability to capture the underlying neural dynamics (e.g. linear) and in their ability to relate the learned dynamics back to the observed behaviour (e.g. no time lag). To this end, we introduce Targeted Neural Dynamical Modeling (TNDM), a nonlinear state-space model that jointly models the neural activity and external behavioural variables. TNDM decomposes neural dynamics into behaviourally relevant and behaviourally irrelevant dynamics; the relevant dynamics are used to reconstruct the behaviour through a flexible linear decoder and both sets of dynamics are used to reconstruct the neural activity through a linear decoder with no time lag. We implement TNDM as a sequential variational autoencoder and validate it on simulated recordings and recordings taken from the premotor and motor cortex of a monkey performing a center-out reaching task. We show that TNDM is able to learn low-dimensional latent dynamics that are highly predictive of behaviour without sacrificing its fit to the neural data.

paragraphs: Neural population recordings contain changing activity associated with behavior as well as other sources of variation. Latent dynamics models try to explain those recordings through a smaller set of hidden processes. This paper develops Targeted Neural Dynamical Modeling to jointly describe neural activity and simultaneously measured behavior while allowing nonlinear dynamics.

TNDM separates its latent dynamics into behaviorally relevant and behaviorally irrelevant components. A flexible linear decoder uses the relevant components to reconstruct behavior. A separate linear decoder uses both components to reconstruct neural activity without a time lag. This structure gives the model a way to preserve variation needed to explain neural recordings while distinguishing the part useful for explaining behavior.

The authors implement the model as a sequential variational autoencoder. They validate it on simulated recordings and premotor and motor cortex recordings from a monkey performing a center-out reaching task. TNDM learns low-dimensional dynamics that strongly predict behavior without sacrificing its fit to neural data. The result supports joint modeling as a way to make neural representations behaviorally informative while retaining explanatory coverage of the recordings.
summary.tldr: TNDM separates behaviorally relevant and irrelevant nonlinear neural dynamics, predicting behavior while preserving fit to neural recordings.

title: Targeted Neural Dynamical Modeling

abstract: Gradient compression is a recent and increasingly popular technique for reducing the communication cost in distributed training of large-scale machine learning models. In this work we focus on developing efficient distributed methods that can work for any compressor satisfying a certain contraction property, which includes both unbiased (after appropriate scaling) and biased compressors such as RandK and TopK. Applied naively, gradient compression introduces errors that either slow down convergence or lead to divergence. A popular technique designed to tackle this issue is error compensation/error feedback. Due to the difficulties associated with analyzing biased compressors, it is not known whether gradient compression with error compensation can be combined with acceleration. In this work, we show for the first time that error compensated gradient compression methods can be accelerated. In particular, we propose and study the error compensated loopless Katyusha method, and establish an accelerated linear convergence rate under standard assumptions. We show through numerical experiments that the proposed method converges with substantially fewer communication rounds than previous error compensated algorithms.

paragraphs: Distributed training requires machines to exchange gradient information, and compressing those messages can reduce communication costs. Compression also introduces errors that can slow convergence or cause divergence. Error compensation, also called error feedback, is a technique for addressing those errors, but its compatibility with acceleration had remained unresolved.

This paper develops an accelerated method for compressors satisfying a specified contraction property. That class includes biased compressors such as TopK and RandK, as well as appropriately scaled unbiased compressors. The distinction matters because biased compression creates particular difficulties for theoretical analysis of error-compensated optimization.

The authors propose an error-compensated version of loopless Katyusha and prove an accelerated linear convergence rate under standard assumptions. Numerical experiments show that it converges in substantially fewer communication rounds than earlier error-compensated algorithms. The result establishes that acceleration and error-compensated compression can coexist within the studied conditions, connecting reduced message sizes with fewer rounds of distributed communication.
summary.tldr: An error-compensated loopless Katyusha method achieves accelerated convergence under stated assumptions and reduces communication rounds in numerical experiments.

title: Error Compensated Distributed SGD Can Be Accelerated

abstract: Learning multimodal representations involves integrating information from multiple heterogeneous sources of data. It is a challenging yet crucial area with numerous real-world applications in multimedia, affective computing, robotics, finance, human-computer interaction, and healthcare. Unfortunately, multimodal research has seen limited resources to study (1) generalization across domains and modalities, (2) complexity during training and inference, and (3) robustness to noisy and missing modalities. In order to accelerate progress towards understudied modalities and tasks while ensuring real-world robustness, we release MultiBench, a systematic and unified large-scale benchmark for multimodal learning spanning 15 datasets, 10 modalities, 20 prediction tasks, and 6 research areas. MultiBench provides an automated end-to-end machine learning pipeline that simplifies and standardizes data loading, experimental setup, and model evaluation. To enable holistic evaluation, MultiBench offers a comprehensive methodology to assess (1) generalization, (2) time and space complexity, and (3) modality robustness. MultiBench introduces impactful challenges for future research, including scalability to large-scale multimodal datasets and robustness to realistic imperfections. To accompany this benchmark, we also provide a standardized implementation of 20 core approaches in multimodal learning spanning innovations in fusion paradigms, optimization objectives, and training approaches. Simply applying methods proposed in different research areas can improve the state-of-the-art performance on 9/15 datasets. Therefore, MultiBench presents a milestone in unifying disjoint efforts in multimodal machine learning research and paves the way towards a better understanding of the capabilities and limitations of multimodal models, all the while ensuring ease of use, accessibility, and reproducibility. MultiBench, our standardized implementations, and leaderboards are publicly available, will be regularly updated, and welcomes inputs from the community.

MultiBench brings 15 datasets, 10 modalities, 20 prediction tasks, and six research areas into a unified benchmark. Its automated pipeline standardizes data loading, experiment setup, and evaluation, reducing differences in how methods are tested.

The benchmark evaluates generalization, training and inference costs, and robustness when modalities are noisy or missing. It also provides standardized implementations of 20 approaches covering different ways to combine information, define learning objectives, and train models. This makes predictive performance one part of a broader assessment that includes resource demands and imperfect inputs.

The authors report that applying approaches from other research areas improves state-of-the-art performance on nine of the fifteen datasets. title: MultiBench: Multiscale Benchmarks for Multimodal Representation Learning

abstract: We introduce Korean Language Understanding Evaluation (KLUE) benchmark. KLUE is a collection of eight Korean natural language understanding (NLU) tasks, including Topic Classification, Semantic Textual Similarity, Natural LanguageInference, Named Entity Recognition, Relation Extraction, Dependency Parsing, Machine Reading Comprehension, and Dialogue State Tracking. We create all of the datasets from scratch in a principled way. We design the tasks to have diverse formats and each task to be built upon various source corpora that respect copyrights. Also, we propose suitable evaluation metrics and organize annotation protocols in a way to ensure quality. To prevent ethical risks in KLUE, we proactively remove examples reflecting social biases, containing toxic content or personally identifiable information (PII). Along with the benchmark datasets, we release pre-trained language models (PLM) for Korean, KLUE-BERT and KLUE-RoBERTa, and find KLUE-Roberta-large outperforms other baselines including multilingual PLMs and existing open-source Korean PLMs. The fine-tuning recipes are publicly open for anyone to reproduce our baseline result. We believe our work will facilitate future research on cross-lingual as well as Korean language models and the creation of similar resources for other languages. KLUE is available at https://klue-benchmark.com.

paragraphs: KLUE creates a shared benchmark for Korean language understanding across eight tasks. These cover topic classification, sentence similarity, inference, named entities, relations, dependency parsing, reading comprehension, and dialogue state tracking. The range of tasks supports evaluation of several aspects of language understanding, with different input and output formats.

The authors build all datasets from scratch using varied source corpora that respect copyright. They establish annotation procedures and suitable evaluation metrics, while proactively removing examples containing social biases, toxic material, or personally identifiable information. These choices make dataset construction and assessment procedures central parts of the benchmark’s design.

The release also includes Korean pretrained models, KLUE-BERT and KLUE-RoBERTa, along with reproducible fine-tuning recipes. In the reported comparisons, KLUE-RoBERTa-large outperforms the evaluated multilingual and existing open-source Korean baselines. Together, the datasets, models, and training instructions provide a common foundation for Korean language research, while the authors also hope to support cross-lingual work and similar resources for other languages.
summary.tldr: KLUE supplies eight Korean language understanding tasks, curated datasets, and pretrained models, with KLUE-RoBERTa-large leading the reported baseline comparisons.

title: KLUE: Korean Language Understanding Evaluation

abstract: Images of a real scene taken with a camera commonly differ from synthetic images of a virtual replica of the same scene, despite advances in light transport simulation and calibration. By explicitly co-developing the Structured-Light Scanning (SLS) hardware and rendering pipeline we are able to achieve negligible per-pixel difference between the real image and the synthesized image on geometrically complex calibration objects with known material properties. This approach provides an ideal test-bed for developing and evaluating data-driven algorithms in the area of 3D reconstruction, as the synthetic data is indistinguishable from real data and can be generated at large scale by simulation. We propose three benchmark challenges using a combination of acquired and synthetic data generated with our system: (1) a denoising benchmark tailored to structured-light scanning, (2) a shape completion benchmark to fill in missing data, and (3) a benchmark for surface reconstruction from dense point clouds. Besides, we provide a large collection of high-resolution scans that allow to use our system and benchmarks without reproduction of the hardware setup on our website: https://geometryprocessing.github.io/scanner-sim

paragraphs: Synthetic images can differ from camera images even when they depict a virtual replica of the same scene. That mismatch complicates using simulation to develop 3D reconstruction algorithms. This paper addresses the issue by designing structured-light scanning hardware and its rendering pipeline together, explicitly connecting the physical acquisition system with the simulation.

On geometrically complex calibration objects with known material properties, the authors achieve negligible differences between real and synthesized images at the pixel level. This stated setting matters: the close agreement is demonstrated on those calibration objects. The approach supports generating large amounts of synthetic data using a system whose real and simulated outputs closely match under the described conditions.

The authors propose three benchmarks combining acquired and synthetic data: removing scanning noise, completing missing shape data, and reconstructing surfaces from dense point clouds. They also release high-resolution scans so researchers can use the system and benchmarks without rebuilding the hardware. The contribution joins acquisition design, simulation fidelity, and evaluation resources around several distinct stages of 3D reconstruction.
summary.tldr: Jointly designed scanning hardware and simulation closely match calibration images and support three 3D reconstruction benchmarks.

title: Hardware Design and Accurate Simulation of Structured-Light Scanning for Benchmarking of 3D Reconstruction Algorithms

abstract: Enabling effective and efficient machine learning (ML) over large-scale graph data (e.g., graphs with billions of edges) can have a great impact on both industrial and scientific applications. However, existing efforts to advance large-scale graph ML have been largely limited by the lack of a suitable public benchmark. Here we present OGB Large-Scale Challenge (OGB-LSC), a collection of three real-world datasets for facilitating the advancements in large-scale graph ML. The OGB-LSC datasets are orders of magnitude larger than existing ones, covering three core graph learning tasks---link prediction, graph regression, and node classification. Furthermore, we provide dedicated baseline experiments, scaling up expressive graph ML models to the massive datasets. We show that expressive models significantly outperform simple scalable baselines, indicating an opportunity for dedicated efforts to further improve graph ML at scale. Moreover, OGB-LSC datasets were deployed at ACM KDD Cup 2021 and attracted more than 500 team registrations globally, during which significant performance improvements were made by a variety of innovative techniques. We summarize the common techniques used by the winning solutions and highlight the current best practices in large-scale graph ML. Finally, we describe how we have updated the datasets after the KDD Cup to further facilitate research advances. The OGB-LSC datasets, baseline code, and all the information about the KDD Cup are available at https://ogb.stanford.edu/docs/lsc/.

This finding shows that the benchmark's size does not eliminate the value of richer modeling and points to opportunities for improving the combination of predictive capability and large-scale execution.

The datasets also supported the ACM KDD Cup 2021, which attracted more than 500 team registrations and produced significant performance improvements through varied techniques. The paper summarizes common approaches among winning solutions and describes subsequent dataset updates. Its contribution combines demanding public tasks, baseline implementations, and experience from a large competition to support continued research on graph learning at scale.
summary.tldr: OGB-LSC provides three massive graph benchmarks where expressive models outperform simple scalable baselines.

title: OGB-LSC: A Large-Scale Challenge for Machine Learning on Graphs

abstract: Over the last two decades, submodular function maximization has been the workhorse of many discrete optimization problems in machine learning applications. Traditionally, the study of submodular functions was based on binary function properties, but recent works began to consider continuous function properties such as the submodularity ratio and the curvature. The monotonicity property of set functions plays a central role in submodular maximization. Nevertheless, no continuous version of this property has been suggested to date (as far as we know), which is unfortunate since submoduar functions that are almost monotone often arise in machine learning applications. In this work we fill this gap by defining the monotonicity ratio, which is a continuous version of the monotonicity property. We then show that for many standard submodular maximization algorithms one can prove new approximation guarantees that depend on the monotonicity ratio; leading to improved approximation ratios for the common machine learning applications of movie recommendation, quadratic programming, image summarization and ride-share optimization.

paragraphs: Submodular maximization appears in many machine learning selection problems. A central property is monotonicity: whether adding items can ever reduce the objective. Traditional analyses often treat this as a yes-or-no distinction, even though applications can involve functions that are close to monotone without satisfying the property completely.

The paper introduces a monotonicity ratio to express this property continuously. This gives the analysis a way to recognize partial monotonicity instead of grouping every departure from monotonicity together. The authors then derive new approximation guarantees for many standard submodular maximization algorithms that depend on this ratio.

These guarantees improve approximation ratios in the discussed applications of movie recommendation, quadratic programming, image summarization, and ride-share optimization. Their significance is that existing algorithmic guarantees can reflect additional structure in the objective, rather than relying only on a binary classification. The contribution is therefore both a measure of partial monotonicity and an analysis showing how that measure can strengthen guarantees for familiar optimization methods.
summary.tldr: A continuous monotonicity ratio yields stronger approximation guarantees for standard submodular maximization algorithms on partially monotone objectives.

title: Using Partial Monotonicity in Submodular Maximization

abstract: Recent works show that adversarial examples exist for random neural networks [Daniely and Schacham, 2020] and that these examples can be found using a single step of gradient ascent [Bubeck et al., 2021]. In this work, we extend this line of work to ``lazy training'' of neural networks -- a dominant model in deep learning theory in which neural networks are provably efficiently learnable. We show that over-parametrized neural networks that are guaranteed to generalize well and enjoy strong computational guarantees remain vulnerable to attacks generated using a single step of gradient ascent.

In this work, we extend this line of work to ``lazy training'' of neural networks -- a dominant model in deep learning theory in which neural networks are provably efficiently learnable. paragraphs: This paper examines whether strong theoretical guarantees for learning a neural network also protect it from adversarial examples. Such examples are inputs deliberately altered to exploit a model's weaknesses. Earlier work had established vulnerability in random neural networks, including attacks constructed with a single gradient-ascent step. The authors extend that investigation to networks undergoing lazy training.

Lazy training is a prominent setting in deep learning theory because it supports proofs that neural networks can be learned efficiently. The paper studies overparameterized networks within this setting that also have guarantees of good generalization. Its result shows that these favorable properties can coexist with vulnerability to attacks produced by just one gradient-ascent step.

The finding separates three desirable properties: efficient learning, generalization, and adversarial robustness. In the analyzed setting, the first two do not establish the third. The contribution is specifically about the vulnerability that remains under lazy training; it does not claim that all neural-network training procedures necessarily have the same behavior.
summary.tldr: Overparameterized networks in the lazy-training setting can generalize well and be efficiently learnable while remaining vulnerable to one-step adversarial attacks.

title: Adversarial Robustness is at Odds with Lazy Training

abstract: Recent studies show that training deep neural networks (DNNs) with Lipschitz constraints are able to enhance adversarial robustness and other model properties such as stability. In this paper, we propose a layer-wise orthogonal training method (LOT) to effectively train 1-Lipschitz convolution layers via parametrizing an orthogonal matrix with an unconstrained matrix. We then efficiently compute the inverse square root of a convolution kernel by transforming the input domain to the Fourier frequency domain. On the other hand, as existing works show that semi-supervised training helps improve empirical robustness, we aim to bridge the gap and prove that semi-supervised learning also improves the certified robustness of Lipschitz-bounded models. We conduct comprehensive evaluations for LOT under different settings. We show that LOT significantly outperforms baselines regarding deterministic l2 certified robustness, and scales to deeper neural networks. Under the supervised scenario, we improve the state-of-the-art certified robustness for all architectures (e.g. from 59.04% to 63.50% on CIFAR-10 and from 32.57% to 34.59% on CIFAR-100 at radius $\rho=36/255$ for 40-layer networks). With semi-supervised learning over unlabelled data, we are able to improve state-of-the-art certified robustness on CIFAR-10 at $\rho=108/255$ from 36.04% to 42.39%. In addition, LOT consistently outperforms baselines on different model architectures with only 1/3 evaluation time.

Such Lipschitz bounds support certified robustness: guarantees concerning perturbations within a specified size. The proposed layer-wise orthogonal training method, LOT, targets convolutional layers with a Lipschitz bound of one, using an unconstrained matrix to parameterize an orthogonal matrix.

summary.tldr: LOT efficiently trains Lipschitz-constrained convolutional networks and improves reported certified robustness, with further gains from semi-supervised learning.

title: LOT: Layer-wise Orthogonal Training on Improving l2 Certified Robustness

abstract: Visual information arriving at the retina is transmitted to the brain by signals in the optic nerve, and the brain must rely solely on these signals to make inferences about the visual world. Previous work has probed the content of these signals by directly reconstructing images from retinal activity using linear regression or nonlinear regression with neural networks. Maximum a posteriori (MAP) reconstruction using retinal encoding models and separately-trained natural image priors offers a more general and principled approach. We develop a novel method for approximate MAP reconstruction that combines a generalized linear model for retinal responses to light, including their dependence on spike history and spikes of neighboring cells, with the image prior implicitly embedded in a deep convolutional neural network trained for image denoising. We use this method to reconstruct natural images from ex vivo simultaneously-recorded spikes of hundreds of retinal ganglion cells uniformly sampling a region of the retina. The method produces reconstructions that match or exceed the state-of-the-art in perceptual similarity and exhibit additional fine detail, while using substantially fewer model parameters than previous approaches. The use of more rudimentary encoding models (a linear-nonlinear-Poisson cascade) or image priors (a 1/f spectral model) significantly reduces reconstruction performance, indicating the essential role of both components in achieving high-quality reconstructed images from the retinal signal.

paragraphs: Reconstructing an image from retinal activity helps reveal what visual information is present in the signals sent toward the brain. This paper develops an approximate maximum a posteriori method, combining a model of how images produce retinal responses with a separate prior describing plausible natural images. Reconstruction therefore draws on both neural evidence and image structure.

The retinal encoding component is a generalized linear model that includes dependence on a cell's spike history and on neighboring cells' spikes. The natural-image prior comes implicitly from a deep convolutional network trained to remove image noise. The authors apply this combination to simultaneously recorded spikes from hundreds of retinal ganglion cells in an ex vivo preparation.

summary.tldr: Combining a retinal response model with a deep-denoiser image prior produces detailed natural-image reconstructions from recorded retinal spikes.

title: Maximum a posteriori natural scene reconstruction from retinal ganglion cells with deep denoiser priors

abstract: Meta-learning hyperparameter optimization (HPO) algorithms from prior experiments is a promising approach to improve optimization efficiency over objective functions from a similar distribution. However, existing methods are restricted to learning from experiments sharing the same set of hyperparameters. In this paper, we introduce the OptFormer, the first text-based Transformer HPO framework that provides a universal end-to-end interface for jointly learning policy and function prediction when trained on vast tuning data from the wild, such as Google’s Vizier database, one of the world’s largest HPO datasets. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that the OptFormer can simultaneously imitate at least 7 different HPO algorithms, which can be further improved via its function uncertainty estimates. Compared to a Gaussian Process, the OptFormer also learns a robust prior distribution for hyperparameter response functions, and can thereby provide more accurate and better calibrated predictions. This work paves the path to future extensions for training a Transformer-based model as a general HPO optimizer.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter optimization can benefit from previous tuning experiments, but existing learned optimizers are often restricted to experiments with the same hyperparameters. OptFormer introduces a text-based Transformer framework intended to learn across more varied tuning records. Its unified interface jointly learns how to propose configurations and how to predict their outcomes.

The framework trains on extensive real-world tuning data, such as Google's Vizier database. Experiments show that it can imitate at least seven distinct hyperparameter optimization algorithms within one model. Its estimates of uncertainty about objective values can further improve the imitated optimization behavior, connecting prediction with the choice of what to evaluate.

Compared with a Gaussian process, OptFormer learns a robust prior over hyperparameter response functions and provides more accurate, better-calibrated predictions in the reported experiments. These findings demonstrate useful shared learning across optimization behaviors and tasks. The paper frames this as progress toward a general Transformer-based optimizer, with a universal interface already provided and broader optimizer capability remaining a direction for future extensions.
summary.tldr: OptFormer learns hyperparameter proposals and outcome predictions from diverse tuning histories, imitating multiple optimizers within a text-based Transformer framework.

title: Towards Learning Universal Hyperparameter Optimizers with Transformers

abstract: Existing long-tailed recognition methods, aiming to train class-balanced models from long-tailed data, generally assume the models would be evaluated on the uniform test class distribution. However, practical test class distributions often violate this assumption (e.g., being either long-tailed or even inversely long-tailed), which may lead existing methods to fail in real applications. In this paper, we study a more practical yet challenging task, called test-agnostic long-tailed recognition, where the training class distribution is long-tailed while the test class distribution is agnostic and not necessarily uniform. In addition to the issue of class imbalance, this task poses another challenge: the class distribution shift between the training and test data is unknown. To tackle this task, we propose a novel approach, called Self-supervised Aggregation of Diverse Experts, which consists of two strategies: (i) a new skill-diverse expert learning strategy that trains multiple experts from a single and stationary long-tailed dataset to separately handle different class distributions; (ii) a novel test-time expert aggregation strategy that leverages self-supervision to aggregate the learned multiple experts for handling unknown test class distributions. We theoretically show that our self-supervised strategy has a provable ability to simulate test-agnostic class distributions. Promising empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on both vanilla and test-agnostic long-tailed recognition. The source code is available at https://github.com/Vanint/SADE-AgnosticLT.

The source code is available at https://github.com/Vanint/SADE-AgnosticLT.

paragraphs: Long-tailed recognition learns from data where some classes are much more common than others. Many methods assume evaluation will give every class equal frequency. This paper studies a broader setting in which the test distribution is unknown and may remain long-tailed or even favor classes that were rare during training.

The proposed method trains multiple experts from the same fixed training dataset. These experts develop different skills for handling different class distributions. At test time, a self-supervised aggregation strategy combines their outputs to address the unknown class frequencies, linking diverse training-time expertise to adaptation during evaluation.

The authors theoretically establish that their self-supervised strategy can simulate test-agnostic class distributions. Experiments report promising results on both conventional and test-agnostic long-tailed recognition. The contribution addresses two connected problems: unequal training data and an unknown change in class frequencies at deployment. Its significance lies in preparing and combining different experts instead of building the entire recognition strategy around a uniform test distribution.
summary.tldr: Diverse experts and self-supervised test-time aggregation help long-tailed recognition adapt to unknown test class distributions.

title: Self-Supervised Aggregation of Diverse Experts for Test-Agnostic Long-Tailed Recognition

abstract: We study Model Predictive Control (MPC) and propose a general analysis pipeline to bound its dynamic regret. The pipeline first requires deriving a perturbation bound for a finite-time optimal control problem. Then, the perturbation bound is used to bound the per-step error of MPC, which leads to a bound on the dynamic regret. Thus, our pipeline reduces the study of MPC to the well-studied problem of perturbation analysis, enabling the derivation of regret bounds of MPC under a variety of settings. To demonstrate the power of our pipeline, we use it to generalize existing regret bounds on MPC in linear time-varying (LTV) systems to incorporate prediction errors on costs, dynamics, and disturbances. Further, our pipeline leads to regret bounds on MPC in systems with nonlinear dynamics and constraints.

paragraphs: Model Predictive Control repeatedly plans over a finite time window, making its performance sensitive to the information used in each planning problem. This paper develops a general route for bounding dynamic regret, a measure of accumulated performance loss relative to an optimal control benchmark. The central contribution is an analysis pipeline that connects planning sensitivity to overall control performance.

The pipeline starts by deriving a perturbation bound for a finite-time optimal control problem. That bound describes how the solution responds to changes in the problem. The authors then use it to bound the controller's error at each step and, from those stepwise errors, obtain a dynamic-regret bound.

This connection allows established perturbation-analysis tools to support regret analysis in several settings. For linear time-varying systems, the authors extend existing bounds to include prediction errors in costs, dynamics, and disturbances. They also derive bounds for systems with nonlinear dynamics and constraints. Applying the pipeline requires an appropriate perturbation bound, making sensitivity analysis the key entry point.
summary.tldr: A perturbation-analysis pipeline bounds Model Predictive Control regret in settings involving prediction errors, nonlinear dynamics, and constraints.

title: Bounded-Regret MPC via Perturbation Analysis: Prediction Error, Constraints, and Nonlinearity

abstract: Standardized and quantified evaluation of machine behaviors is a crux of understanding LLMs. In this study, we draw inspiration from psychometric studies by leveraging human personality theory as a tool for studying machine behaviors. Originating as a philosophical quest for human behaviors, the study of personality delves into how individuals differ in thinking, feeling, and behaving. Toward building and understanding human-like social machines, we are motivated to ask: Can we assess machine behaviors by leveraging human psychometric tests in a **principled** and **quantitative** manner? If so, can we induce a specific personality in LLMs? To answer these questions, we introduce the Machine Personality Inventory (MPI) tool for studying machine behaviors; MPI follows standardizedpersonality tests, built upon the Big Five Personality Factors (Big Five) theory and personality assessment inventories. By systematically evaluating LLMs with MPI, we provide the first piece of evidence demonstrating the efficacy of MPI in studying LLMs behaviors. We further devise a Personality Prompting (P$^2$) method to induce LLMs with specific personalities in a **controllable** way, capable of producing diverse and verifiable behaviors. We hope this work sheds light on future studies by adopting personality as the essential indicator for various downstream tasks, and could further motivate research into equally intriguing human-like machine behaviors.

paragraphs: This paper uses human personality assessment as a structured way to study language-model behavior. The central questions are whether psychometric tests can provide principled, quantitative measurements of machine behavior and whether prompts can induce particular personality patterns. The focus is on observable responses assessed through a standardized framework.

The authors introduce the Machine Personality Inventory, or MPI, drawing on established personality inventories and the Big Five framework. They systematically evaluate language models with this tool and report initial evidence that it is useful for studying their behavior. The contribution is a common assessment approach through which differences in model responses can be examined quantitatively.

The paper also introduces Personality Prompting, abbreviated P², to induce specific personalities in a controllable manner. The authors report diverse behaviors that can be checked through assessment. Taken together, the measurement tool and prompting method connect behavioral evaluation with behavioral steering. The proposed use of personality as an indicator for downstream tasks remains a direction for future research, rather than a demonstrated result across those tasks.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces a personality-based inventory for evaluating language-model behavior and a prompting method for controllably inducing personality patterns.

title: Evaluating and Inducing Personality in Pre-trained Language Models

abstract: This paper explores a hierarchical prompting mechanism for the hierarchical image classification (HIC) task. Different from prior HIC methods, our hierarchical prompting is the first to explicitly inject ancestor-class information as a tokenized hint that benefits the descendant-class discrimination. We think it well imitates human visual recognition, i.e., humans may use the ancestor class as a prompt to draw focus on the subtle differences among descendant classes. We model this prompting mechanism into a Transformer with Hierarchical Prompting (TransHP). TransHP consists of three steps: 1) learning a set of prompt tokens to represent the coarse (ancestor) classes, 2) on-the-fly predicting the coarse class of the input image at an intermediate block, and 3) injecting the prompt token of the predicted coarse class into the intermediate feature. Though the parameters of TransHP maintain the same for all input images, the injected coarse-class prompt conditions (modifies) the subsequent feature extraction and encourages a dynamic focus on relatively subtle differences among the descendant classes. Extensive experiments show that TransHP improves image classification on accuracy (e.g., improving ViT-B/16 by +2.83% ImageNet classification accuracy), training data efficiency (e.g., +12.69% improvement under 10% ImageNet training data), and model explainability. Moreover, TransHP also performs favorably against prior HIC methods, showing that TransHP well exploits the hierarchical information. The code is available at: https://github.com/WangWenhao0716/TransHP.
