paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning builds a policy from an existing dataset. Diffusion-DICE starts from a distributional interpretation of DICE methods: their optimal stationary distribution ratio describes a transformation from the data-collection policy toward the optimized policy. The paper uses a diffusion model to carry out this transformation directly.

The key mathematical result splits the optimal policy's score function into a behavior-policy score and a guidance gradient determined by the optimal distribution ratio. A diffusion model trained on the dataset supplies the first component. The authors introduce an objective that learns the guidance component using only actions from the dataset, keeping this training step grounded in observed actions.

Because the resulting distribution can have multiple modes, guidance may lead to locally optimal choices. Diffusion-DICE therefore generates several candidate actions and selects among them to pursue the global optimum. The authors report that this guide-then-select approach minimizes exploitation of value-function errors. A toy example illustrates that failure mechanism in previous methods, and benchmark experiments demonstrate strong performance for Diffusion-DICE.
summary.tldr: Diffusion-DICE learns diffusion guidance from dataset actions and selects among generated candidates to reduce exploitation of value-function errors in offline reinforcement learning.

title: Diffusion-DICE: In-Sample Diffusion Guidance for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Existing video multi-modal sentiment analysis mainly focuses on the sentiment expression of people within the video, yet often neglects the induced sentiment of viewers while watching the videos. Induced sentiment of viewers is essential for inferring the public response to videos and has broad application in analyzing public societal sentiment, effectiveness of advertising and other areas. The micro videos and the related comments provide a rich application scenario for viewers’ induced sentiment analysis. In light of this, we introduces a novel research task, Multimodal Sentiment Analysis for Comment Response of Video Induced(MSA-CRVI), aims to infer opinions and emotions according to comments response to micro video. Meanwhile, we manually annotate a dataset named Comment Sentiment toward to Micro Video (CSMV) to support this research. It is the largest video multi-modal sentiment dataset in terms of scale and video duration to our knowledge, containing 107, 267 comments and 8, 210 micro videos with a video duration of 68.83 hours. To infer the induced sentiment of comment should leverage the video content, we propose the Video Content-aware Comment Sentiment Analysis (VC-CSA) method as a baseline to address the challenges inherent in this new task. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method is showing significant improvements over other established baselines. We make the dataset and source code publicly available at https://github.com/IEIT-AGI/MSA-CRVI.

paragraphs: Video sentiment analysis often studies emotions expressed by people appearing in a video. This paper instead examines viewers’ reactions through the comments they leave. It introduces a task for inferring opinions and emotions in responses to micro videos, with potential applications in understanding public reactions and assessing advertising effectiveness.

To support the task, the authors manually annotate CSMV, a dataset containing 107,267 comments and 8,210 micro videos spanning 68.83 hours. They describe it as the largest video multimodal sentiment dataset by scale and duration to their knowledge. The paired video-and-comment setting provides material for studying responses in relation to the content that prompted them.

The proposed baseline, VC-CSA, uses video content when analyzing comment sentiment. This connects the interpretation of a response to the video it addresses. Experiments report significant improvements over established baselines, supporting the value of video-aware analysis for this task. The contribution combines a new research target, annotated data, and a method for using the relevant multimodal context.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces a video-comment sentiment task, a large annotated dataset, and a baseline that uses video content to interpret viewer reactions.

title: Infer Induced Sentiment of Comment Response to Video: A New Task, Dataset and Baseline

abstract: Precise image segmentation provides clinical study with instructive information. Despite the remarkable progress achieved in medical image segmentation, there is still an absence of a 3D foundation segmentation model that can segment a wide range of anatomical categories with easy user interaction. In this paper, we propose a 3D foundation segmentation model, named SegVol, supporting universal and interactive volumetric medical image segmentation. By scaling up training data to 90K unlabeled Computed Tomography (CT) volumes and 6K labeled CT volumes, this foundation model supports the segmentation of over 200 anatomical categories using semantic and spatial prompts. To facilitate efficient and precise inference on volumetric images, we design a zoom-out-zoom-in mechanism. Extensive experiments on 22 anatomical segmentation tasks verify that SegVol outperforms the competitors in 19 tasks, with improvements up to 37.24\% compared to the runner-up methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness and importance of specific designs by ablation study. We expect this foundation model can promote the development of volumetric medical image analysis. The model and code are publicly available at https://github.com/BAAI-DCAI/SegVol.

paragraphs: Volumetric medical-image segmentation identifies anatomical structures within a 3D scan. This paper addresses the need for a single foundation model that covers many anatomical categories while allowing users to specify what they want segmented. SegVol combines broad anatomical coverage with semantic and spatial prompts for interactive use.

The model is trained using 90,000 unlabeled CT volumes and 6,000 labeled CT volumes, and supports more than 200 anatomical categories. Its zoom-out-zoom-in mechanism is designed to make inference on volumetric images both efficient and precise. Together, these choices address the breadth of structures the model can handle and the demands of processing three-dimensional inputs.

Across 22 anatomical segmentation tasks, SegVol outperforms competitors on 19, with reported improvements reaching 37.24% over runner-up methods. Ablation studies examine the contributions of specific design choices. These results support the model’s usefulness across the evaluated segmentation tasks, while the prompt-based interface provides a way to direct that capability toward the anatomical structure a user needs.
summary.tldr: SegVol supports prompt-driven segmentation of over 200 anatomical categories in CT volumes and outperforms competitors on 19 of 22 evaluated tasks.

title: SegVol: Universal and Interactive Volumetric Medical Image Segmentation

abstract: Cross-domain few-shot learning (CDFSL) is proposed to transfer knowledge from large-scale source-domain datasets to downstream target-domain datasets with only a few training samples. However, Vision Transformer (ViT), as a strong backbone network to achieve many top performances, is still under-explored in the CDFSL task in its transferability against large domain gaps. In this paper, we find an interesting phenomenon of ViT in the CDFSL task: by simply multiplying a temperature (even as small as 0) to the attention in ViT blocks, the target-domain performance consistently increases, even though the attention map is downgraded to a uniform map. In this paper, we delve into this phenomenon for an interpretation. Through experiments, we interpret this phenomenon as a remedy for the ineffective target-domain attention caused by the query-key attention mechanism under large domain gaps. Based on it, we further propose a simple but effective method for the CDFSL task to boost ViT's transferability by resisting the learning of query-key parameters and encouraging that of non-query-key ones. Experiments on four CDFSL datasets validate the rationale of our interpretation and method, showing we can consistently outperform state-of-the-art methods. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Zoilsen/Attn_Temp_CDFSL.

paragraphs: Cross-domain few-shot learning asks a model trained on a large source dataset to adapt to a different domain using very few examples. This paper investigates Vision Transformers in that setting, especially when the source and target differ substantially. It examines whether their learned attention remains useful after this change in the data.

The authors observe that multiplying attention by a temperature improves target-domain performance in their experiments, even when a zero temperature makes the attention map uniform. They interpret this behavior as a remedy for ineffective target-domain attention produced by the query-key mechanism under large domain gaps. The observation links a simple attention adjustment to a specific source of transfer difficulty.

Building on that interpretation, the proposed method discourages learning in query-key parameters while encouraging learning in the remaining parameters. Experiments on four cross-domain few-shot datasets support the explanation and report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The result suggests that controlling which transformer components adapt can improve transfer when only a small target training set is available.
summary.tldr: Adjusting attention temperature and restraining query-key learning improve Vision Transformer transfer across domains in few-shot experiments.

title: Attention Temperature Matters in ViT-Based Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning

abstract: We explore the potential of self-play training for large language models (LLMs) in a two-player adversarial language game called Adversarial Taboo. In this game, an attacker and a defender communicate around a target word only visible to the attacker. The attacker aims to induce the defender to speak the target word unconsciously, while the defender tries to infer the target word from the attacker's utterances. To win the game, both players must have sufficient knowledge about the target word and high-level reasoning ability to infer and express in this information-reserved conversation. Hence, we are curious about whether LLMs' reasoning ability can be further enhanced by Self-Playing this Adversarial language Game (SPAG). With this goal, we select several open-source LLMs and let each act as the attacker and play with a copy of itself as the defender on an extensive range of target words. Through reinforcement learning on the game outcomes, we observe that the LLMs' performances uniformly improve on a broad range of reasoning benchmarks. Furthermore, iteratively adopting this self-play process can continuously promote LLMs' reasoning abilities. The code is available at https://github.com/Linear95/SPAG.

paragraphs: This paper explores whether a competitive language game can provide useful training for general reasoning. In Adversarial Taboo, an attacker knows a hidden target word and tries to make a defender say it unknowingly. The defender instead tries to infer the target from the attacker's messages, creating a conversation with deliberately unequal information.

The proposed SPAG process has each selected open-source language model play the attacker against a copy of itself as defender across many target words. Reinforcement learning then uses game outcomes as training feedback. Both roles require knowledge of the target and reasoning about what to communicate or infer from the conversation.

The authors report improvements across a broad range of reasoning benchmarks for the tested models. Repeating the self-play process produces further gains in their experiments. The significance is that learning from outcomes in this particular language game transfers to reasoning evaluations beyond the game itself, supporting self-play as a potential source of training signals for language-model reasoning.
summary.tldr: SPAG improves tested language models' reasoning through reinforcement learning from self-play in an adversarial hidden-word game.

title: Self-playing Adversarial Language Game Enhances LLM Reasoning

abstract: Transformer-based autoregressive sampling has been the major bottleneck for slowing down large language model inferences. One effective way to accelerate inference is Speculative Decoding, which employs a small model to sample a sequence of draft tokens and a large model to validate. Given its empirical effectiveness, the theoretical understanding of Speculative Decoding is falling behind. This paper tackles this gap by conceptualizing the decoding problem via markov chain abstraction and studying the key properties, output quality and inference acceleration, from a theoretical perspective. Our analysis covers the theoretical limits of speculative decoding, batch algorithms, and output quality-inference acceleration tradeoffs. Our results reveal the fundamental connections between different components of LLMs via total variation distances and show how they jointly affect the efficiency of decoding algorithms.

paragraphs: Autoregressive language models generate text through repeated sampling steps, making generation a major inference bottleneck. Speculative decoding accelerates this process by asking a smaller model to propose several tokens and a larger model to validate them. Although this approach has demonstrated practical benefits, the paper argues that its theoretical explanation has lagged behind its empirical use.

The authors represent decoding through a Markov-chain abstraction and study both output quality and computational acceleration within that framework. Their analysis considers theoretical limits, batch algorithms, and tradeoffs between quality and speed. This puts several aspects of speculative decoding into a common mathematical setting, allowing their relationships to be examined together.

A central finding connects different model components through total variation distances, which describe differences between probability distributions. The analysis shows how these relationships jointly affect decoding efficiency. Its contribution is therefore an explanation of the factors governing speculative decoding, including how quality requirements interact with acceleration, rather than a claim that one speedup applies across all model combinations.
summary.tldr: A Markov-chain analysis explains speculative decoding's theoretical limits and how differences between model distributions affect speed and output quality.

title: A Theoretical Perspective for Speculative Decoding Algorithm

abstract:
Flow Matching (FM) (also referred to as stochastic interpolants or rectified flows) stands out as a class of generative models that aims to bridge in finite time the target distribution $
u^\star$ with an auxiliary distribution $\mu$ leveraging a fixed coupling $\pi$ and a bridge which can either be deterministic or stochastic. These two ingredients define a path measure which can then be approximated by learning the drift of its Markovian projection. The main contribution of this paper is to provide relatively mild assumption on $
u^\star$, $\mu$ and $\pi$ to obtain non-asymptotics guarantees for Diffusion Flow Matching (DFM) models using as bridge the conditional distribution associated with the Brownian motion. More precisely, it establishes bounds on the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the target distribution and the one generated by such DFM models under moment conditions on the score of $
u^\star$, $\mu$ and $\pi$, and a standard $\mathrm{L}^2$-drift-approximation error assumption.

paragraphs: Flow matching connects an auxiliary distribution with a target distribution over a finite time interval. A coupling specifies how the two distributions are related, while a deterministic or stochastic bridge defines paths between them. Learning the drift of a Markovian projection provides a way to approximate the resulting path distribution for generation.

This paper studies Diffusion Flow Matching with a bridge based on the conditional distribution associated with Brownian motion. Its main contribution is a non-asymptotic bound on Kullback–Leibler divergence between the target distribution and the distribution produced by the learned model. Such a bound quantifies distributional error without relying only on a limiting argument.

The guarantees require moment conditions on the scores of the target distribution, auxiliary distribution, and coupling, together with a standard squared-error assumption on the learned drift. The authors characterize these assumptions as relatively mild. The result connects the quality of drift approximation and the regularity of the underlying distributions to a formal guarantee for this particular diffusion flow-matching construction.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes non-asymptotic KL error bounds for Brownian-bridge Diffusion Flow Matching under score-moment and drift-approximation assumptions.

title: Theoretical guarantees in KL for Diffusion Flow Matching

abstract: Algorithms for bilevel optimization often encounter Hessian computations, which are prohibitive in high dimensions. While recent works offer first-order methods for unconstrained bilevel problems, the constrained setting remains relatively underexplored. We present first-order linearly constrained optimization methods with finite-time hypergradient stationarity guarantees. For linear equality constraints, we attain $\epsilon$-stationarity in $\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ gradient oracle calls, which is nearly-optimal. For linear inequality constraints, we attain $(\delta,\epsilon)$-Goldstein stationarity in $\widetilde{O}(d{\delta^{-1} \epsilon^{-3}})$ gradient oracle calls, where $d$ is the upper-level dimension. Finally, we obtain for the linear inequality setting dimension-free rates of $\widetilde{O}({\delta^{-1} \epsilon^{-4}})$ oracle complexity under the additional assumption of oracle access to the optimal dual variable. Along the way, we develop new nonsmooth nonconvex optimization methods with inexact oracles. Our numerical experiments verify these guarantees.

Finally, we obtain for the linear inequality setting dimension-free rates of $\widetilde{O}({\delta^{-1} \epsilon^{-4}})$ oracle complexity under the additional assumption of oracle access to the optimal dual variable. paragraphs: Bilevel optimization places one optimization problem inside another. Algorithms for these problems often require Hessian computations, which become costly in high dimensions. This paper develops first-order methods for problems with linear constraints, extending a direction previously explored mainly for unconstrained settings. It provides finite-time guarantees for reaching specified forms of stationarity.

For linear equality constraints, the methods reach epsilon-stationarity using approximately epsilon to the power of minus two gradient-oracle calls, with logarithmic factors suppressed. The authors characterize this rate as nearly optimal. For linear inequality constraints, they obtain a Goldstein stationarity guarantee with complexity approximately d times delta to the power of minus one times epsilon to the power of minus three, where d is the upper-level dimension.

A second inequality-constrained result removes the dimension dependence, but requires oracle access to the optimal dual variable and has an epsilon-to-the-minus-four dependence. That additional access assumption is essential to the stated dimension-free guarantee. The work also develops methods for nonsmooth, nonconvex optimization with inexact oracles, and reports numerical experiments supporting the theoretical guarantees.
summary.tldr: First-order methods provide finite-time stationarity guarantees for bilevel problems with linear constraints, including a conditional dimension-free result.

title: First-Order Methods for Linearly Constrained Bilevel Optimization

abstract: Hypothesis selection, also known as density estimation, is a fundamental problem in statistics and learning theory. Suppose we are given a sample set from an unknown distribution $P$ and a finite class of candidate distributions (called hypotheses) $\mathcal{H} \coloneqq \{H_1, H_2, \ldots, H_n\}$. The aim is to design an algorithm that selects a distribution $\hat H$ in $\mathcal{H}$ that best fits the data. The algorithm's accuracy is measured based on the distance between $\hat{H}$ and $P$ compared to the distance of the closest distribution in $\mathcal{H}$ to $P$ (denoted by $OPT$). Concretely, we aim for $\|\hat{H} - P\|_{TV}$ to be at most $ \alpha \cdot OPT + \epsilon$ for some small $\epsilon$ and $\alpha$. While it is possible to decrease the value of $\epsilon$ as the number of samples increases, $\alpha$ is an inherent characteristic of the algorithm. In fact, one cannot hope to achieve $\alpha < 3$ even when there are only two candidate hypotheses, unless the number of samples is proportional to the domain size of $P$ [Bousquet, Kane, Moran '19]. Finding the best $\alpha$ has been one of the main focuses of studies of the problem since early work of [Devroye, Lugosi '01]. Prior to our work, no algorithm was known that achieves $\alpha = 3$ in near-linear time. We provide the first algorithm that operates in almost linear time ($\tilde{O}(n/\epsilon^3)$ time) and achieves $\alpha = 3$. This result improves upon a long list of results in hypothesis selection. Previously known algorithms either had worse time complexity, a larger factor $\alpha$, or extra assumptions about the problem setting.In addition to this algorithm, we provide another (almost) linear-time algorithm with better dependency on the additive accuracy parameter $\epsilon$, albeit with a slightly worse accuracy parameter, $\alpha = 4$.
originalAbstract: Hypothesis selection, also known as density estimation, is a fundamental problem in statistics and learning theory. Suppose we are given a sample set from an unknown distribution $P$ and a finite class of candidate distributions (called hypotheses) $\mathcal{H} \coloneqq \{H_1, H_2, \ldots, H_n\}$. The aim is to design an algorithm that selects a distribution $\hat H$ in $\mathcal{H}$ that best fits the data. The algorithm's accuracy is measured based on the distance between $\hat{H}$ and $P$ compared to the distance of the closest distribution in $\mathcal{H}$ to $P$ (denoted by $OPT$). Concretely, we aim for $\|\hat{H} - P\|_{TV}$ to be at most $ \alpha \cdot OPT + \epsilon$ for some small $\epsilon$ and $\alpha$. While it is possible to decrease the value of $\epsilon$ as the number of samples increases, $\alpha$ is an inherent characteristic of the algorithm. In fact, one cannot hope to achieve $\alpha < 3$ even when there are only two candidate hypotheses, unless the number of samples is proportional to the domain size of $P$ [Bousquet, Kane, Moran '19]. Finding the best $\alpha$ has been one of the main focuses of studies of the problem since early work of [Devroye, Lugosi '01]. Prior to our work, no algorithm was known that achieves $\alpha = 3$ in near-linear time. We provide the first algorithm that operates in almost linear time ($\tilde{O}(n/\epsilon^3)$ time) and achieves $\alpha = 3$. This result improves upon a long list of results in hypothesis selection. Previously known algorithms either had worse time complexity, a larger factor $\alpha$, or extra assumptions about the problem setting.In addition to this algorithm, we provide another (almost) linear-time algorithm with better dependency on the additive accuracy parameter $\epsilon$, albeit with a slightly worse accuracy parameter, $\alpha = 4$.

paragraphs: Hypothesis selection chooses a distribution from a finite list using samples from an unknown distribution. The goal is to select a candidate whose total variation distance from the truth is close to that of the best available candidate. The guarantee has two parts: a multiplicative factor on the best candidate’s error and a small additive error.

The paper gives the first almost-linear-time algorithm achieving multiplicative factor three. Its runtime is approximately n divided by epsilon cubed, with logarithmic factors suppressed, where n is the number of candidates and epsilon is the additive accuracy parameter. Earlier algorithms required more time, accepted a worse multiplicative factor, or imposed additional assumptions.

The significance of three comes from a lower bound: achieving a smaller factor can require samples proportional to the distribution’s domain size, even with only two candidates. The result therefore combines the optimal factor in that sense with almost-linear dependence on candidate count. A second algorithm improves the dependence on additive accuracy while accepting factor four, offering a different trade-off between runtime and approximation quality.
summary.tldr: A new hypothesis-selection algorithm achieves approximation factor three in almost-linear time in the number of candidate distributions.

title: Optimal Hypothesis Selection in (Almost) Linear Time

abstract: Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) has shown great promise in achieving humanlevel reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), and has recently been extended to MLLMs. Nevertheless, reasoning about videos, which is a fundamental aspect of human intelligence, remains a persistent challenge due to the complex logic, temporal and causal structures inherent in video data. To fill this gap, we propose VideoRFT, a novel approach that extends the RFT paradigm to cultivate human-like video reasoning capabilities in MLLMs. VideoRFT follows the standard two-stage scheme in RFT: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with chain-of-thought (CoT) annotations, followed by reinforcement learning (RL) to improve generalization. A central challenge to achieve this in the video domain lies in the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality video CoT datasets. We address this by building a multi-expert-driven, cognition-inspired CoT curation pipeline. First, we devise a cognition-inspired prompting strategy to elicit a reasoning LLM to generate preliminary CoTs based solely on rich, structured, and literal representations of video content. Subsequently, these CoTs are revised by a MLLM conditioned on the actual video, ensuring visual consistency and reducing visual hallucinations. This pipeline results in two new datasets, i.e.VideoRFT-CoT-102K for SFT and VideoRFT-RL-310K for RL. To further strengthen the RL phase, we introduce a novel semantic-consistency reward that explicitly promotes the alignment between textual reasoning and visual evidence. This reward encourages the model to produce coherent, context-aware reasoning outputs grounded in visual input. Extensive experiments show that VideoRFT achieves state-of-the-art performance on six video reasoning benchmarks.

paragraphs: Reasoning about video requires connecting visual evidence with events, timing, and causal relationships. VideoRFT applies a two-stage training process to this challenge: supervised learning from annotated reasoning chains, followed by reinforcement learning intended to improve generalization. A central obstacle is obtaining enough high-quality reasoning annotations grounded in the actual videos.

The authors build a curation pipeline in which a reasoning language model first drafts chains from rich, structured, literal descriptions of video content. A multimodal model then revises those drafts while viewing the video. This second pass checks visual consistency and reduces hallucinations. The pipeline produces VideoRFT-CoT-102K for supervised training and VideoRFT-RL-310K for reinforcement learning.

During reinforcement learning, a semantic-consistency reward explicitly encourages agreement between textual reasoning and visual evidence. This makes grounding part of the optimization objective as well as the annotation process. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on six video reasoning benchmarks. The results support combining curated reasoning examples with a reward that encourages the model’s explanations to remain connected to what the video shows.
summary.tldr: VideoRFT combines video-grounded reasoning data and a semantic-consistency reward to improve multimodal video reasoning.

title: VideoRFT: Incentivizing Video Reasoning Capability in MLLMs via Reinforced Fine-Tuning

abstract: Autoregressive language models dominate modern text generation, yet their sequential nature introduces fundamental limitations: decoding is slow, and maintaining global coherence remains challenging. Diffusion models offer a promising alternative by enabling parallel generation and flexible control; however, their application to text generation is hindered by the high dimensionality of token-level representations. We introduce Cosmos, a novel approach to text generation that operates entirely in a compressed, smooth latent space tailored specifically for diffusion. This space is learned using an autoencoder trained simultaneously for token-level reconstruction and alignment with frozen activations from a pretrained language encoder, providing robust semantic grounding and enabling effective perturbation‑based augmentations. Empirically, we demonstrate that text representations can be compressed up to $8\times$ while maintaining generation quality comparable to token‑level diffusion models. Furthermore, increasing the latent sequence length allows \textsc{Cosmos} to surpass both diffusion‑based and autoregressive baselines. We evaluate Cosmos on four diverse generative tasks including story generation, question generation, summarization, and detoxification and compare it with various generative paradigms. Cosmos achieves comparable or superior generation quality while offering more than $2\times$ faster inference. Code is released at https://github.com/MeshchaninovViacheslav/cosmos.

paragraphs: Text diffusion offers parallel generation, but operating on representations for every token creates a high-dimensional modeling problem. Cosmos moves diffusion into a shorter, smooth latent representation. The goal is to reduce the amount of representation the generation process must handle while retaining the information needed to produce meaningful text.

An autoencoder learns this space through two simultaneous objectives. It must reconstruct the original tokens and align its representations with fixed activations from a pretrained language encoder. Reconstruction preserves recoverable text content, while alignment supplies semantic grounding. The resulting space also supports augmentations formed by perturbing the representations.

Experiments show compression of up to eight times with generation quality comparable to token-level diffusion models. Increasing the latent sequence length lets Cosmos outperform the evaluated diffusion and autoregressive baselines. Across story generation, question generation, summarization, and detoxification, it achieves comparable or better quality with more than twice the inference speed. Together, these results show that the design and size of the latent representation can support both efficient generation and strong output quality.
summary.tldr: Cosmos performs text diffusion in a compressed, semantically grounded latent space, achieving competitive quality with faster inference.

title: Cosmos: Compressed and Smooth Latent Space for Text Diffusion Modeling

abstract: We prove that the classic REINFORCE stochastic policy gradient (SPG) method converges to globally optimal policies in finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with $\textit{any}$ constant learning rate. To avoid the need for small or decaying learning rates, we introduce two key innovations in the stochastic bandit setting, which we then extend to MDPs. $\textbf{First}$, we identify a new exploration property of SPG: the online SPG method samples every action infinitely often (i.o.), improving on previous results that only guaranteed at least two actions would be sampled i.o. This means SPG inherently achieves asymptotic exploration without modification. $\textbf{Second}$, we eliminate the assumption of unique mean reward values, a condition that previous convergence analyses in the bandit setting relied on, but that does not translate to MDPs. Our results deepen the theoretical understanding of SPG in both bandit problems and MDPs, with a focus on how it handles the exploration-exploitation trade-off when standard optimization and stochastic approximation methods cannot be applied, as is the case with large constant learning rates.

paragraphs: The paper proves that REINFORCE converges to globally optimal policies in finite-horizon Markov decision processes with any constant learning rate. The result removes the need for a small or shrinking learning rate in this convergence analysis. Its significance is theoretical: it concerns eventual optimality, including step sizes for which standard optimization arguments do not apply.

The proof begins with stochastic bandits and establishes a stronger exploration property. Online stochastic policy gradient samples every action infinitely often, extending previous results that guaranteed this for at least two actions. This shows that the method itself supplies asymptotic exploration in the analyzed setting, without an added exploration modification.

The authors also remove an assumption that mean rewards must be distinct. That matters because the earlier bandit assumption does not carry over to general Markov decision processes. Together, these advances enable the extension from bandits to finite-horizon decision problems. summary.tldr: REINFORCE is proved to converge to globally optimal policies in finite-horizon MDPs with any constant learning rate.

title: REINFORCE Converges to Optimal Policies with Any Learning Rate

abstract: Existing research in low-level vision has shifted its focus from "one-by-one" task-specific methods to "all-in-one" multi-task unified architectures. However, current all-in-one image restoration approaches primarily aim to improve overall performance across a limited number of tasks. In contrast, how to incrementally add new image restoration capabilities on top of an existing model — that is, task-incremental learning — has been largely unexplored. To fill this research gap, we propose a minimalistic and universal paradigm for task-incremental learning called MINI. It addresses the problem of parameter interference across different tasks through a simple yet effective mechanism, enabling nearly forgetting-free task-incremental learning. Specifically, we design a special meta-convolution called MINI-Conv, which generates parameters solely through lightweight embeddings instead of complex convolutional networks or MLPs. This not only significantly reduces the number of parameters and computational overhead but also achieves complete parameter isolation across different tasks. Moreover, MINI-Conv can be seamlessly integrated as a plug-and-play replacement for any convolutional layer within existing backbone networks, endowing them with incremental learning capabilities. Therefore, our method is highly generalizable. Finally, we demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing incremental learning approaches across five common image restoration tasks. Moreover, the near forgetting-free nature of our method makes it highly competitive even against all-in-one image restoration methods trained in a full-supervised manner. Our code is available at https://github.com.

paragraphs: Image restoration models increasingly handle several tasks within one architecture, but adding a new capability after training raises a different problem: updates for the new task can interfere with parameters supporting earlier tasks. MINI addresses this incremental setting, aiming to extend an existing model while retaining the restoration abilities it already learned.

Its central component is MINI-Conv, a replacement for convolutional layers that generates parameters from lightweight embeddings. This avoids using more complex convolutional networks or multilayer perceptrons for parameter generation. The method completely isolates parameters across tasks, addressing interference while reducing parameter counts and computational overhead. Its compatibility with existing convolutional layers makes the approach broadly applicable across backbone networks.

Across five common restoration tasks, the authors report state-of-the-art results against existing incremental learning methods. They describe forgetting as nearly absent, rather than claiming that all previous performance is perfectly preserved. The resulting models are also competitive with fully supervised all-in-one methods, suggesting that adding capabilities incrementally can remain effective without training every task together.
summary.tldr: MINI isolates task parameters through lightweight convolution replacements, enabling image restoration models to gain capabilities with nearly no forgetting.

title: A Minimalistic Unified Framework for Incremental Learning across Image Restoration Tasks

abstract: Clinical decision‑making routinely demands reasoning over heterogeneous data, yet existing multimodal language models (MLLMs) remain largely vision‑centric and fail to generalize across clinical specialties. To bridge this gap, we introduce QoQ-Med-7B/32B, the first open generalist clinical foundation model that jointly reasons across medical images, time‑series signals, and text reports. QoQ-Med is trained with Domain‑aware Relative Policy Optimization (DRPO), a novel reinforcement‑learning objective that hierarchically scales normalized rewards according to domain rarity and modality difficulty, mitigating performance imbalance caused by skewed clinical data distributions. Trained on 2.61 million instruction tuning pairs spanning 9 clinical domains, we show that DRPO training boosts diagnostic performance by 43% in macro‑F1 on average across all visual domains as compared to other critic-free training methods like GRPO. Furthermore, with QoQ-Med trained on intensive segmentation data, it is able to highlight salient regions related to the diagnosis, with an IoU 10x higher than open models while reaching the performance of OpenAI o4-mini. To foster reproducibility and downstream research, we release (i) the full model weights, (ii) the modular training pipeline, and (iii) all intermediate reasoning traces.

summary.tldr: QoQ-Med uses domain-aware reward scaling to improve clinical reasoning across images, time-series signals, and text reports.

title: QoQ-Med: Building Multimodal Clinical Foundation Models with Domain-Aware GRPO Training

abstract: The energy paradigm, exemplified by Hopfield networks, offers a principled framework for memory in neural systems by interpreting dynamics as descent on an energy surface. While powerful for static associative memories, it falls short in modeling sequential memory, where transitions between memories are essential. We introduce the Exponential Dynamic Energy Network (EDEN), a novel architecture that extends the energy paradigm to temporal domains by evolving the energy function over multiple timescales. EDEN combines a static high-capacity energy network with a slow, asymmetrically interacting modulatory population, enabling robust and controlled memory transitions. We formally derive short-timescale energy functions that govern local dynamics and use them to analytically compute memory escape times, revealing a phase transition between static and dynamic regimes. The analysis of capacity, defined as the number of memories that can be stored with minimal error rate as a function of the dimensions of the state space (number of feature neurons), for EDEN shows that it achieves exponential sequence memory capacity $\mathcal{O}(\gamma^N)$, outperforming the linear capacity $\mathcal{O}(N)$ of conventional models. Furthermore, EDEN's dynamics resemble the activity of time and ramping cells observed in the human brain during episodic memory tasks, grounding its biological relevance. By unifying static and sequential memory within a dynamic energy framework, EDEN offers a scalable and interpretable model for high-capacity temporal memory in both artificial and biological systems.

paragraphs: Energy-based memory models describe recall as movement toward stable states on an energy surface. That perspective naturally supports static memories, but sequential memory also requires leaving one state and moving to another. EDEN extends this framework by allowing the energy function to evolve across multiple timescales.

The architecture couples a static, high-capacity memory network with a slower modulatory population whose interactions are asymmetric. Together, these components enable controlled transitions between memories. The authors derive energy functions for short-timescale dynamics and use them to calculate memory escape times, revealing a phase transition between regimes that remain static and those that move through memories.

It establishes exponential sequence capacity for EDEN, compared with the linear capacity of conventional models. The dynamics also resemble time-cell and ramping-cell activity observed during human episodic memory tasks. That resemblance supports biological relevance while the mathematical analysis provides an interpretable account of sequential recall.
summary.tldr: EDEN evolves an energy-based memory system over multiple timescales, enabling controlled memory sequences with analytically established exponential capacity.

title: Exponential Dynamic Energy Network for High Capacity Sequence Memory

abstract: Estimating the uncertainty of responses from Large Language Models (LLMs) remains a critical challenge. While recent Bayesian methods have demonstrated effectiveness in quantifying uncertainty through low-rank weight updates, they typically require complex fine-tuning or post-training procedures. In this paper, we propose **T**raining-**F**ree **B**ayesianization (**TFB**), a simple yet theoretically grounded framework that efficiently transforms trained low-rank adapters into Bayesian ones without additional training. TFB systematically searches for the maximally acceptable level of variance in the weight posterior, constrained within a family of low-rank isotropic Gaussian distributions. Our theoretical analysis shows that under mild conditions, this search process is equivalent to KL-regularized variational optimization, a generalized form of variational inference. Through comprehensive experiments, we show that TFB achieves superior uncertainty estimation and generalization compared to existing methods while eliminating the need for complex Bayesianization training procedures.

paragraphs: Training-Free Bayesianization converts an already trained low-rank language-model adapter into a Bayesian adapter for uncertainty estimation. Existing Bayesian approaches using low-rank weight updates can require complex additional training procedures. This paper instead starts from the learned adapter and searches for an appropriate distribution over its weights without further training.

The search seeks the largest acceptable posterior variance within a restricted family of low-rank isotropic Gaussian distributions. That family specifies the form uncertainty can take, while the search determines its acceptable magnitude. The method thus adds uncertainty around trained weights through variance selection, avoiding a new Bayesian fine-tuning procedure.

The theoretical result is conditional: under mild conditions, this search is equivalent to KL-regularized variational optimization, a generalized form of variational inference. Experiments report better uncertainty estimation and generalization than existing methods. Together, the analysis and results support a comparatively simple route to Bayesian adapters, while keeping the scope clear: the method operates on trained low-rank adapters and searches within the stated posterior family.
summary.tldr: TFB adds Bayesian uncertainty to trained low-rank adapters by searching posterior variance without additional training.

title: Training-Free Bayesianization for Low-Rank Adapters of Large Language Models

abstract: In recent years, nonlinear dynamic system identification using artificial neural networks has garnered attention due to its broad potential applications across science and engineering. However, purely data-driven approaches often struggle with extrapolation and may yield physically implausible forecasts. Furthermore, the learned dynamics can exhibit instabilities, making it difficult to apply such models safely and robustly. This article introduces stable port-Hamiltonian neural networks, a machine learning architecture that incorporates physical biases of energy conservation and dissipation while ensuring global Lyapunov stability of the learned dynamics. Through illustrative and real-world examples, we demonstrate that these strong inductive biases facilitate robust learning of stable dynamics from sparse data, while avoiding instability and surpassing purely data-driven approaches in accuracy and physically meaningful generalization. Furthermore, the model's applicability and potential for data-driven surrogate modeling are showcased on multi-physics simulation data.

paragraphs: Neural networks can learn nonlinear system dynamics from observations, but accurate fits do not automatically provide physically plausible or stable forecasts. Purely data-driven models can struggle when extrapolating and may learn unstable behavior. This paper introduces an architecture that builds physical structure and stability into the learned dynamics.

Stable port-Hamiltonian neural networks incorporate biases based on energy conservation and dissipation while ensuring global Lyapunov stability. These constraints shape the kinds of dynamics the model can represent. The approach therefore uses physical knowledge as part of the learning architecture, connecting predictions to energy behavior and a mathematical stability property.

Illustrative and real-world examples show robust learning of stable dynamics from sparse data. The authors report better accuracy and more physically meaningful generalization than purely data-driven approaches, while avoiding instability. They also demonstrate applicability on multi-physics simulation data for surrogate modeling. The results support the usefulness of strong physical biases when the learning objective includes stability and plausible behavior beyond the available observations.
summary.tldr: Stable port-Hamiltonian neural networks embed energy conservation, dissipation, and global stability into models that learn dynamics from sparse data.

title: Stable Port-Hamiltonian Neural Networks

abstract: By incorporating visual inputs, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) extend LLMs to support visual reasoning. However, this integration also introduces new vulnerabilities, making MLLMs susceptible to multimodal jailbreak attacks and hindering their safe deployment. Existing defense methods, including Image-to-Text Translation, Safe Prompting, and Multimodal Safety Tuning, attempt to address this by aligning multimodal inputs with LLMs’ built-in safeguards. Yet, they fall short in uncovering root causes of multimodal vulnerabilities, particularly how harmful multimodal tokens trigger jailbreak in MLLMs? Consequently, they remain vulnerable to text-driven multimodal attacks, often exhibiting overdefensive behaviors and imposing heavy training overhead. To bridge this gap, we present an comprehensive analysis of where, how and which harmful multimodal tokens bypass safeguards in MLLMs. Surprisingly, we find that less than 1% tokens in early-middle layers are responsible for inducing unsafe behaviors, highlighting the potential of precisely removing a small subset of harmful tokens, without requiring safety tuning, can still effectively improve safety against jailbreaks. Motivated by this, we propose Safe Prune-then-Restore (SafePTR), an training-free defense framework that selectively prunes harmful tokens at vulnerable layers while restoring benign features at subsequent layers. Without incurring additional computational overhead, SafePTR significantly enhances the safety of MLLMs while preserving efficiency. Extensive evaluations across three MLLMs and five benchmarks demonstrate SafePTR’s state-of-the-art performance in mitigating jailbreak risks without compromising utility.

Yet, they fall short in uncovering root causes of multimodal vulnerabilities, particularly how harmful multimodal tokens trigger jailbreak in MLLMs? Consequently, they remain vulnerable to text-driven multimodal attacks, often exhibiting overdefensive behaviors and imposing heavy training overhead. To bridge this gap, we present an comprehensive analysis of where, how and which harmful multimodal tokens bypass safeguards in MLLMs. Surprisingly, we find that less than 1% tokens in early-middle layers are responsible for inducing unsafe behaviors, highlighting the potential of precisely removing a small subset of harmful tokens, without requiring safety tuning, can still effectively improve safety against jailbreaks. Motivated by this, we propose Safe Prune-then-Restore (SafePTR), an training-free defense framework that selectively prunes harmful tokens at vulnerable layers while restoring benign features at subsequent layers. Without incurring additional computational overhead, SafePTR significantly enhances the safety of MLLMs while preserving efficiency. Extensive evaluations across three MLLMs and five benchmarks demonstrate SafePTR’s state-of-the-art performance in mitigating jailbreak risks without compromising utility.

paragraphs: Adding visual inputs gives language models new capabilities but also creates pathways for multimodal jailbreaks. SafePTR starts by investigating where harmful information bypasses safeguards inside these models. The authors report that, in their analysis, fewer than 1% of tokens in early-to-middle layers are responsible for inducing unsafe behavior.

That concentration motivates a selective intervention. SafePTR removes harmful tokens at vulnerable layers, then restores benign features in later layers. The restoration step is part of preserving useful information while suppressing the harmful influence. The framework requires no safety tuning, and the authors report that it adds no computational overhead.

Evaluations span three multimodal language models and five benchmarks. The paper reports state-of-the-art jailbreak mitigation without compromising utility, supporting the value of intervening on a small subset of internal tokens. The significance is both explanatory and practical: the analysis identifies a concentrated source of vulnerability, and the defense uses that finding to target particular layers and tokens. The reported results concern the evaluated models and attacks rather than establishing immunity to every possible jailbreak.
summary.tldr: SafePTR removes a small subset of harmful internal tokens and restores benign features to improve multimodal jailbreak resistance without training.

title: SafePTR: Token-Level Jailbreak Defense in Multimodal LLMs via Prune-then-Restore Mechanism

abstract: Foundation Models (FMs) have demonstrated remarkable success in fields like computer vision and natural language processing, yet their application to combinatorial optimization remains underexplored. Optimization problems, often modeled as graphs, pose unique challenges due to their diverse structures, varying distributions, and NP-hard complexity. To address these challenges, we propose OPTFM, the first graph foundation model for general combinatorial optimization. OPTFM introduces a scalable multi-view graph transformer with hybrid self-attention and cross-attention to model large-scale heterogeneous graphs in $O(N)$ time complexity while maintaining semantic consistency throughout the attention computation. A Dual-level pre-training framework integrates node-level graph reconstruction and instance-level contrastive learning, enabling robust and adaptable representations at multiple levels. Experimental results across diverse optimization tasks show that models trained on OPTFM embeddings without fine-tuning consistently outperform task-specific approaches, establishing a new benchmark for solving combinatorial optimization problems.

paragraphs: Combinatorial optimization problems can often be represented as graphs, but their structures and data distributions vary substantially. OPTFM seeks to learn reusable graph representations across these problems. The goal is to support multiple optimization tasks with a shared pretrained model, rather than requiring each task to begin with its own representation learning.

Pretraining operates at two levels. Node-level graph reconstruction teaches local structural information, while instance-level contrastive learning develops representations that distinguish and relate whole problem instances.

This indicates that the learned embeddings carry useful information across the evaluated tasks. The efficiency claim concerns the model’s graph processing, while the task results demonstrate the practical value of its shared representations for combinatorial optimization.
summary.tldr: OPTFM learns reusable graph embeddings with linear-time attention and dual-level pretraining, outperforming task-specific approaches across tested optimization tasks.

title: OPTFM: A Scalable Multi-View Graph Transformer for Hierarchical Pre-Training in Combinatorial Optimization

abstract: This work introduces a novel approach, Pairwise Epistemic Estimators (PairEpEsts), for epistemic uncertainty estimation in ensemble models for regression tasks using pairwise-distance estimators (PaiDEs). By utilizing the pairwise distances between model components, PaiDEs establish bounds on entropy. We leverage this capability to enhance the performance of Bayesian Active Learning by Disagreement (BALD). Notably, unlike sample-based Monte Carlo estimators, PairEpEsts can estimate epistemic uncertainty up to 100 times faster and demonstrate superior performance in higher dimensions. To validate our approach, we conducted a varied series of regression experiments on commonly used benchmarks: 1D sinusoidal data, *Pendulum*, *Hopper*, *Ant*, and *Humanoid*, demonstrating PairEpEsts’ advantage over baselines in high-dimensional regression active learning.

paragraphs: An ensemble of regression models can express uncertainty through disagreement among its component predictions. Epistemic uncertainty concerns what the model does not yet know, making it useful for deciding which additional observations to acquire. Estimating it with Monte Carlo sampling can, however, be computationally expensive.

Pairwise Epistemic Estimators use distances between ensemble components to estimate this uncertainty. The approach builds on pairwise-distance estimators that establish bounds on entropy, a measure of uncertainty. The authors use those bounds to enhance Bayesian Active Learning by Disagreement, connecting a more efficient uncertainty calculation to the selection of informative training examples.

Experiments include one-dimensional sinusoidal regression and the Pendulum, Hopper, Ant, and Humanoid benchmarks. The authors report uncertainty estimation up to 100 times faster than sample-based Monte Carlo methods and stronger performance in higher dimensions. Their active-learning results show advantages over baselines in high-dimensional regression, supporting the value of pairwise comparisons when repeated sampling becomes costly.
summary.tldr: Pairwise comparisons between ensemble components enable faster epistemic uncertainty estimation and improve high-dimensional regression active learning.

title: Epistemic Uncertainty Estimation in Regression Ensemble Models with Pairwise Epistemic Estimators

abstract: State‑space models (SSMs) have become a cornerstone for unraveling brain dynamics, revealing how latent neural states evolve over time and give rise to observed signals. By combining deep learning’s flexibility with SSMs’ principled dynamical structure, recent studies have achieved powerful fits to functional neuroimaging data. However, most approaches still view the brain as a set of loosely connected regions or impose oversimplified network priors—falling short of a truly holistic, self‐organized dynamical system perspective. Brain functional connectivity (FC) at each time point naturally forms a symmetric positive–definite (SPD) matrix, which lives on a curved Riemannian manifold rather than in Euclidean space. Capturing the trajectories of these SPD matrices is key to understanding how coordinated networks support cognition and behavior. To this end, we introduce *GeoDynamics*, a geometric state‑space neural network that tracks latent brain‐state trajectories directly on the high‑dimensional SPD manifold. *GeoDynamics* embeds each connectivity matrix into a manifold‑aware recurrent framework, learning smooth, geometry‑respecting transitions that reveal task‐driven state changes and early markers of Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and autism. Beyond neuroscience, we validate *GeoDynamics* on human action recognition benchmarks (UTKinect, Florence, HDM05), demonstrating its scalability and robustness in modeling complex spatiotemporal dynamics across diverse domains.

paragraphs: GeoDynamics models how patterns of brain connectivity evolve over time. The paper represents functional connectivity at each time point as a symmetric positive-definite matrix, an object belonging to a curved geometric space. It argues that tracking these matrices with their geometry intact can better express coordinated network dynamics than treating brain regions as loosely connected components.

The proposed geometric state-space neural network places connectivity matrices inside a manifold-aware recurrent framework. It learns smooth transitions between latent brain states while respecting the structure of the positive-definite matrix space. This links a model of temporal change with a representation of the brain's connectivity as a whole.

The paper reports that the learned trajectories reveal task-driven state changes and early markers associated with Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and autism. It also evaluates GeoDynamics on the UTKinect, Florence, and HDM05 human action recognition benchmarks, supporting its stated scalability and robustness beyond neuroscience. The broader contribution is a way to model changing structured relationships while preserving their non-Euclidean geometry.
summary.tldr: GeoDynamics tracks evolving brain connectivity with a state-space neural network that respects the curved geometry of connectivity matrices.

title: GeoDynamics: A Geometric State‑Space Neural Network for Understanding Brain Dynamics on Riemannian Manifolds

abstract: We propose a novel collaborative multi-agent optimization framework for adaptive training in multi-label image classification, fundamentally advancing beyond static decision rules and isolated automation. Our method deploys a set of distributed, task-specific agents, each responsible for dynamically orchestrating critical training components—including data augmentation, optimization methods, learning rate schedules, and loss functions—according to evolving visual-semantic relationships and training states. Each agent employs an advanced non-stationary multi-armed bandit algorithm, integrating both $\epsilon$-greedy and upper confidence bound strategies, to judiciously balance exploration with exploitation throughout the training lifecycle. A hierarchical composite reward mechanism synergizes overall classification accuracy, rare class recognition, and training stability, fostering both independent optimization and implicit collaborative behavior among agents. The framework further leverages refined techniques such as dual-rate exponential moving average smoothing and structured mixed-precision training to enhance robustness and computational efficiency. Extensive experiments across benchmarks including Pascal VOC, COCO, Yeast, and Mediamill demonstrate that our approach achieves superior mean average precision and rare-class F1 scores compared to state-of-the-art methods, while also exhibiting rapid convergence and remarkable cross-domain generalization. Our results indicate that collaborative multi-agent adaptive optimization offers a scalable and principled solution for self-optimizing deep learning in complex multi-label scenarios.

paragraphs: MAT-Agent treats training configuration as a collection of decisions that should adapt as learning progresses. The findings suggest that coordinated adaptation of several training components can improve both overall classification and recognition of less common classes. The paper presents this as a scalable approach to self-optimizing training in complex multi-label settings.
summary.tldr: MAT-Agent coordinates specialized agents that adapt training choices to improve multi-label classification, including recognition of rare classes.

title: MAT-Agent: Adaptive Multi-Agent Training Optimization

abstract: Many decision-making tasks, where both accuracy and efficiency matter, still require human supervision. For example, tasks like traffic officers reviewing hour-long dashcam footage or researchers screening conference videos can benefit from concise summaries that reduce cognitive load and save time. Yet current vision-language models (VLMs) often produce verbose, redundant outputs that hinder task performance. Existing video caption evaluation depends on costly human annotations and overlooks the summaries' utility in downstream tasks. We address these gaps with $\underline{\textbf{V}}$ideo-to-text $\underline{\textbf{I}}$nformation $\underline{\textbf{B}}$ottleneck $\underline{\textbf{E}}$valuation (VIBE), an annotation-free method that scores VLM outputs using two metrics: $\textit{grounding}$ (how well the summary aligns with visual content) and $\textit{utility}$ (how informative it is for the task). VIBE selects from randomly sampled VLM outputs by ranking them according to the two scores to support effective human decision-making. Human studies on $\texttt{LearningPaper24}$, $\texttt{SUTD-TrafficQA}$, and $\texttt{LongVideoBench}$ show that summaries selected by VIBE consistently improve performance—boosting task accuracy by up to $61.23$% and reducing response time by $75.77$% compared to naive VLM summaries or raw video.

summary.tldr: VIBE selects video summaries using annotation-free grounding and task-utility scores, improving human decision accuracy and speed in reported studies.

title: VIBE: Annotation-Free Video-to-Text Information Bottleneck Evaluation for TL;DR

abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) using diverse datasets is crucial for enhancing their overall performance across various domains. In practical scenarios, existing methods based on modeling the mixture proportions of data composition often struggle with data whose domain labels are missing, imprecise or non-normalized, while methods based on data selection usually encounter difficulties in balancing multi-domain performance. To address these challenges, in this work, we investigate the role of data diversity in enhancing the overall abilities of LLMs by empirically constructing contrastive data pools and theoretically deriving explanations. Building upon the insights gained, we propose a new method that gives the LLM a dual identity: an output model to cognitively probe and select data based on diversity reward, as well as an input model to be tuned with the selected data. Extensive experiments show that the proposed method notably boosts performance across domain-undetermined data and a series of foundational downstream tasks when applied to various advanced LLMs. We release our code and hope this study can shed light on the understanding of data diversity and advance feedback-driven data-model co-design for LLMs.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a language model across multiple domains requires deciding which data to use. Methods that set domain mixture proportions become difficult to apply when domain labels are absent, inconsistent, or unclear. Data selection methods face a related problem: selecting useful examples while maintaining performance across multiple domains.

This paper investigates diversity as a basis for making those choices. The authors construct contrasting data pools to study its effects empirically and develop theoretical explanations. Their method assigns the language model two roles. In one role, it probes candidate data and selects examples using a diversity reward. In the other, it is fine-tuned on the selected examples, connecting data choice directly to model improvement.

Experiments across several advanced language models report improved performance on data with undetermined domains and on a range of foundational downstream tasks. The findings support diversity-guided selection as a way to improve broad capabilities when conventional domain categories are unreliable. The broader contribution is a feedback-driven relationship between the model selecting its training material and the model learning from that material.
summary.tldr: The method uses a language model to select diverse fine-tuning data, improving performance when domain labels are missing or unreliable.

title: Diversity as a Reward: Fine-Tuning LLMs on a Mixture of Domain-Undetermined Data

abstract: The current mainstream and state-of-the-art anomaly detection (AD) methods are substantially established on pretrained feature networks yielded by ImageNet pre- training. However, regardless of supervised or self-supervised pretraining, the pretraining process on ImageNet does not match the goal of anomaly detection (i.e., pretraining in natural images doesn’t aim to distinguish between normal and abnormal). Moreover, natural images and industrial image data in AD scenarios typically have the distribution shift. The two issues can cause ImageNet-pretrained features to be suboptimal for AD tasks. To further promote the development of the AD field, pretrained representations specially for AD tasks are eager and very valuable. To this end, we propose a novel AD representation learning framework specially designed for learning robust and discriminative pretrained representa- tions for industrial anomaly detection. Specifically, closely surrounding the goal of anomaly detection (i.e., focus on discrepancies between normals and anoma- lies), we propose angle- and norm-oriented contrastive losses to maximize the angle size and norm difference between normal and abnormal features simulta- neously. To avoid the distribution shift from natural images to AD images, our pretraining is performed on a large-scale AD dataset, RealIAD. To further alle- viate the potential shift between pretraining data and downstream AD datasets, we learn the pretrained AD representations based on the class-generalizable repre- sentation, residual features. For evaluation, based on five embedding-based AD methods, we simply replace their original features with our pretrained represen- tations. Extensive experiments on five AD datasets and five backbones consis- tently show the superiority of our pretrained features. The code is available at https://github.com/xcyao00/ADPretrain.

paragraphs: Industrial anomaly detectors often reuse features learned from ImageNet, even though recognizing natural images differs from separating normal industrial examples from defects. ADPretrain addresses both this mismatch in training goals and the difference between natural and industrial imagery. It aims to supply representations explicitly trained for anomaly detection.

The framework trains on the large industrial anomaly dataset RealIAD. Its contrastive objectives separate normal and abnormal features in two ways: by increasing the angle between them and by increasing the difference in their magnitudes. It also learns through residual features, which the authors describe as generalizable across classes, to reduce potential differences between pretraining data and downstream datasets.

The evaluation replaces the original features in five embedding-based anomaly detection methods with ADPretrain representations. Across five datasets and five backbone architectures, the experiments consistently favor the new features. This makes the contribution useful at the representation level: existing detection methods can benefit from features whose training objective and source imagery more closely match their task.
summary.tldr: ADPretrain improves industrial anomaly detection by pretraining features to distinguish normal examples from anomalies on industrial data.

title: ADPretrain: Advancing Industrial Anomaly Detection via Anomaly Representation Pretraining

abstract: Pre-trained Large language models (LLMs) have shown impressive advancements in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) analysis and causal discovery. Considering the unique nature of the causal discovery field, which focuses on extracting causal graphs from observed data, research on LLMs in this field is still at an early exploratory stage. As a subfield of causal discovery, effective connectivity (EC) has received even less attention, and LLM-based approaches in EC remain unexplored. Existing LLM-based approaches for causal discovery typically rely on iterative querying to assess the causal influence between variable pairs, without any model adaptation or fine-tuning, making them ill-suited for handling the cross-modal gap and complex causal structures. To this end, we propose BrainEC-LLM, the first method to fine-tune LLMs for estimating brain EC from fMRI data. Specifically, multiscale decomposition mixing module decomposes fMRI time series data into short-term and long-term multiscale trends, then mixing them in bottom-up (fine to coarse) and top-down (coarse to fine) manner to extract multiscale temporal variations. And cross attention is applied with pre-trained word embeddings to ensure consistency between the fMRI input and pre-trained natural language. The experimental results on simulated and real resting-state fMRI datasets demonstrate that BrainEC-LLM can achieve superior performance when compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: BrainEC-LLM adapts a pretrained language model to estimate brain effective connectivity from fMRI recordings. The task concerns directed influences between brain regions. The authors argue that existing language-model approaches to causal discovery, which repeatedly ask about pairs of variables without adapting the model, are poorly suited to the differences between brain measurements and language.

The method first separates fMRI time series into patterns at multiple scales, including shorter and longer trends. It mixes information from fine scales toward coarse scales and in the reverse direction, allowing the representation to incorporate temporal variation at different resolutions. Cross attention then connects these representations with pretrained word embeddings to align the input with the language model.

The authors present this as the first approach to fine-tune language models specifically for brain effective connectivity estimation. Evaluations on simulated and real resting-state fMRI datasets report superior performance against state-of-the-art baselines. The contribution combines model adaptation with multiscale processing, addressing both the input mismatch and the complexity of temporal relationships.
summary.tldr: BrainEC-LLM combines multiscale fMRI processing with language-model fine-tuning to estimate directed relationships between brain regions.

title: BrainEC-LLM: Brain Effective Connectivity Estimation by Multiscale Mixing LLM

abstract: We propose Metric Automata Theory, an elegant generalisation of classic Automata Theory to continuous dynamical systems, that constitutes a unifying theory of all kinds of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), including widely-adopted architectures such as xLSTM and State Space Models (SSMs). The theory allows one to analyse RNNs both in the finite and unbounded precision settings seamlessly, while utilising fundamental results of Automata Theory. It also provides a novel notion of robustness that guarantees numerical stability and contributes to stability of learning. We employ the theory to prove a comprehensive set of expressivity results for widely-adopted RNNs, with a focus on robustness and finite-precision. Notably, we contrast the capabilities of xLSTM and SSMs for robustly modelling all star-free regular languages—xLSTM can do so, while SSMs cannot robustly recognize the FLIP-FLOP language. Thus we give a novel perspective on the importance of non-linear recurrences, giving insight for why xLSTM shows superior performance to SSMs on several tasks. We provide an improved understanding of the capabilities of Mamba, a popular SSM model. We show that Mamba is not generally capable of recognising the star-free languages under finite-precision, which is seemingly in contrast with the existing theoretical and empirical results for SSMs. We clarify the picture, by showing that Mamba admits a piecewise-linearly separable state space that allows it to approximate star-free languages, with some length-generalisation abilities. At the same time, Mamba does not admit such state spaces for languages like Parity. This explains why empirically Mamba performs well on star-free languages, and fails on Parity.

The theory distinguishes what these architectures can represent robustly. This offers a theoretical perspective on the importance of nonlinear recurrence and insight into xLSTM’s stronger performance on several tasks.

The analysis also clarifies Mamba’s capabilities. Under finite precision, Mamba cannot generally recognize star-free languages, but its state space can be separated in a piecewise-linear way that supports approximations with some generalization to longer sequences. The authors show that this state-space structure is unavailable for languages such as Parity. This distinction reconciles limitations on exact recognition with reported empirical success on star-free languages and failure on Parity.
summary.tldr: Metric Automata Theory explains how robustness and numerical precision shape the sequence-recognition capabilities of recurrent architectures.

title: Metric Automata Theory: A Unifying Theory of RNNs

abstract: Conventional wisdom attributes the mysterious generalization abilities of overparameterized neural networks to gradient descent (and its variants). The recent volume hypothesis challenges this view: it posits that these generalization abilities persist even when gradient descent is replaced by Guess & Check (G&C), i.e., by randomly drawing weight settings until one that fits the training data is found. The validity of the volume hypothesis for wide and deep neural networks remains an open question. In this paper, we theoretically investigate this question for matrix factorization (with linear and non-linear activation): a canonical testbed in neural network theory. We first prove that generalization under G&C deteriorates with increasing width, establishing what is, to our knowledge, the first canonical case where G&C is provably inferior to gradient descent. Conversely, we prove that generalization under G&C improves with increasing depth, revealing a stark contrast between wide and deep networks, which we further validate empirically. These findings suggest that even in simple settings, there may not be a simple answer to the question of whether neural networks need gradient descent to generalize well.

paragraphs: Why can a neural network fit its training examples and still perform well on unseen data? One explanation emphasizes gradient descent. The volume hypothesis proposes that good generalization could persist even with Guess & Check: repeatedly drawing random weights until finding a setting that fits the training data. This paper tests that idea theoretically in matrix factorization.

The analysis covers matrix factorization with both linear and nonlinear activation, a setting used to study neural-network behavior. The authors prove that generalization under Guess & Check worsens as width increases. This supplies a concrete case in which random search for a fitting solution is provably inferior to gradient descent, challenging a broad interpretation of the volume hypothesis.

Depth produces the opposite result: the authors prove that increasing depth improves generalization under Guess & Check, and empirically validate the width-depth contrast. The findings therefore depend on how a model is expanded. They suggest that even in relatively simple theoretical settings, the importance of gradient descent cannot be captured by one answer applying equally to width and depth.
summary.tldr: In matrix-factorization models, random fitting generalizes worse with increasing width but better with increasing depth, complicating claims about gradient descent's necessity.

title: Do Neural Networks Need Gradient Descent to Generalize? A Theoretical Study

abstract: Recent multimodal embedding approaches leveraging multimodal large language models (MLLMs) fine-tuned with contrastive learning (CL) have shown promising results, yet the underlying reasons behind their superiority remain underexplored. This work argues that a crucial advantage of MLLM-based approaches stems from implicit cross-modal alignment achieved during generative pretraining, where the language decoder learns to exploit multimodal signals within a shared representation space for generating unimodal outputs. Through analysis of anisotropy and kernel similarity structure, we empirically confirm that latent alignment emerges within MLLM representations, allowing CL to serve as a lightweight refinement stage. Leveraging this insight, we propose a Language-Centric Omnimodal Embedding framework, termed LCO-Embed. Extensive experiments across diverse backbones and benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness, achieving state-of-the-art performance across modalities. Furthermore, we identify a Generation-Representation Scaling Law (GRSL), showing that the representational capabilities gained through contrastive refinement scale positively with the MLLM's generative capabilities. This suggests that improving generative abilities evolves as an effective paradigm for enhancing representation quality. We provide a theoretical explanation of GRSL, which formally links the MLLM's generative quality to the upper bound on its representation performance, and validate it on a challenging, low-resource visual-document retrieval task, showing that continual generative pretraining before CL can further enhance the potential of a model's embedding capabilities. Codes, models, and resources are available at https://github.com/LCO-Embedding/LCO-Embedding.

Its theoretical account connects generative quality to an upper bound on representation performance.
