Together, these findings suggest that strengthening generation can be a productive route to better representations.
summary.tldr: LCO-Embed builds on cross-modal alignment acquired during generative pretraining, linking stronger generation with better embeddings after contrastive refinement.

title: Scaling Language-centric Omnimodal Representation Learning

abstract: Diffusion LLMs have emerged as a promising alternative to conventional autoregressive LLMs, offering substantial potential for improving runtime efficiency. However, existing diffusion models fail to provably enforce user-specified formal constraints, such as regular expressions, which makes them unreliable for tasks that require structured outputs, such as fixed-schema JSON generation. Unlike autoregressive models, which generate tokens sequentially, diffusion LLMs predict a block of tokens in parallel. This parallelism makes traditional constrained decoding algorithms, designed to enforce constraints with sequential token prediction, ineffective at preserving the true output distribution. To address this limitation, we propose DINGO, a dynamic programming-based constrained decoding strategy that is both efficient and provably distribution-preserving. DINGO enables sampling of output strings with the highest probability under the model’s predicted distribution while strictly adhering to any user-specified regular expression. On standard symbolic math and JSON generation benchmarks, DINGO achieves up to a $68$\% points of improvement over unconstrained inference. The code is available at [**DINGO**](https://github.com/uiuc-focal-lab/DINGO).

paragraphs: Diffusion language models predict blocks of tokens in parallel, creating opportunities for faster generation. That same parallelism complicates enforcing formal output requirements, such as a regular expression describing valid structured text. Constraint-handling algorithms built around sequential token generation do not preserve the intended output distribution when transferred directly to this setting.

DINGO addresses this problem with a constrained decoding strategy based on dynamic programming. The authors establish that the strategy preserves the distribution while strictly satisfying a user-specified regular expression. It enables sampling of high-probability valid strings under the model's predicted distribution. This connects two requirements that matter together: producing an admissible output and retaining the model's probability structure.

The paper evaluates DINGO on symbolic mathematics and JSON generation benchmarks, reporting improvements of up to 68 percentage points over unconstrained inference. That is a maximum reported gain across the evaluated settings, rather than a uniform improvement. The contribution makes formal constraints compatible with parallel diffusion generation and provides evidence that enforcing those constraints can substantially improve results on tasks where output structure matters.
summary.tldr: DINGO provides provably distribution-preserving decoding for diffusion language models while enforcing user-specified regular expressions.

title: DINGO: Constrained Inference for Diffusion LLMs

abstract: Vector-Quantized Variational Autoencoders (VQVAEs) have enabled strong performance in generative modeling by mapping continuous data to learnable codes. In this work, we identify a surprising yet consistent phenomenon that we term \emph{dimensional collapse}: despite using high-dimensional embeddings, VQVAEs tend to compress their representations into a much smaller subspace, typically only 4 to 10 dimensions. We provide an in-depth analysis of this phenomenon and reveal its relation to model performance and learning dynamics. Interestingly, VQVAEs naturally gravitate toward this low-dimensional regime, and enforcing higher-dimensional usage (e.g., via rank regularization) could lead to degraded performance. To overcome this low-dimensionality limitation, we propose \textbf{Divide-and-Conquer VQ (DCVQ)}, which partitions the latent space into multiple low-dimensional subspaces, each quantized independently. By design, each subspace respects the model’s preference for low dimensionality, while their combination expands the overall capacity. Our results show that DCVQ overcomes the inherent dimensional bottleneck and achieves improved reconstruction quality across image datasets.

paragraphs: Vector-quantized variational autoencoders represent continuous inputs through learned discrete codes. This paper finds that their apparently high-dimensional embeddings often occupy a much smaller subspace, typically just four to ten dimensions. The authors call this pattern dimensional collapse and analyze its relationship to model performance and learning dynamics.

A central observation is that directly forcing representations to use more dimensions can degrade performance. The models appear to favor a low-dimensional regime, so increasing effective dimensionality through rank regularization is not automatically beneficial. This motivates a remedy that accommodates the observed learning behavior while expanding the capacity available to the overall representation.

Divide-and-Conquer VQ partitions the latent space into several low-dimensional subspaces and quantizes each independently. Each component can operate in the regime the model tends to prefer, while their combination provides greater overall capacity. Results across image datasets show improved reconstruction quality and support the method as a way to overcome the observed bottleneck. The design turns the collapse analysis into a concrete change in how quantization is organized.
summary.tldr: DCVQ improves reconstruction by combining independently quantized low-dimensional subspaces to address dimensional collapse in VQVAEs.

title: Dimensional Collapse in VQVAEs: Evidence and Remedies

abstract: We show that several popular discounted reward natural actor-critics, including the popular NAC-LSTD and eNAC algorithms, do not generate unbiased estimates of the natural policy gradient as claimed. We derive the first unbiased discounted reward natural actor-critics using batch and iterative approaches to gradient estimation. We argue that the bias makes the existing algorithms more appropriate for the average reward setting. We also show that, when Sarsa(lambda) is guaranteed to converge to an optimal policy, the objective function used by natural actor-critics is concave, so policy gradient methods are guaranteed to converge to globally optimal policies as well.
originalAbstract: We show that several popular discounted reward natural actor-critics, including the popular NAC-LSTD and eNAC algorithms, do not generate unbiased estimates of the natural policy gradient as claimed. We derive the first unbiased discounted reward natural actor-critics using batch and iterative approaches to gradient estimation. We argue that the bias makes the existing algorithms more appropriate for the average reward setting. We also show that, when Sarsa(lambda) is guaranteed to converge to an optimal policy, the objective function used by natural actor-critics is concave, so policy gradient methods are guaranteed to converge to globally optimal policies as well.

paragraphs: Natural actor-critic algorithms update a policy using an estimated natural policy gradient. This paper examines whether several popular methods actually estimate the intended gradient without bias in the discounted reward setting. It shows that NAC-LSTD and eNAC, among others, fail to provide unbiased estimates despite claims that they do.

The authors derive unbiased natural actor-critic methods for discounted rewards using both batch and iterative gradient estimation. This addresses the mismatch between the quantity existing algorithms claim to estimate and the estimates they produce. They also argue that the identified bias makes those existing algorithms more appropriate for average reward problems, distinguishing two reward objectives that require different treatment.

A separate theoretical result concerns global optimality. Under conditions where Sarsa(lambda) is guaranteed to reach an optimal policy, the authors show that the natural actor-critic objective is concave. Policy gradient methods consequently also receive a global convergence guarantee in that setting. This conclusion depends on the stated condition; it does not establish global convergence for policy gradient methods in general.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies bias in popular discounted reward natural actor-critics, derives unbiased alternatives, and establishes a conditional global convergence result.

title: Bias in Natural Actor-Critic Algorithms

abstract: We describe a novel approach to optimizing matrix problems involving nuclear norm regularization and apply it to the matrix completion problem. We combine methods from non-smooth and smooth optimization. At each step we use the proximal gradient to select an active subspace. We then find a smooth, convex relaxation of the smaller subspace problems and solve these using second order methods. We apply our methods to matrix completion problems including Netflix dataset, and show that they are more than 6 times faster than state-of-the-art nuclear norm solvers. Also, this is the first paper to scale nuclear norm solvers to the Yahoo-Music dataset, and the first time in the literature that the efficiency of nuclear norm solvers can be compared and even compete with non-convex solvers like Alternating Least Squares (ALS).

paragraphs: Nuclear norm regularization is used in matrix optimization problems such as filling in missing matrix entries. This paper develops a solver that combines nonsmooth and smooth optimization to make these problems more efficient. Its main strategy is to select a smaller active subspace and concentrate subsequent optimization there.

At each step, a proximal gradient operation chooses the active subspace. The authors then construct a smooth, convex relaxation of the resulting smaller problem and solve it with second-order methods. The two components serve complementary purposes: one identifies a subspace to work in, while the other performs more focused optimization within that reduced setting.

On matrix completion problems including Netflix data, the methods are reported to run more than six times faster than state-of-the-art nuclear norm solvers. The paper also reports scaling such solvers to Yahoo-Music for the first time. Its comparisons show that their efficiency can compete with nonconvex methods such as alternating least squares, demonstrating that the choice of solver can substantially change the practical cost of nuclear norm optimization.
summary.tldr: Selecting active subspaces and solving smaller smooth problems substantially accelerates nuclear norm minimization in the reported matrix completion experiments.

title: Nuclear Norm Minimization via Active Subspace Selection

abstract: Matrix completion concerns the recovery of a low-rank matrix from a subset of its revealed entries, and nuclear norm minimization has emerged as an effective surrogate for this combinatorial problem. Here, we show that nuclear norm minimization can recover an arbitrary n \times n matrix of rank r from O(nr log^2(n)) revealed entries, provided that revealed entries are drawn proportionally to the local row and column coherences (closely related to leverage scores) of the underlying matrix. Our results are order-optimal up to logarithmic factors, and extend existing results for nuclear norm minimization which require strong incoherence conditions on the types of matrices that can be recovered, due to assumed uniformly distributed revealed entries. We further provide extensive numerical evidence that a proposed two-phase sampling algorithm can perform nearly as well as local-coherence sampling and without requiring a priori knowledge of the matrix coherence structure. Finally, we apply our results to quantify how weighted nuclear norm minimization can improve on unweighted minimization given an arbitrary set of sampled entries.

paragraphs: Matrix completion reconstructs a low-rank matrix from a subset of its entries. This paper studies how the choice of observed entries affects recovery by nuclear norm minimization. Earlier guarantees based on uniformly sampled entries require strong incoherence conditions, which restrict how concentrated the matrix's structure can be.

The main result replaces those matrix restrictions with a suitable sampling rule. For an arbitrary n-by-n rank-r matrix, recovery is possible from O(nr log²(n)) entries when sampling probabilities are proportional to local row and column coherences. These quantities are closely related to leverage scores. The bound is optimal in order up to logarithmic factors, connecting recovery efficiency to where observations are collected.

Because the required coherence structure may not be known beforehand, the authors propose a two-phase sampling procedure. Numerical evidence indicates that it can perform nearly as well as sampling with that knowledge. They also quantify benefits of weighted nuclear norm minimization for an arbitrary observed set, showing how recovery can benefit from accounting for the distribution of available entries.
summary.tldr: Sampling according to local matrix coherence enables strong recovery guarantees without the usual incoherence restrictions.

title: Coherent Matrix Completion

abstract: Language modelling is a fundamental building block of natural language processing. However, in practice the size of the vocabulary limits the distributions applicable for this task: specifically, one has to either resort to local optimization methods, such as those used in neural language models, or work with heavily constrained distributions. In this work, we take a step towards overcoming these difficulties. We present a method for global-likelihood optimization of a Markov random field language model exploiting long-range contexts in time independent of the corpus size. We take a variational approach to optimizing the likelihood and exploit underlying symmetries to greatly simplify learning. We demonstrate the efficiency of this method both for language modelling and for part-of-speech tagging.

paragraphs: Language models need to represent relationships among words while handling large vocabularies. The paper describes a practical tension: flexible models often rely on local optimization, while more manageable alternatives impose strong restrictions on the distributions they can represent. It proposes a Markov random field language model that can use context extending across longer stretches of text.

The learning method takes a variational approach to optimizing likelihood. It also uses symmetries within the model to simplify the computation. These symmetries are central to the contribution: the authors exploit shared structure in the problem to make a demanding learning objective more manageable. They describe their approach as global-likelihood optimization with time independent of corpus size.

The paper demonstrates computational efficiency in both language modeling and part-of-speech tagging. These applications show how the proposed learning method can support different language tasks. The contribution is a step toward combining richer contextual dependencies with efficient likelihood optimization, rather than a claim that vocabulary-related difficulties have been completely resolved.
summary.tldr: A variational method exploits model symmetries to efficiently learn Markov random field language models with long-range context.

title: A Fast Variational Approach for Learning Markov Random Field Language Models

abstract: We investigate the statistical efficiency of a nonparametric Gaussian process method for a nonlinear tensor estimation problem. Low-rank tensor estimation has been used as a method to learn higher order relations among several data sources in a wide range of applications, such as multi-task learning, recommendation systems, and spatiotemporal analysis. We consider a general setting where a common linear tensor learning is extended to a nonlinear learning problem in reproducing kernel Hilbert space and propose a nonparametric Bayesian method based on the Gaussian process method. We prove its statistical convergence rate without assuming any strong convexity, such as restricted strong convexity. Remarkably, it is shown that our convergence rate achieves the minimax optimal rate. We apply our proposed method to multi-task learning and show that our method significantly outperforms existing methods through numerical experiments on real-world data sets.

paragraphs: Tensor estimation models higher-order relationships among several data sources, with applications including multi-task learning, recommendation, and spatiotemporal analysis. This paper studies the statistical efficiency of a nonlinear version of that problem. It extends a common linear tensor-learning formulation into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space and proposes a nonparametric Bayesian estimator based on Gaussian processes.

In the problem setting analyzed, this means that the estimator matches the best achievable worst-case statistical rate, giving a precise efficiency claim for the proposed nonlinear method.

The authors also apply the estimator to multi-task learning and evaluate it on real-world datasets. They report substantial improvements over existing methods in those experiments. The paper thus combines a statistical optimality result for its formulation with empirical evidence that the nonlinear Gaussian-process approach can improve practical multi-task prediction.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian-process tensor estimator achieves a minimax-optimal convergence rate without strong-convexity assumptions and improves reported multi-task learning results.

title: Gaussian process nonparametric tensor estimator and its minimax optimality

abstract: In statistical relational learning, the link prediction problem is key to automatically understand the structure of large knowledge bases. As in previous studies, we propose to solve this problem through latent factorization. However, here we make use of complex valued embeddings. The composition of complex embeddings can handle a large variety of binary relations, among them symmetric and antisymmetric relations. Compared to state-of-the-art models such as Neural Tensor Network and Holographic Embeddings, our approach based on complex embeddings is arguably simpler, as it only uses the Hermitian dot product, the complex counterpart of the standard dot product between real vectors. Our approach is scalable to large datasets as it remains linear in both space and time, while consistently outperforming alternative approaches on standard link prediction benchmarks.

Compared to state-of-the-art models such as Neural Tensor Network and Holographic Embeddings, our approach based on complex embeddings is arguably simpler, as it only uses the Hermitian dot product, the complex counterpart of the standard dot product between real vectors. paragraphs: The paper addresses link prediction in knowledge bases: estimating which relationships hold between entities. It uses latent factorization, representing relational structure through learned embeddings. Its distinguishing choice is to use complex-valued embeddings, giving the model a way to express a broad range of binary relationships within a relatively simple mathematical construction.

The composition of these embeddings can represent both symmetric and antisymmetric relations. This distinction matters because some relationships behave the same way when the two entities exchange positions, while others depend on their order. The scoring construction uses the Hermitian dot product, a counterpart of the ordinary dot product for complex vectors. The authors describe it as arguably simpler than Neural Tensor Networks and Holographic Embeddings.

The approach retains linear space and time requirements, supporting its use with large datasets. On standard link-prediction benchmarks, it consistently outperforms the alternative approaches evaluated. The findings show that complex-valued representations can provide useful relational expressiveness while keeping the model’s core operation simple and its computational requirements scalable.
summary.tldr: Complex-valued embeddings model varied relation types with a simple Hermitian dot product and outperform alternatives on standard link-prediction benchmarks.

title: Complex Embeddings for Simple Link Prediction

abstract: We present a Monte Carlo sampler using a modified Nosé-Poincaré Hamiltonian along with Riemannian preconditioning. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo samplers allow better exploration of the state space as opposed to random walk-based methods, but, from a molecular dynamics perspective, may not necessarily provide samples from the canonical ensemble. Nosé-Hoover samplers rectify that shortcoming, but the resultant dynamics are not Hamiltonian. Furthermore, usage of these algorithms on large real-life datasets necessitates the use of stochastic gradients, which acts as another potentially destabilizing source of noise. In this work, we propose dynamics based on a modified Nosé-Poincaré Hamiltonian augmented with Riemannian manifold corrections. The resultant symplectic sampling algorithm samples from the canonical ensemble while using structural cues from the Riemannian preconditioning matrices to efficiently traverse the parameter space. We also propose a stochastic variant using additional terms in the Hamiltonian to correct for the noise from the stochastic gradients. We show strong performance of our algorithms on synthetic datasets and high-dimensional Poisson factor analysis-based topic modeling scenarios.

paragraphs: The paper develops a Monte Carlo sampler that combines a modified Nosé–Poincaré Hamiltonian with Riemannian preconditioning. Its motivation joins several concerns: effective exploration, sampling from the canonical ensemble, and stability when stochastic gradients introduce noise. The authors seek dynamics that address these concerns within a Hamiltonian framework.

Their modified dynamics include corrections associated with the Riemannian manifold. The resulting symplectic algorithm samples from the canonical ensemble and uses structural information in the preconditioning matrices to traverse parameter space efficiently. This connects the geometry used to guide movement with the dynamics governing the sampling procedure.

For large-data settings, the authors also propose a stochastic version with additional Hamiltonian terms that correct for stochastic-gradient noise. This directly addresses the potentially destabilizing effect identified in their motivation. Experiments show strong performance on synthetic datasets and high-dimensional topic-modeling problems based on Poisson factor analysis. The contribution is both a geometry-aware sampling construction and a noise-corrected variant, with empirical support in the reported sampling applications.
summary.tldr: A modified Hamiltonian sampler combines Riemannian geometry with canonical-ensemble sampling and a stochastic-gradient noise correction.

title: Robust Monte Carlo Sampling using Riemannian Nosé-Poincaré Hamiltonian Dynamics

abstract: We present spectral methods of moments for learning sequential models from a single trajectory, in stark contrast with the classical literature that assumes the availability of multiple i.i.d. trajectories. Our approach leverages an efficient SVD-based learning algorithm for weighted automata and provides the first rigorous analysis for learning many important models using dependent data. We state and analyze the algorithm under three increasingly difficult scenarios: probabilistic automata, stochastic weighted automata, and reactive predictive state representations controlled by a finite-state policy. Our proofs include novel tools for studying mixing properties of stochastic weighted automata.

We state and analyze the algorithm under three increasingly difficult scenarios: probabilistic automata, stochastic weighted automata, and reactive predictive state representations controlled by a finite-state policy. Our proofs include novel tools for studying mixing properties of stochastic weighted automata.

paragraphs: Learning a sequential model from one trajectory means working with observations that depend on one another. This differs from the classical assumption that multiple independent, identically distributed trajectories are available. The paper develops spectral methods of moments for this single-trajectory setting, addressing the dependence within the data directly in its analysis.

The approach builds on an efficient learning algorithm for weighted automata based on singular value decomposition. The authors state and analyze it across three increasingly difficult settings: probabilistic automata, stochastic weighted automata, and reactive predictive state representations controlled by a finite-state policy. This progression extends the analysis from sequential probabilistic models to a setting where a policy influences the observed process.

The proofs introduce tools for studying the mixing properties of stochastic weighted automata. These properties are relevant to understanding how dependence persists along a trajectory. The main contribution is a rigorous foundation for learning several important sequential model classes from dependent data, broadening the circumstances in which spectral learning can be justified.
summary.tldr: Spectral methods learn sequential models from one dependent trajectory, with rigorous analysis extending to finite-state policy control.

title: Spectral Learning from a Single Trajectory under Finite-State Policies

abstract: We consider the problem of approximating a given matrix by a low-rank matrix so as to minimize the entrywise $\ell_p$-approximation error, for any $p \geq 1$; the case $p = 2$ is the classical SVD problem. We obtain the first provably good approximation algorithms for this robust version of low-rank approximation that work for every value of $p$. Our algorithms are simple, easy to implement, work well in practice, and illustrate interesting tradeoffs between the approximation quality, the running time, and the rank of the approximating matrix.

Our algorithms are simple, easy to implement, work well in practice, and illustrate interesting tradeoffs between the approximation quality, the running time, and the rank of the approximating matrix.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to replace a matrix with a simpler, low-rank matrix while controlling the errors in its individual entries. It measures those errors using an entrywise ℓp objective, allowing any p of at least one. The familiar singular value decomposition problem appears as the special case p = 2, placing the work within a broader family of approximation problems.

The authors provide approximation algorithms with provable quality guarantees across this entire range of p. Their stated novelty is obtaining the first such algorithms that work for every value in the specified range. The guarantee concerns how well the algorithms approximate the objective; the abstract does not claim that they always find an exact optimum.

The algorithms also expose tradeoffs among approximation quality, computation time, and the rank of the matrix they produce. These competing quantities make the contribution more than a single accuracy result: they describe different ways to balance simplicity and computational effort. The authors report that the methods are straightforward to implement and perform well in practice.
summary.tldr: The paper gives provably good low-rank approximation algorithms for every entrywise ℓp objective with p ≥ 1, exposing tradeoffs in quality, runtime, and rank.

title: Algorithms for $\ell_p$ Low-Rank Approximation

abstract: Bandit methods for black-box optimisation, such as Bayesian optimisation, are used in a variety of applications including hyper-parameter tuning and experiment design. Recently, multi-fidelity methods have garnered considerable attention since function evaluations have become increasingly expensive in such applications. Multi-fidelity methods use cheap approximations to the function of interest to speed up the overall optimisation process. However, most multi-fidelity methods assume only a finite number of approximations. On the other hand, in many practical applications, a continuous spectrum of approximations might be available. For instance, when tuning an expensive neural network, one might choose to approximate the cross validation performance using less data $N$ and/or few training iterations $T$. Here, the approximations are best viewed as arising out of a continuous two dimensional space $(N,T)$. In this work, we develop a Bayesian optimisation method, BOCA, for this setting. We characterise its theoretical properties and show that it achieves better regret than than strategies which ignore the approximations. BOCA outperforms several other baselines in synthetic and real experiments.

paragraphs: Black-box optimization becomes expensive when every evaluation requires substantial computation or experimentation. Multi-fidelity methods reduce this burden by using cheaper approximations of the desired function. This paper addresses a setting where approximation quality is adjustable across a continuous space, rather than restricted to a finite menu of choices.

For neural-network tuning, the abstract illustrates this space with the amount of training data and the number of training iterations. Changing either quantity changes the approximation used to assess a candidate configuration. BOCA, the proposed Bayesian optimization method, is designed for this richer setting, where approximation choices have multiple adjustable dimensions.

The authors characterize BOCA theoretically and establish better regret than strategies that ignore the available approximations. They also report that BOCA outperforms several baselines in synthetic and real experiments. These findings support treating the approximation space as part of the optimization problem itself. The central contribution is a method that can use a spectrum of cheaper evaluations to improve the search for a good solution to the expensive target problem.
summary.tldr: BOCA uses continuously adjustable approximations to improve Bayesian optimization of expensive black-box functions.

title: Multi-fidelity Bayesian Optimisation with Continuous Approximations

abstract: How many samples are sufficient to guarantee that the eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix are close to those of the actual covariance matrix? For a wide family of distributions, including distributions with finite second moment and sub-gaussian distributions supported in a centered Euclidean ball, we prove that the inner product between eigenvectors of the sample and actual covariance matrices decreases proportionally to the respective eigenvalue distance and the number of samples. Our findings imply non-asymptotic concentration bounds for eigenvectors and eigenvalues and carry strong consequences for the non-asymptotic analysis of PCA and its applications. For instance, they provide conditions for separating components estimated from $O(1)$ samples and show that even few samples can be sufficient to perform dimensionality reduction, especially for low-rank covariances.

paragraphs: Covariance-based dimensionality reduction uses directions estimated from a finite dataset, while the corresponding population directions are unknown. This paper asks when the eigenvectors of a sample covariance matrix reliably reflect those of the actual covariance matrix. The question directly concerns how much data is sufficient for useful estimates.

The authors prove bounds relating inner products between sample and population eigenvectors to sample count and separation between the respective eigenvalues. Greater separation and more samples control overlap across different eigendirections. Their analysis covers a wide family of distributions, including finite-second-moment distributions and sub-Gaussian distributions supported in a centered Euclidean ball.

The resulting concentration bounds apply to both eigenvectors and eigenvalues at finite sample sizes, providing tools for non-asymptotic PCA analysis. In particular, the paper gives conditions under which estimated components can be separated using only a constant number of samples. It also shows that few samples can suffice for dimensionality reduction, especially when the covariance is low rank; these are conditional possibilities rather than universal sample guarantees.
summary.tldr: Finite-sample covariance bounds explain conditions under which PCA directions and useful dimensionality reduction can be recovered from few observations.

title: How Close Are the Eigenvectors of the Sample and Actual Covariance Matrices?

abstract: Understanding how users navigate in a network is of high interest in many applications. We consider a setting where only aggregate node-level traffic is observed and tackle the task of learning edge transition probabilities. We cast it as a preference learning problem, and we study a model where choices follow Luce’s axiom. In this case, the $O(n)$ marginal counts of node visits are a sufficient statistic for the $O(n^2)$ transition probabilities. We show how to make the inference problem well-posed regardless of the network’s structure, and we present ChoiceRank, an iterative algorithm that scales to networks that contains billions of nodes and edges. We apply the model to two clickstream datasets and show that it successfully recovers the transition probabilities using only the network structure and marginal (node-level) traffic data. Finally, we also consider an application to mobility networks and apply the model to one year of rides on New York City’s bicycle-sharing system.

paragraphs: Network traffic summaries may reveal how often each location is visited without revealing which connections people traverse. ChoiceRank addresses the problem of estimating transition probabilities along edges from these aggregate node counts. It formulates navigation as preference learning, using a model in which choices obey Luce’s axiom.

Under that model, the node-level visit counts are sufficient statistics for the transition probabilities. This is a substantial compression: the abstract describes O(n) counts supporting inference about O(n²) probabilities. The claim depends on the choice model; it does not mean that arbitrary patterns of network movement can be recovered from node totals alone.

The paper shows how to make inference well-posed regardless of network structure and introduces an iterative algorithm that scales to billions of nodes and edges. Two clickstream applications demonstrate successful recovery using network structure and node-level traffic. An additional application uses one year of New York City bicycle-sharing rides, extending the investigation from web navigation to mobility.
summary.tldr: ChoiceRank estimates network transition probabilities from aggregate node traffic under a Luce choice model.

title: ChoiceRank: Identifying Preferences from Node Traffic in Networks

abstract: A deep neural network (DNN) consists of a nonlinear transformation from an input to a feature representation, followed by a common softmax linear classifier. Though many efforts have been devoted to designing a proper architecture for nonlinear transformation, little investigation has been done on the classifier part. In this paper, we show that a properly designed classifier can improve robustness to adversarial attacks and lead to better prediction results. Specifically, we define a Max-Mahalanobis distribution (MMD) and theoretically show that if the input distributes as a MMD, the linear discriminant analysis (LDA) classifier will have the best robustness to adversarial examples. We further propose a novel Max-Mahalanobis linear discriminant analysis (MM-LDA) network, which explicitly maps a complicated data distribution in the input space to a MMD in the latent feature space and then applies LDA to make predictions. Our results demonstrate that the MM-LDA networks are significantly more robust to adversarial attacks, and have better performance in class-biased classification.

Our results demonstrate that the MM-LDA networks are significantly more robust to adversarial attacks, and have better performance in class-biased classification.

paragraphs: A neural classifier combines a learned feature transformation with a final decision rule. This paper focuses on that decision rule and asks how its design can improve resistance to adversarial examples. The authors introduce a Max-Mahalanobis distribution and establish a theoretical result: if classifier inputs follow that distribution, linear discriminant analysis has the best adversarial robustness.

The proposed MM-LDA network turns this conditional result into an architectural objective. It explicitly maps a complicated input distribution toward a Max-Mahalanobis distribution in the latent feature space, then applies linear discriminant analysis to classify those features. The feature representation and final classifier are therefore designed around the same distributional target.

The reported results show significantly greater robustness to adversarial attacks and better performance in class-biased classification. These findings support attention to the classifier component when designing robust neural networks. The theoretical optimum remains tied to its distributional condition, while the network’s practical value is demonstrated through the reported robustness and classification results.
summary.tldr: MM-LDA shapes learned features around a distribution with a conditional robustness guarantee for its final classifier.

title: Max-Mahalanobis Linear Discriminant Analysis Networks

abstract: Categorical distributions are ubiquitous in machine learning, e.g., in classification, language models, and recommendation systems. However, when the number of possible outcomes is very large, using categorical distributions becomes computationally expensive, as the complexity scales linearly with the number of outcomes. To address this problem, we propose augment and reduce (A&R), a method to alleviate the computational complexity. A&R uses two ideas: latent variable augmentation and stochastic variational inference. It maximizes a lower bound on the marginal likelihood of the data. Unlike existing methods which are specific to softmax, A&R is more general and is amenable to other categorical models, such as multinomial probit. On several large-scale classification problems, we show that A&R provides a tighter bound on the marginal likelihood and has better predictive performance than existing approaches.

paragraphs: Categorical models assign probabilities to discrete outcomes, such as classes, words, or recommended items. When the outcome set becomes very large, their computational cost becomes a bottleneck because it grows linearly with the number of possibilities. This paper introduces augment and reduce, or A&R, to ease that computational burden.

A&R combines latent variable augmentation with stochastic variational inference. The augmentation introduces additional hidden variables into the modeling approach, while variational inference provides a tractable learning objective: a lower bound on the data's marginal likelihood. Training seeks to improve this bound instead of directly handling the original likelihood in its expensive form.

The method also broadens applicability beyond approaches designed specifically for softmax, extending to categorical models such as multinomial probit. Across several large-scale classification problems, the authors report a tighter likelihood bound and better predictions than existing approaches. The findings therefore concern both the quality of the approximation used during learning and its usefulness for classification.
summary.tldr: A&R combines latent variables and stochastic variational inference to make large categorical models more tractable while improving reported classification performance.

title: Augment and Reduce: Stochastic Inference for Large Categorical Distributions

abstract: We consider optimization problems in which the objective requires an inner loop with many steps or is the limit of a sequence of increasingly costly approximations. Meta-learning, training recurrent neural networks, and optimization of the solutions to differential equations are all examples of optimization problems with this character. In such problems, it can be expensive to compute the objective function value and its gradient, but truncating the loop or using less accurate approximations can induce biases that damage the overall solution. We propose randomized telescope (RT) gradient estimators, which represent the objective as the sum of a telescoping series and sample linear combinations of terms to provide cheap unbiased gradient estimates. We identify conditions under which RT estimators achieve optimization convergence rates independent of the length of the loop or the required accuracy of the approximation. We also derive a method for tuning RT estimators online to maximize a lower bound on the expected decrease in loss per unit of computation. We evaluate our adaptive RT estimators on a range of applications including meta-optimization of learning rates, variational inference of ODE parameters, and training an LSTM to model long sequences.

paragraphs: Some optimization objectives require a long inner computation or increasingly accurate approximations to a limiting quantity. Examples include meta-learning, recurrent network training, and optimizing differential equation solutions. Computing full gradients can be expensive, while simply stopping early can introduce bias that harms the eventual solution. The paper seeks a cheaper gradient without that truncation bias.

Randomized telescope estimators express the objective through a telescoping series, whose successive terms account for changes between approximations. They sample linear combinations of those terms to produce inexpensive, unbiased gradient estimates. The authors identify conditions under which optimization convergence rates do not depend on inner-loop length or the required approximation accuracy.

The method also adapts its estimators during optimization, maximizing a lower bound on expected loss reduction per unit of computation. Evaluations cover learning-rate meta-optimization, variational inference of differential equation parameters, and LSTM training on long sequences. The central contribution is a conditional route to efficient optimization without replacing the intended gradient with a systematically biased shortcut.
summary.tldr: Randomized telescoping sums provide cheap unbiased gradients for expensive iterative objectives, with conditional convergence guarantees and online adaptation.

title: Efficient optimization of loops and limits with randomized telescoping sums

abstract: Dealing with high variance is a significant challenge in model-free reinforcement learning (RL). Existing methods are unreliable, exhibiting high variance in performance from run to run using different initializations/seeds. Focusing on problems arising in continuous control, we propose a functional regularization approach to augmenting model-free RL. In particular, we regularize the behavior of the deep policy to be similar to a policy prior, i.e., we regularize in function space. We show that functional regularization yields a bias-variance trade-off, and propose an adaptive tuning strategy to optimize this trade-off. When the policy prior has control-theoretic stability guarantees, we further show that this regularization approximately preserves those stability guarantees throughout learning. We validate our approach empirically on a range of settings, and demonstrate significantly reduced variance, guaranteed dynamic stability, and more efficient learning than deep RL alone.

In particular, we regularize the behavior of the deep policy to be similar to a policy prior, i.e., we regularize in function space. paragraphs: Model-free reinforcement learning can produce substantially different results across runs with different initializations or random seeds. This paper addresses that variability in continuous control by encouraging a learned policy to behave similarly to a policy prior. The regularization acts on the policy's behavior, described as function-space regularization, rather than merely constraining its numerical parameters.

The authors show that this introduces a bias-variance trade-off. Guidance from the prior can reduce variability, while also influencing which behavior the learner favors. They propose an adaptive tuning strategy to manage that trade-off as learning proceeds, making the strength of the prior's influence part of the learning approach.

The stability result has a specific condition: when the prior policy has control-theoretic stability guarantees, regularization approximately preserves those guarantees throughout learning. Across their empirical settings, the authors report significantly lower variance and more efficient learning than deep reinforcement learning alone, alongside dynamic stability. The contribution therefore connects reproducibility of learning outcomes with prior control knowledge, while retaining the stated qualification on stability preservation.
summary.tldr: Regularizing learned control policies toward a prior reduces performance variability and can approximately preserve the prior's stability guarantees.

title: Control Regularization for Reduced Variance Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We consider the decentralized exploration problem: a set of players collaborate to identify the best arm by asynchronously interacting with the same stochastic environment. The objective is to insure privacy in the best arm identification problem between asynchronous, collaborative, and thrifty players. In the context of a digital service, we advocate that this decentralized approach allows a good balance between conflicting interests: the providers optimize their services, while protecting privacy of users and saving resources. We define the privacy level as the amount of information an adversary could infer by intercepting all the messages concerning a single user. We provide a generic algorithm DECENTRALIZED ELIMINATION, which uses any best arm identification algorithm as a subroutine. We prove that this algorithm insures privacy, with a low communication cost, and that in comparison to the lower bound of the best arm identification problem, its sample complexity suffers from a penalty depending on the inverse of the probability of the most frequent players. Then, thanks to the genericity of the approach, we extend the proposed algorithm to the non-stationary bandits. Finally, experiments illustrate and complete the analysis.

paragraphs: This paper studies how multiple players can collaboratively identify the best option in a stochastic environment while acting asynchronously. The players need to share useful information without communicating excessively or exposing too much about an individual. The motivating tradeoff is between improving a digital service, protecting users, and conserving resources.

The authors define privacy through the information an adversary could infer after intercepting all messages concerning one user. Their algorithm, DECENTRALIZED ELIMINATION, wraps an existing best-arm identification algorithm rather than requiring a particular underlying procedure. This generic construction makes the collaboration mechanism usable with different best-arm identification methods.

The analysis proves privacy under the paper's definition and a low communication cost. It also identifies a sample-complexity penalty relative to the best-arm identification lower bound, depending on the inverse probability of the most frequent players. Thus, participation patterns enter the learning cost. The authors further extend the approach to non-stationary bandits, where the environment changes, and use experiments to illustrate and supplement the analysis.
summary.tldr: DECENTRALIZED ELIMINATION enables asynchronous best-arm identification with privacy guarantees, low communication, and a participation-dependent sampling penalty.

title: Decentralized Exploration in Multi-Armed Bandits

abstract: Most modern text-to-speech architectures use a WaveNet vocoder for synthesizing high-fidelity waveform audio, but there have been limitations, such as high inference time, in practical applications due to its ancestral sampling scheme. The recently suggested Parallel WaveNet and ClariNet has achieved real-time audio synthesis capability by incorporating inverse autoregressive flow (IAF) for parallel sampling. However, these approaches require a two-stage training pipeline with a well-trained teacher network and can only produce natural sound by using probability distillation along with heavily-engineered auxiliary loss terms. We propose FloWaveNet, a flow-based generative model for raw audio synthesis. FloWaveNet requires only a single-stage training procedure and a single maximum likelihood loss, without any additional auxiliary terms, and it is inherently parallel due to the characteristics of generative flow. The model can efficiently sample raw audio in real-time, with clarity comparable to previous two-stage parallel models. The code and samples for all models, including our FloWaveNet, are available on GitHub.

paragraphs: Generating high-fidelity waveform audio can be slow when synthesis follows an ancestral sampling procedure. Earlier parallel approaches, including Parallel WaveNet and ClariNet, enable real-time synthesis but require a trained teacher, a second training stage, and additional loss terms. FloWaveNet targets both synthesis speed and the complexity of that training pipeline.

The proposed model uses a generative flow for raw audio. Its structure permits parallel sampling, and training uses a single maximum-likelihood objective in one stage. No auxiliary loss terms are required. This joins two practical properties in one model: parallel waveform generation and a training procedure that does not depend on the two-stage teacher-based setup described in the abstract.

The authors report efficient real-time sampling with audio clarity comparable to earlier two-stage parallel models. The stated outcome is therefore comparable clarity alongside a simpler training procedure, rather than a claim of universally superior sound quality. By making real-time synthesis compatible with a single training objective, FloWaveNet offers a different route to practical raw-audio generation.
summary.tldr: FloWaveNet generates raw audio in real time using a parallel flow model trained in one stage with a single likelihood objective.

title: FloWaveNet : A Generative Flow for Raw Audio

abstract: The well known domain shift issue causes model performance to degrade when deployed to a new target domain with different statistics to training. Domain adaptation techniques alleviate this, but need some instances from the target domain to drive adaptation. Domain generalisation is the recently topical problem of learning a model that generalises to unseen domains out of the box, and various approaches aim to train a domain-invariant feature extractor, typically by adding some manually designed losses. In this work, we propose a learning to learn approach, where the auxiliary loss that helps generalisation is itself learned. Beyond conventional domain generalisation, we consider a more challenging setting of heterogeneous domain generalisation, where the unseen domains do not share label space with the seen ones, and the goal is to train a feature representation that is useful off-the-shelf for novel data and novel categories. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that our method outperforms state-of-the-art solutions in both settings.

paragraphs: A model can lose accuracy when deployed on data whose statistics differ from its training data. Domain generalization aims to prepare a model for unseen domains without needing target-domain examples to drive adaptation. Many approaches encourage broadly useful features by adding manually designed auxiliary losses during training.

This paper instead learns the auxiliary loss itself through a learning-to-learn approach. The aim is to discover a training signal that helps the feature representation generalize. This moves part of the design problem from selecting a fixed loss by hand to learning how feature training should be guided.

The authors also study heterogeneous domain generalization, where unseen domains contain categories outside the label spaces of the training domains. Here the desired output is a feature representation useful for both new data and new categories. Experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art methods in conventional and heterogeneous settings. These results support the learned-loss approach for representation transfer under both kinds of change, rather than only shifts among familiar categories.
summary.tldr: Feature-Critic learns an auxiliary training loss that improves feature generalization to unseen domains, including domains with new categories.

title: Feature-Critic Networks for Heterogeneous Domain Generalization

abstract: We study high-dimensional estimators with the trimmed $\ell_1$ penalty, which leaves the h largest parameter entries penalty-free. While optimization techniques for this nonconvex penalty have been studied, the statistical properties have not yet been analyzed. We present the first statistical analyses for M-estimation, and characterize support recovery, $\ell_\infty$ and $\ell_2$ error of the trimmed $\ell_1$ estimates as a function of the trimming parameter h. Our results show different regimes based on how h compares to the true support size. Our second contribution is a new algorithm for the trimmed regularization problem, which has the same theoretical convergence rate as difference of convex (DC) algorithms, but in practice is faster and finds lower objective values. Empirical evaluation of $\ell_1$ trimming for sparse linear regression and graphical model estimation indicate that trimmed $\ell_1$ can outperform vanilla $\ell_1$ and non-convex alternatives. Our last contribution is to show that the trimmed penalty is beneficial beyond M-estimation, and yields promising results for two deep learning tasks: input structures recovery and network sparsification.

Our results show different regimes based on how h compares to the true support size. Our second contribution is a new algorithm for the trimmed regularization problem, which has the same theoretical convergence rate as difference of convex (DC) algorithms, but in practice is faster and finds lower objective values. Empirical evaluation of $\ell_1$ trimming for sparse linear regression and graphical model estimation indicate that trimmed $\ell_1$ can outperform vanilla $\ell_1$ and non-convex alternatives. Our last contribution is to show that the trimmed penalty is beneficial beyond M-estimation, and yields promising results for two deep learning tasks: input structures recovery and network sparsification.

paragraphs: The trimmed ℓ1 penalty changes sparse estimation by leaving the h largest parameter entries unpenalized. This paper studies how that choice affects statistical behavior, addressing a gap left by earlier optimization-focused work. Its analysis covers recovery of the nonzero parameter locations and estimation errors measured in the ℓ∞ and ℓ2 norms.

The results distinguish regimes according to how h compares with the true number of nonzero parameters. This makes the trimming parameter central to understanding the estimator. The authors also introduce an optimization algorithm with the same theoretical convergence rate as difference-of-convex algorithms, while reporting faster practical execution and lower attained objective values.

Experiments in sparse linear regression and graphical model estimation indicate that trimming can outperform ordinary ℓ1 regularization and nonconvex alternatives. The paper additionally reports promising results for recovering input structure and sparsifying deep networks. Together, the contributions connect statistical analysis, an optimization procedure, and applications, while treating the empirical advantages as possibilities demonstrated in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes trimmed ℓ1 regularization, develops a practical optimizer, and reports benefits for sparse estimation and two deep learning tasks.

title: Trimming the $\ell_1$ Regularizer: Statistical Analysis, Optimization, and Applications to Deep Learning

abstract: Modern convolutional networks are not shift-invariant, as small input shifts or translations can cause drastic changes in the output. Commonly used downsampling methods, such as max-pooling, strided-convolution, and average-pooling, ignore the sampling theorem. The well-known signal processing fix is anti-aliasing by low-pass filtering before downsampling. However, simply inserting this module into deep networks leads to performance degradation; as a result, it is seldomly used today. We show that when integrated correctly, it is compatible with existing architectural components, such as max-pooling. The technique is general and can be incorporated across layer types and applications, such as image classification and conditional image generation. In addition to increased shift-invariance, we also observe, surprisingly, that anti-aliasing boosts accuracy in ImageNet classification, across several commonly-used architectures. This indicates that anti-aliasing serves as effective regularization. Our results demonstrate that this classical signal processing technique has been undeservingly overlooked in modern deep networks.

This paper connects that instability to common downsampling operations, including pooling and strided convolutions, that overlook the sampling theorem. It revisits the signal-processing remedy of applying a low-pass filter before reducing spatial resolution.

The central issue is how to integrate this anti-aliasing step into a neural network. Simply inserting a filtering module can hurt performance. The paper shows that a suitable integration is compatible with existing components such as max-pooling, and that the technique can be used across layer types and applications, including image classification and conditional image generation.

The reported results show increased shift-invariance and improved ImageNet classification accuracy across several commonly used architectures. The authors interpret the accuracy gains as evidence that anti-aliasing provides effective regularization. The contribution is therefore both greater stability under image translations and an observed improvement in predictive performance through a carefully incorporated classical signal-processing technique.
summary.tldr: Properly integrated anti-aliasing makes convolutional networks more stable under image shifts and improves ImageNet accuracy across several tested architectures.

title: Making Convolutional Networks Shift-Invariant Again

abstract: In standard classification problems, the assumption is that the entity making the decision (the principal ) has access to all the samples. However, in many contexts, she either does not have direct access to the samples, or can inspect only a limited set of samples and does not know which are the most relevant ones. In such cases, she must rely on another party (the agent ) to either provide the samples or point out the most relevant ones. If the agent has a different objective, then the principal cannot trust the submitted samples to be representative. She must set a policy for how she makes decisions, keeping in mind the agent’s incentives. In this paper, we introduce a theoretical framework for this problem and provide key structural and computational results.

paragraphs: Standard classification often assumes the decision-maker can access all relevant samples. This paper considers situations where access is indirect or inspection capacity is limited. The decision-maker, called the principal, must rely on another party, called the agent, either to supply samples or to identify which samples deserve attention.

The difficulty arises when the agent's objective differs from the principal's. In that case, the selected evidence may reflect what benefits the agent rather than what represents the available information. The principal therefore needs a decision policy that accounts for the agent's incentives. Sample selection becomes part of the decision problem itself, rather than a neutral step that happens before classification.

The paper introduces a theoretical framework for this setting and establishes structural and computational results. Its contribution is to make strategic control over evidence an explicit object of analysis. This framing matters whenever a decision depends on samples chosen by someone with a potentially different goal, because the policy must consider how those samples are selected.
summary.tldr: A theoretical framework studies classification when another party strategically selects the samples shown to the decision-maker.

title: When Samples Are Strategically Selected

abstract: In computer vision applications, such as domain adaptation (DA), few shot learning (FSL) and zero-shot learning (ZSL), we encounter new objects and environments, for which insufficient examples exist to allow for training “models from scratch,” and methods that adapt existing models, trained on the presented training environment, to the new scenario are required. We propose a novel visual attribute encoding method that encodes each image as a low-dimensional probability vector composed of prototypical part-type probabilities. The prototypes are learnt to be representative of all training data. At test-time we utilize this encoding as an input to a classifier. At test-time we freeze the encoder and only learn/adapt the classifier component to limited annotated labels in FSL; new semantic attributes in ZSL. We conduct extensive experiments on benchmark datasets. Our method outperforms state-of-art methods trained for the specific contexts (ZSL, FSL, DA).

paragraphs: The paper addresses visual recognition when new objects or environments provide too little labeled data to train a model from scratch. It brings together domain adaptation, few-shot learning, and zero-shot learning through a common image representation. The central aim is to make knowledge learned from the training environment usable in a new setting.

Each image is encoded as a compact probability vector whose entries describe prototypical part types. These prototypes are learned to represent the training data as a whole. A classifier then operates on this encoding. At test time, the encoder stays fixed, so adaptation occurs in the classifier rather than requiring the image representation itself to be relearned.

For few-shot learning, the classifier uses the limited available labels; for zero-shot learning, it uses new semantic attributes. This division gives the same representation a role across different forms of scarce supervision. Benchmark experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art methods specialized for domain adaptation, few-shot learning, and zero-shot learning, supporting the usefulness of the shared encoding across the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A fixed encoding of prototypical visual parts supports classifier adaptation with few labels or semantic attributes across several recognition settings.

title: Learning Classifiers for Target Domain with Limited or No Labels

abstract: Variational inference (VI) and Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) are approximate posterior inference algorithms that are often said to have complementary strengths, with VI being fast but biased and MCMC being slower but asymptotically unbiased. In this paper, we analyze gradient-based MCMC and VI procedures and find theoretical and empirical evidence that these procedures are not as different as one might think. In particular, a close examination of the Fokker-Planck equation that governs the Langevin dynamics (LD) MCMC procedure reveals that LD implicitly follows a gradient flow that corresponds to a variational inference procedure based on optimizing a nonparametric normalizing flow. This result suggests that the transient bias of LD (due to the Markov chain not having burned in) may track that of VI (due to the optimizer not having converged), up to differences due to VI’s asymptotic bias and parameterization. Empirically, we find that the transient biases of these algorithms (and their momentum-accelerated counterparts) do evolve similarly. This suggests that practitioners with a limited time budget may get more accurate results by running an MCMC procedure (even if it’s far from burned in) than a VI procedure, as long as the variance of the MCMC estimator can be dealt with (e.g., by running many parallel chains).

paragraphs: Variational inference and Markov chain Monte Carlo are often presented as contrasting ways to approximate a posterior distribution: one optimizes a tractable approximation, while the other samples through a chain. This paper investigates a closer relationship between their gradient-based forms, focusing on how their errors evolve before either procedure has settled.

Analyzing the Fokker-Planck equation for Langevin dynamics, the authors show that its probability distribution follows a gradient flow corresponding to variational inference with a nonparametric normalizing flow. This connection suggests that bias from an incompletely run sampling chain may evolve similarly to bias from unfinished variational optimization. Differences from the variational parameterization and its eventual approximation bias still matter.

Experiments find similar evolution of these transient biases, including for momentum-accelerated versions. The practical implication is conditional: with limited computation time, an MCMC procedure might produce more accurate estimates even before burn-in is complete, provided its estimator variance can be controlled. Running many parallel chains is offered as one way to address that variance.
summary.tldr: Langevin sampling and variational inference share a gradient-flow connection that helps explain their similar transient biases.

title: Black-Box Variational Inference as a Parametric Approximation to Langevin Dynamics

abstract: Implicit stochastic models, where the data-generation distribution is intractable but sampling is possible, are ubiquitous in the natural sciences. The models typically have free parameters that need to be inferred from data collected in scientific experiments. A fundamental question is how to design the experiments so that the collected data are most useful. The field of Bayesian experimental design advocates that, ideally, we should choose designs that maximise the mutual information (MI) between the data and the parameters. For implicit models, however, this approach is severely hampered by the high computational cost of computing posteriors and maximising MI, in particular when we have more than a handful of design variables to optimise. In this paper, we propose a new approach to Bayesian experimental design for implicit models that leverages recent advances in neural MI estimation to deal with these issues. We show that training a neural network to maximise a lower bound on MI allows us to jointly determine the optimal design and the posterior. Simulation studies illustrate that this gracefully extends Bayesian experimental design for implicit models to higher design dimensions.

paragraphs: Scientific models often allow simulated observations even when the probability of a particular observation cannot be evaluated tractably. Experiments must still be chosen to reveal the model's unknown parameters. Bayesian experimental design expresses this goal through mutual information: designs should make the resulting data informative about those parameters.

For these implicit models, calculating posterior distributions and optimizing mutual information can be expensive, especially when many experimental choices must be adjusted together. The paper proposes using a neural network to estimate information through a lower bound on mutual information. Training against this bound allows experimental design and posterior determination to be handled jointly.

Simulation studies show that the approach extends Bayesian experimental design to higher-dimensional design spaces. The contribution is a way to connect the selection of informative experiments with inference about the parameters those experiments investigate. The optimization uses an information bound, so its computational approach should be understood through that objective rather than as direct, unrestricted evaluation of mutual information.
summary.tldr: Neural mutual-information estimation jointly supports experimental design and posterior inference for models that can be simulated but have intractable distributions.

title: Bayesian Experimental Design for Implicit Models by Mutual Information Neural Estimation

abstract: In this work, we propose WaveFlow, a small-footprint generative flow for raw audio, which is directly trained with maximum likelihood. It handles the long-range structure of 1-D waveform with a dilated 2-D convolutional architecture, while modeling the local variations using expressive autoregressive functions. WaveFlow provides a unified view of likelihood-based models for 1-D data, including WaveNet and WaveGlow as special cases. It generates high-fidelity speech as WaveNet, while synthesizing several orders of magnitude faster as it only requires a few sequential steps to generate very long waveforms with hundreds of thousands of time-steps. Furthermore, it can significantly reduce the likelihood gap that has existed between autoregressive models and flow-based models for efficient synthesis. Finally, our small-footprint WaveFlow has only 5.91M parameters, which is 15{\texttimes} smaller than WaveGlow. It can generate 22.05 kHz high-fidelity audio 42.6{\texttimes} faster than real-time (at a rate of 939.3 kHz) on a V100 GPU without engineered inference kernels.

paragraphs: WaveFlow is a compact generative model for raw audio trained directly by maximum likelihood. It combines a dilated two-dimensional convolutional architecture for long-range waveform structure with autoregressive functions for local variation. This design addresses both broad temporal organization and fine changes in the audio signal.

The framework includes WaveNet and WaveGlow as special cases, providing a shared perspective on likelihood-based models for one-dimensional data. WaveFlow needs only a few sequential generation steps even for waveforms with hundreds of thousands of time steps. The authors report speech fidelity comparable to WaveNet with synthesis several orders of magnitude faster, and a substantial reduction in the likelihood gap between autoregressive and efficient flow-based models.

These findings connect compact model size, rapid generation, and high-fidelity speech within the evaluated setup, illustrating the benefits of combining flow-based generation with expressive local autoregressive modeling.
summary.tldr: WaveFlow combines long-range convolutions and local autoregressive modeling to generate high-fidelity speech quickly with a compact flow-based model.

title: WaveFlow: A Compact Flow-based Model for Raw Audio

abstract: Coastal communities are at high risk of natural hazards due to unremitting global warming and sea level rise. Both the catastrophic impacts, e.g., tidal flooding and storm surges, and the long-term impacts, e.g., beach erosion, inundation of low lying areas, and saltwater intrusion into aquifers, cause economic, social, and ecological losses. Creating policies through appropriate modeling of the responses of stakeholders, such as government, businesses, and residents, to climate change and sea level rise scenarios can help to reduce these losses. In this work, we propose a Markov decision process (MDP) formulation for an agent (government) which interacts with the environment (nature and residents) to deal with the impacts of climate change, in particular sea level rise. Through theoretical analysis we show that a reasonable government’s policy on infrastructure development ought to be proactive and based on detected sea levels in order to minimize the expected total cost, as opposed to a straightforward government that reacts to observed costs from nature. We also provide a deep reinforcement learning-based scenario planning tool considering different government and resident types in terms of cooperation, and different sea level rise projections by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

paragraphs: Coastal adaptation involves more than predicting physical damage: government decisions interact with residents’ responses as sea levels change. This paper models that interaction as a Markov decision process. The government acts as the decision maker, while nature and residents form the environment with which it interacts. The formulation focuses on the consequences of climate change, particularly sea level rise.

The theoretical analysis compares approaches to infrastructure development through their expected total costs. Within the model, it supports proactive decisions based on detected sea levels over a straightforward strategy that reacts to costs already imposed by nature. The distinction matters because observed environmental conditions can inform investment before the costs driving a reactive policy have materialized.

The authors also provide a scenario planning tool based on deep reinforcement learning. It incorporates different levels of cooperation among government and resident types, alongside NOAA sea level rise projections. Together, the model and tool connect physical scenarios with stakeholder behavior, allowing infrastructure policies to be studied as continuing decisions within a changing social and environmental system.
summary.tldr: An MDP model supports proactive coastal infrastructure decisions based on sea levels and provides a reinforcement learning tool for exploring adaptation scenarios.

title: A Markov Decision Process Model for Socio-Economic Systems Impacted by Climate Change

abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) variants approximately minimize divergences between the model and the data distribution using a discriminator. Wasserstein GANs (WGANs) enjoy superior empirical performance, however, unlike in f-GANs, the discriminator does not provide an estimate for the ratio between model and data densities, which is useful in applications such as inverse reinforcement learning. To overcome this limitation, we propose an new training objective where we additionally optimize over a set of importance weights over the generated samples. By suitably constraining the feasible set of importance weights, we obtain a family of objectives which includes and generalizes the original f-GAN and WGAN objectives. We show that a natural extension outperforms WGANs while providing density ratios as in f-GAN, and demonstrate empirical success on distribution modeling, density ratio estimation and image generation.

Wasserstein GANs (WGANs) enjoy superior empirical performance, however, unlike in f-GANs, the discriminator does not provide an estimate for the ratio between model and data densities, which is useful in applications such as inverse reinforcement learning. To overcome this limitation, we propose an new training objective where we additionally optimize over a set of importance weights over the generated samples. By suitably constraining the feasible set of importance weights, we obtain a family of objectives which includes and generalizes the original f-GAN and WGAN objectives. We show that a natural extension outperforms WGANs while providing density ratios as in f-GAN, and demonstrate empirical success on distribution modeling, density ratio estimation and image generation.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial networks learn by comparing a generated distribution with the data distribution through a discriminator. The paper starts from a tradeoff between two families of these models. Wasserstein GANs have strong empirical performance, while f-GANs provide estimates of the ratio between model and data densities. Those ratios are useful beyond generation, including in inverse reinforcement learning.

The authors introduce a training objective that also optimizes importance weights assigned to generated samples. These weights become part of the optimization rather than leaving the objective fixed in its original form. By changing the constraints on which weights are permitted, the approach produces a family of objectives that includes both the original f-GAN and Wasserstein GAN objectives.

This construction connects the two families within a common framework and supports extensions beyond either original objective. The authors report that a natural extension outperforms Wasserstein GANs while retaining density-ratio estimation. Experiments cover distribution modeling, density-ratio estimation, and image generation. The stated benefit is therefore both a unifying formulation and an empirically successful way to combine useful capabilities.
summary.tldr: Optimizing weights on generated samples connects f-GAN and Wasserstein GAN objectives while supporting strong generation and density-ratio estimation.

title: Bridging the Gap Between f-GANs and Wasserstein GANs

abstract: Can deep neural networks learn to solve any task, and in particular problems of high complexity? This question attracts a lot of interest, with recent works tackling computationally hard tasks such as the traveling salesman problem and satisfiability. In this work we offer a different perspective on this question. Given the common assumption that NP != coNP we prove that any polynomial-time sample generator for an NP-hard problem samples, in fact, from an easier sub-problem. We empirically explore a case study, Conjunctive Query Containment, and show how common data generation techniques generate biased data-sets that lead practitioners to over-estimate model accuracy. Our results suggest that machine learning approaches that require training on a dense uniform sampling from the target distribution cannot be used to solve computationally hard problems, the reason being the difficulty of generating sufficiently large and unbiased training sets.
