paragraphs: When neural networks are applied to computationally difficult problems, attention often centers on what the model can learn. This paper examines an earlier obstacle: producing representative training examples. A model may appear successful on an NP-hard task if the procedure that generates its data actually concentrates on an easier part of that task.

Assuming NP is not equal to coNP, the authors prove that any polynomial-time sample generator for an NP-hard problem samples from an easier subproblem. The assumption is central to the stated theorem. The result shifts the discussion toward the computational difficulty of supplying training data, rather than treating data generation as a straightforward prerequisite to learning.

The empirical case study examines Conjunctive Query Containment. Common generation techniques produce biased datasets that lead practitioners to overestimate model accuracy. The authors consequently suggest that methods requiring dense, uniform samples from the target distribution cannot solve computationally hard problems through that route, because generating sufficiently large unbiased datasets is itself an obstacle.
summary.tldr: Under NP ≠ coNP, efficient sample generation for NP-hard problems targets easier subproblems, exposing a potential source of misleading learning results.

title: It’s Not What Machines Can Learn, It’s What We Cannot Teach

abstract: Modeling the time-series of high-dimensional, longitudinal data is important for predicting patient disease progression. However, existing neural network based approaches that learn representations of patient state, while very flexible, are susceptible to overfitting. We propose a deep generative model that makes use of a novel attention-based neural architecture inspired by the physics of how treatments affect disease state. The result is a scalable and accurate model of high-dimensional patient biomarkers as they vary over time. Our proposed model yields significant improvements in generalization and, on real-world clinical data, provides interpretable insights into the dynamics of cancer progression.

The result is a scalable and accurate model of high-dimensional patient biomarkers as they vary over time. paragraphs: Predicting disease progression requires modeling how many patient measurements evolve over time. Neural networks can learn flexible representations of a patient’s state, but that flexibility also makes them susceptible to overfitting. The paper addresses this tension in the modeling of high-dimensional longitudinal data, where the goal is to capture changing patient biomarkers.

The authors propose a deep generative model with an attention-based neural architecture inspired by the physics of treatment effects on disease state. This connects the model’s design to the process being studied: patients’ conditions evolve while treatments affect that evolution. The approach brings this treatment-related structure into a flexible neural model of temporal measurements.

The resulting model is described as scalable and accurate, with significant improvements in generalization. On real clinical data, it also provides interpretable insights into the dynamics of cancer progression. These findings connect two goals of patient-state modeling: making predictions that generalize and producing representations whose behavior can help explain observed disease dynamics.
summary.tldr: A treatment-inspired attention architecture improves generalization in patient time-series modeling and provides interpretable insights into cancer progression.

title: Neural Pharmacodynamic State Space Modeling

abstract: We present and analyze a momentum-based gradient method for training linear classifiers with an exponentially-tailed loss (e.g., the exponential or logistic loss), which maximizes the classification margin on separable data at a rate of O(1/t^2). This contrasts with a rate of O(1/log(t)) for standard gradient descent, and O(1/t) for normalized gradient descent. The momentum-based method is derived via the convex dual of the maximum-margin problem, and specifically by applying Nesterov acceleration to this dual, which manages to result in a simple and intuitive method in the primal. This dual view can also be used to derive a stochastic variant, which performs adaptive non-uniform sampling via the dual variables.
originalAbstract: We present and analyze a momentum-based gradient method for training linear classifiers with an exponentially-tailed loss (e.g., the exponential or logistic loss), which maximizes the classification margin on separable data at a rate of O(1/t^2). This contrasts with a rate of O(1/log(t)) for standard gradient descent, and O(1/t) for normalized gradient descent. The momentum-based method is derived via the convex dual of the maximum-margin problem, and specifically by applying Nesterov acceleration to this dual, which manages to result in a simple and intuitive method in the primal. This dual view can also be used to derive a stochastic variant, which performs adaptive non-uniform sampling via the dual variables.

paragraphs: For linearly separable data, a classifier can correctly divide the classes while leaving different amounts of separation around its decision boundary. Margin maximization seeks the largest such separation. This paper presents a momentum-based gradient method for linear classifiers trained with losses whose tails decay exponentially, including exponential and logistic loss.

The authors establish a margin-maximization rate of O(1/t²), where t counts iterations. They contrast this with O(1/log(t)) for standard gradient descent and O(1/t) for normalized gradient descent. Under the stated separability and loss conditions, the analysis therefore gives a substantially faster rate for approaching the maximum margin, rather than merely showing that the training objective decreases.

The algorithm comes from applying Nesterov acceleration to the convex dual of the maximum-margin problem. Although derived in the dual formulation, it yields a simple momentum method in the original variables. The same viewpoint also produces a stochastic variant whose dual variables guide adaptive, nonuniform sampling, connecting accelerated optimization with the choice of training examples.
summary.tldr: Dual acceleration yields a momentum method with an O(1/t²) margin-maximization rate for separable linear classification with exponentially tailed losses.

title: Fast margin maximization via dual acceleration

abstract: Bilevel optimization has arisen as a powerful tool for many machine learning problems such as meta-learning, hyperparameter optimization, and reinforcement learning. In this paper, we investigate the nonconvex-strongly-convex bilevel optimization problem. For deterministic bilevel optimization, we provide a comprehensive convergence rate analysis for two popular algorithms respectively based on approximate implicit differentiation (AID) and iterative differentiation (ITD). For the AID-based method, we orderwisely improve the previous convergence rate analysis due to a more practical parameter selection as well as a warm start strategy, and for the ITD-based method we establish the first theoretical convergence rate. Our analysis also provides a quantitative comparison between ITD and AID based approaches. For stochastic bilevel optimization, we propose a novel algorithm named stocBiO, which features a sample-efficient hypergradient estimator using efficient Jacobian- and Hessian-vector product computations. We provide the convergence rate guarantee for stocBiO, and show that stocBiO outperforms the best known computational complexities orderwisely with respect to the condition number $\kappa$ and the target accuracy $\epsilon$. We further validate our theoretical results and demonstrate the efficiency of bilevel optimization algorithms by the experiments on meta-learning and hyperparameter optimization.

For the AID-based method, we orderwisely improve the previous convergence rate analysis due to a more practical parameter selection as well as a warm start strategy, and for the ITD-based method we establish the first theoretical convergence rate. Our analysis also provides a quantitative comparison between ITD and AID based approaches. For stochastic bilevel optimization, we propose a novel algorithm named stocBiO, which features a sample-efficient hypergradient estimator using efficient Jacobian- and Hessian-vector product computations. We provide the convergence rate guarantee for stocBiO, and show that stocBiO outperforms the best known computational complexities orderwisely with respect to the condition number $\kappa$ and the target accuracy $\epsilon$. We further validate our theoretical results and demonstrate the efficiency of bilevel optimization algorithms by the experiments on meta-learning and hyperparameter optimization.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves an outer optimization problem whose objective depends on the solution of an inner problem. This structure appears in meta-learning and hyperparameter selection. The paper studies the setting where the outer problem can be nonconvex while the inner problem is strongly convex, providing analysis and algorithm designs specifically for that setting.

For deterministic problems, the authors analyze two ways to compute how inner optimization affects the outer objective: approximate implicit differentiation and differentiation through optimization iterations. Practical parameter choices and reuse of previous solutions improve the known convergence-rate analysis for the implicit approach. The paper also establishes the first convergence rate for the iterative approach and quantitatively compares the two.

For stochastic problems, the authors introduce stocBiO, which estimates the outer gradient using efficient Jacobian-vector and Hessian-vector products. Its guarantees improve the order of known computational complexity bounds in both condition number and target accuracy. Experiments on meta-learning and hyperparameter optimization support the theoretical findings and demonstrate the algorithms’ efficiency.
summary.tldr: Improved analysis and a sample-efficient stochastic algorithm advance bilevel optimization with a nonconvex outer problem and strongly convex inner problem.

title: Bilevel Optimization: Convergence Analysis and Enhanced Design

abstract: Planning, the ability to analyze the structure of a problem in the large and decompose it into interrelated subproblems, is a hallmark of human intelligence. While deep reinforcement learning (RL) has shown great promise for solving relatively straightforward control tasks, it remains an open problem how to best incorporate planning into existing deep RL paradigms to handle increasingly complex environments. One prominent framework, Model-Based RL, learns a world model and plans using step-by-step virtual rollouts. This type of world model quickly diverges from reality when the planning horizon increases, thus struggling at long-horizon planning. How can we learn world models that endow agents with the ability to do temporally extended reasoning? In this work, we propose to learn graph-structured world models composed of sparse, multi-step transitions. We devise a novel algorithm to learn latent landmarks that are scattered (in terms of reachability) across the goal space as the nodes on the graph. In this same graph, the edges are the reachability estimates distilled from Q-functions. On a variety of high-dimensional continuous control tasks ranging from robotic manipulation to navigation, we demonstrate that our method, named L3P, significantly outperforms prior work, and is oftentimes the only method capable of leveraging both the robustness of model-free RL and generalization of graph-search algorithms. We believe our work is an important step towards scalable planning in reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Planning with a learned world model often means predicting one step after another into the future. Errors can accumulate as the planning horizon grows, causing imagined trajectories to diverge from reality. This paper proposes a graph-based world model that represents sparse, multi-step transitions to support reasoning over longer spans.

The method, L3P, learns latent landmarks as graph nodes. These landmarks are spread across the goal space according to reachability, so their placement reflects how goals can be reached. Graph edges contain reachability estimates distilled from Q-functions. Planning can therefore work with connections between landmarks rather than relying entirely on a long chain of one-step predictions.

Across high-dimensional continuous-control tasks involving robotic manipulation and navigation, L3P significantly outperforms prior work. The authors report that it is often the only evaluated method able to combine model-free reinforcement learning’s robustness with graph search’s generalization. The findings support learned landmark graphs as a promising representation for temporally extended planning in the tested environments.
summary.tldr: L3P learns a graph of latent landmarks and multi-step reachability estimates to improve long-horizon planning in continuous-control tasks.

title: World Model as a Graph: Learning Latent Landmarks for Planning

abstract: Multi-label classification tasks such as OCR and multi-object recognition are a major focus of the growing machine learning as a service industry. While many multi-label APIs are available, it is challenging for users to decide which API to use for their own data and budget, due to the heterogeneity in their prices and performance. Recent work has shown how to efficiently select and combine single label APIs to optimize performance and cost. However, its computation cost is exponential in the number of labels, and is not suitable for settings like OCR. In this work, we propose FrugalMCT, a principled framework that adaptively selects the APIs to use for different data in an online fashion while respecting the user’s budget. It allows combining ML APIs’ predictions for any single data point, and selects the best combination based on an accuracy estimator. We run systematic experiments using ML APIs from Google, Microsoft, Amazon, IBM, Tencent, and other providers for tasks including multi-label image classification, scene text recognition, and named entity recognition. Across these tasks, FrugalMCT can achieve over 90% cost reduction while matching the accuracy of the best single API, or up to 8% better accuracy while matching the best API’s cost.

paragraphs: Machine-learning APIs differ in both price and accuracy, making the best choice depend on a user’s data and budget. The problem becomes harder when an input can have many labels, as in text or multi-object recognition. Earlier selection approaches for single-label APIs have computation costs that grow exponentially with the number of labels.

FrugalMCT addresses this problem by choosing APIs adaptively as data arrive, subject to the user’s budget. It can combine predictions from multiple APIs for a single input. An accuracy estimator guides the choice of combination, allowing the framework to make different service choices for different data points.

The authors evaluate services from several providers on multi-label image classification, scene text recognition, and named entity recognition. Across these tasks, they report that FrugalMCT can reduce cost by more than 90% while matching the best single API’s accuracy, or improve accuracy by up to 8% at that API’s cost. These are alternative observed tradeoffs, showing how adaptive selection and combination can improve the usefulness of existing services.
summary.tldr: FrugalMCT adaptively selects and combines classification APIs to improve accuracy-cost tradeoffs within a user’s budget.

title: Efficient Online ML API Selection for Multi-Label Classification Tasks

abstract: In general-sum games the interaction of self-interested learning agents commonly leads to collectively worst-case outcomes, such as defect-defect in the iterated prisoner’s dilemma (IPD). To overcome this, some methods, such as Learning with Opponent-Learning Awareness (LOLA), directly shape the learning process of their opponents. However, these methods are myopic since only a small number of steps can be anticipated, are asymmetric since they treat other agents as naive learners, and require the use of higher-order derivatives, which are calculated through white-box access to an opponent’s differentiable learning algorithm. To address these issues, we propose Model-Free Opponent Shaping (M-FOS). M-FOS learns in a meta-game in which each meta-step is an episode of the underlying game. The meta-state consists of the policies in the underlying game and the meta-policy produces a new policy to be used in the next episode. M-FOS then uses generic model-free optimisation methods to learn meta-policies that accomplish long-horizon opponent shaping. Empirically, M-FOS near-optimally exploits naive learners and other, more sophisticated algorithms from the literature. For example, to the best of our knowledge, it is the first method to learn the well-known ZD extortion strategy in the IPD. In the same settings, M-FOS leads to socially optimal outcomes under meta-self-play. Finally, we show that M-FOS can be scaled to high-dimensional settings.

Opponent-shaping methods try to change this by influencing how other agents learn, but existing approaches can look ahead only a few updates, treat opponents as naive, and require access to their differentiable learning algorithms. Model-Free Opponent Shaping addresses these issues through a meta-game.

Generic model-free optimization then learns how these episode-level choices can shape opponents over longer horizons, avoiding the need to differentiate through an opponent’s learning procedure.

Empirically, M-FOS nearly optimally exploits both naive learners and more sophisticated methods. The authors report learning a zero-determinant extortion strategy in the iterated prisoner’s dilemma, which they describe as a first to their knowledge. In the same settings, meta-self-play produces socially optimal outcomes. They also demonstrate scaling to high-dimensional settings, showing that the framework can support both exploitation and mutually beneficial behavior depending on the interaction.
summary.tldr: M-FOS learns episode-level policy updates that shape opponents over long horizons, producing strong exploitation and socially optimal meta-self-play in the evaluated settings.

title: Model-Free Opponent Shaping

abstract: Selective regression allows abstention from prediction if the confidence to make an accurate prediction is not sufficient. In general, by allowing a reject option, one expects the performance of a regression model to increase at the cost of reducing coverage (i.e., by predicting on fewer samples). However, as we show, in some cases, the performance of a minority subgroup can decrease while we reduce the coverage, and thus selective regression can magnify disparities between different sensitive subgroups. Motivated by these disparities, we propose new fairness criteria for selective regression requiring the performance of every subgroup to improve with a decrease in coverage. We prove that if a feature representation satisfies the sufficiency criterion or is calibrated for mean and variance , then the proposed fairness criteria is met. Further, we introduce two approaches to mitigate the performance disparity across subgroups: (a) by regularizing an upper bound of conditional mutual information under a Gaussian assumption and (b) by regularizing a contrastive loss for conditional mean and conditional variance prediction. The effectiveness of these approaches is demonstrated on synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Selective regression lets a model abstain when it lacks confidence in a numerical prediction. Predicting on fewer examples is usually expected to improve accuracy among those retained. The paper shows that this overall expectation can hide a fairness problem: a minority subgroup’s performance can worsen as coverage decreases, increasing disparities between sensitive groups.

The authors propose fairness criteria requiring every subgroup’s performance to improve as the system becomes more selective. They prove sufficient conditions for meeting these criteria: a feature representation can satisfy the sufficiency criterion, or it can be calibrated for both mean and variance. These results connect subgroup behavior under abstention to properties of the learned representation.

Two proposed interventions aim to reduce the resulting disparities. One regularizes an upper bound on conditional mutual information under a Gaussian assumption. The other uses a contrastive loss for predictions of conditional means and variances. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate their effectiveness. The work makes subgroup performance across coverage levels an explicit objective when designing models that may refuse to predict.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies subgroup harms from selective regression and develops fairness criteria, sufficient conditions, and mitigation methods.

title: Selective Regression under Fairness Criteria

abstract: Coded distributed computation has become common practice for performing gradient descent on large datasets to mitigate stragglers and other faults. This paper proposes a novel algorithm that encodes the partial derivatives themselves and furthermore optimizes the codes by performing lossy compression on the derivative codewords by maximizing the information contained in the codewords while minimizing the information between the codewords. The utility of this application of coding theory is a geometrical consequence of the observed fact in optimization research that noise is tolerable, sometimes even helpful, in gradient descent based learning algorithms since it helps avoid overfitting and local minima. This stands in contrast with much current conventional work on distributed coded computation which focuses on recovering all of the data from the workers. A second further contribution is that the low-weight nature of the coding scheme allows for asynchronous gradient updates since the code can be iteratively decoded; i.e., a worker’s task can immediately be updated into the larger gradient. The directional derivative is always a linear function of the direction vectors; thus, our framework is robust since it can apply linear coding techniques to general machine learning frameworks such as deep neural networks.

paragraphs: Distributed gradient computation must cope with slow workers and other faults. Coding schemes can help, but many approaches focus on recovering all worker data. This paper instead encodes partial derivatives directly and introduces lossy compression into the resulting derivative codewords, focusing on information useful for gradient-based learning.

The compression objective seeks to preserve information within codewords while reducing information shared between them. Its motivation comes from the observation that gradient descent can tolerate noise and that noise can sometimes help avoid overfitting and local minima. This supports allowing some information loss in the coded derivatives rather than treating exact recovery as the only useful outcome.

The scheme’s low-weight codes also allow iterative decoding, so a completed worker task can immediately contribute to the larger gradient update. That property enables asynchronous updates. Finally, the authors exploit the linear dependence of directional derivatives on direction vectors to apply linear coding techniques even within general machine learning frameworks such as deep neural networks. The contribution links compression, coding, and asynchronous optimization.
summary.tldr: Coding and compressing derivatives directly enables iterative decoding and asynchronous gradient updates in distributed learning.

title: Lightweight Projective Derivative Codes for Compressed Asynchronous Gradient Descent

abstract: Differentiable simulators promise faster computation time for reinforcement learning by replacing zeroth-order gradient estimates of a stochastic objective with an estimate based on first-order gradients. However, it is yet unclear what factors decide the performance of the two estimators on complex landscapes that involve long-horizon planning and control on physical systems, despite the crucial relevance of this question for the utility of differentiable simulators. We show that characteristics of certain physical systems, such as stiffness or discontinuities, may compromise the efficacy of the first-order estimator, and analyze this phenomenon through the lens of bias and variance. We additionally propose an $\alpha$-order gradient estimator, with $\alpha \in [0,1]$, which correctly utilizes exact gradients to combine the efficiency of first-order estimates with the robustness of zero-order methods. We demonstrate the pitfalls of traditional estimators and the advantages of the $\alpha$-order estimator on some numerical examples.
originalAbstract: Differentiable simulators promise faster computation time for reinforcement learning by replacing zeroth-order gradient estimates of a stochastic objective with an estimate based on first-order gradients. However, it is yet unclear what factors decide the performance of the two estimators on complex landscapes that involve long-horizon planning and control on physical systems, despite the crucial relevance of this question for the utility of differentiable simulators. We show that characteristics of certain physical systems, such as stiffness or discontinuities, may compromise the efficacy of the first-order estimator, and analyze this phenomenon through the lens of bias and variance. We additionally propose an $\alpha$-order gradient estimator, with $\alpha \in [0,1]$, which correctly utilizes exact gradients to combine the efficiency of first-order estimates with the robustness of zero-order methods. We demonstrate the pitfalls of traditional estimators and the advantages of the $\alpha$-order estimator on some numerical examples.

paragraphs: Differentiable simulators provide derivatives that could make reinforcement learning more efficient than relying on zeroth-order gradient estimates. Whether these derivatives produce better estimates is less clear in physical control problems involving complex landscapes and long planning horizons. This paper investigates factors that can undermine the expected benefit.

The authors show that physical characteristics such as stiffness and discontinuities may compromise first-order gradient estimation. They analyze these effects through bias and variance, examining the quality of the resulting estimate rather than assuming that access to derivatives makes it preferable. The stated difficulty concerns certain physical systems, so it does not imply that first-order methods are always ineffective.

The proposed alternative is an α-order gradient estimator, with α between zero and one, that combines exact-gradient information with zeroth-order estimation. It aims to bring together first-order efficiency and zeroth-order robustness. Numerical examples illustrate weaknesses of traditional estimators and advantages of this combined approach. The findings make simulator differentiation a question of estimator suitability as well as derivative availability.
summary.tldr: Differentiable simulators can yield problematic policy-gradient estimates, motivating an estimator that combines first-order information with zeroth-order robustness.

title: Do Differentiable Simulators Give Better Policy Gradients?

abstract: Disease-related representations play a crucial role in image-based disease prediction such as cancer diagnosis, due to its considerable generalization capacity. However, it is still a challenge to identify lesion characteristics in obscured images, as many lesions are obscured by other tissues. In this paper, to learn the representations for identifying obscured lesions, we propose a disentanglement learning strategy under the guidance of alpha blending generation in an encoder-decoder framework (DAB-Net). Specifically, we take mammogram mass benign/malignant classification as an example. In our framework, composite obscured mass images are generated by alpha blending and then explicitly disentangled into disease-related mass features and interference glands features. To achieve disentanglement learning, features of these two parts are decoded to reconstruct the mass and the glands with corresponding reconstruction losses, and only disease-related mass features are fed into the classifier for disease prediction. Experimental results on one public dataset DDSM and three in-house datasets demonstrate that the proposed strategy can achieve state-of-the-art performance. DAB-Net achieves substantial improvements of 3.9%~4.4% AUC in obscured cases. Besides, the visualization analysis shows the model can better disentangle the mass and glands in the obscured image, suggesting the effectiveness of our solution in exploring the hidden characteristics in this challenging problem.

The paper studies this problem through benign-versus-malignant classification of mammogram masses. Its goal is to learn features that describe the mass even when surrounding gland tissue obscures the visual evidence needed for classification.

The proposed DAB-Net uses alpha blending to generate composite images containing obscured masses. An encoder-decoder framework then separates their representations into mass-related features and interfering gland features. Each feature group must support reconstruction of its corresponding image component. These reconstruction objectives guide the separation, while only the mass-related features are passed to the disease classifier.

Experiments on the public DDSM dataset and three in-house datasets show that the strategy can achieve state-of-the-art performance, with reported AUC improvements of 3.9%–4.4% on obscured cases. Visualization analysis also suggests better separation of masses from glands. Together, these findings support the proposed use of explicit separation to recover diagnostically relevant characteristics under tissue overlap.
summary.tldr: DAB-Net learns to separate mammogram mass features from obscuring gland tissue, improving benign-versus-malignant classification in the reported experiments.

title: Disentangling Disease-related Representation from Obscure for Disease Prediction

abstract: The REINFORCE algorithm \cite{williams1992simple} is popular in policy gradient (PG) for solving reinforcement learning (RL) problems. Meanwhile, the theoretical form of PG is from \cite{sutton1999policy}. Although both formulae prescribe PG, their precise connections are not yet illustrated. Recently, \citeauthor{nota2020policy} (\citeyear{nota2020policy}) have found that the ambiguity causes implementation errors. Motivated by the ambiguity and implementation incorrectness, we study PG from a perturbation perspective. In particular, we derive PG in a unified framework, precisely clarify the relation between PG implementation and theory, and echos back the findings by \citeauthor{nota2020policy}. Diving into factors contributing to empirical successes of the existing erroneous implementations, we find that small approximation error and the experience replay mechanism play critical roles.

paragraphs: Policy-gradient methods improve a reinforcement-learning policy by estimating how changes to it affect performance. The paper addresses an ambiguity between the familiar REINFORCE algorithm and the theoretical policy-gradient formula. Although both describe policy gradients, their precise relationship had not been clearly explained, and previous work connected that ambiguity to implementation errors.

The authors approach the problem through perturbation: examining how performance responds when the policy changes. They derive policy gradients within a unified framework and use it to clarify the relationship between theory and implementation. This analysis also supports earlier findings about incorrect implementations, making the connection between a mathematical expression and its computational use more explicit.

The paper then asks why some erroneous implementations nevertheless work well empirically. It identifies small approximation errors and experience replay as critical contributors to that success. The findings help separate theoretical correctness from observed effectiveness: an implementation may perform well for identifiable reasons even when it does not precisely implement the intended policy-gradient formula.
summary.tldr: A perturbation-based framework clarifies policy-gradient theory and implementation, identifying small approximation errors and experience replay as reasons some incorrect implementations still work.

title: Understanding Policy Gradient Algorithms: A Sensitivity-Based Approach

abstract: This work examines the deep disconnect between existing theoretical analyses of gradient-based algorithms and the practice of training deep neural networks. Specifically, we provide numerical evidence that in large-scale neural network training (e.g., ImageNet + ResNet101, and WT103 + TransformerXL models), the neural network’s weights do not converge to stationary points where the gradient of the loss is zero. Remarkably, however, we observe that even though the weights do not converge to stationary points, the progress in minimizing the loss function halts and training loss stabilizes. Inspired by this observation, we propose a new perspective based on ergodic theory of dynamical systems to explain it. Rather than studying the evolution of weights, we study the evolution of the distribution of weights. We prove convergence of the distribution of weights to an approximate invariant measure, thereby explaining how the training loss can stabilize without weights necessarily converging to stationary points. We further discuss how this perspective can better align optimization theory with empirical observations in machine learning practice.

paragraphs: Optimization theory often studies whether training approaches a stationary point, where the loss gradient is zero. This paper presents numerical evidence that large-scale neural network training can behave differently. In the studied image and language models, weights do not converge to stationary points even though further loss reduction stops and the training loss stabilizes.

To explain this behavior, the authors shift attention from the trajectory of individual weights to the evolution of their distribution. They draw on ergodic theory, which studies the long-run behavior of dynamical systems. This perspective allows stable statistical behavior to be considered even when the parameters themselves do not settle at a stationary point.

The paper proves convergence of the weight distribution to an approximate invariant measure. Such a distribution provides a way to explain stable training loss without requiring stationary-point convergence of the weights. The contribution links the reported observations with a different theoretical object of study, offering a route toward optimization analyses that better reflect the behavior seen in the training examples.
summary.tldr: An approximate invariant distribution of weights explains how training loss can stabilize without weights converging to stationary points.

title: Neural Network Weights Do Not Converge to Stationary Points: An Invariant Measure Perspective

abstract: We study robustness to test-time adversarial attacks in the regression setting with $\ell_p$ losses and arbitrary perturbation sets. We address the question of which function classes are PAC learnable in this setting. We show that classes of finite fat-shattering dimension are learnable in both the realizable and agnostic settings. Moreover, for convex function classes, they are even properly learnable. In contrast, some non-convex function classes provably require improper learning algorithms. Our main technique is based on a construction of an adversarially robust sample compression scheme of a size determined by the fat-shattering dimension. Along the way, we introduce a novel agnostic sample compression scheme for real-valued functions, which may be of independent interest.

Our main technique is based on a construction of an adversarially robust sample compression scheme of a size determined by the fat-shattering dimension. paragraphs: This paper asks when regression can be learned reliably if an adversary may alter inputs at test time. It considers real-valued predictions, a family of losses called l_p losses, and arbitrary sets of permitted perturbations. The central question concerns learnability: which classes of functions admit statistical guarantees under these adversarial conditions?

The authors show that finite fat-shattering dimension, a measure of the complexity of a real-valued function class, is sufficient for robust PAC learning. Their result covers both realizable settings and agnostic settings. For convex function classes, the learner can also be proper, meaning that its output belongs to the original function class. Some non-convex classes, however, provably require outputs outside that class.

The main construction compresses training information into a smaller representation that still supports adversarially robust learning. Its size is controlled by the fat-shattering dimension. The work also introduces an agnostic compression scheme for real-valued functions. These results connect robustness to statistical complexity while showing that the requirement to stay inside the original class can materially change what learning is possible.
summary.tldr: Finite fat-shattering dimension suffices for adversarially robust regression learning, although some non-convex classes require learners to output functions outside the class.

title: Adversarially Robust PAC Learnability of Real-Valued Functions

abstract: The Shapley value is widely regarded as a trustworthy attribution metric. However, when people use Shapley values to explain the attribution of input variables of a deep neural network (DNN), it usually requires a very high computational cost to approximate relatively accurate Shapley values in real-world applications. Therefore, we propose a novel network architecture, the HarsanyiNet, which makes inferences on the input sample and simultaneously computes the exact Shapley values of the input variables in a single forward propagation. The HarsanyiNet is designed on the theoretical foundation that the Shapley value can be reformulated as the redistribution of Harsanyi interactions encoded by the network.

paragraphs: Shapley values attribute a model's prediction to its input variables, but obtaining accurate values for deep networks is usually computationally expensive. This paper addresses that cost by changing the network architecture. HarsanyiNet is designed to produce a prediction and the exact Shapley values of its inputs during the same forward pass.

The construction rests on a theoretical relationship between Shapley values and Harsanyi interactions encoded by the network. These interactions describe contributions involving combinations of input variables. Reformulating attribution as a redistribution of those interactions gives the architecture a way to compute individual variable contributions alongside its ordinary inference computation.

The key result is exact attribution in a single forward propagation for this proposed architecture. This connects the form of the predictive model directly to the tractability of explaining it. The contribution is consequently an architecture with built-in attribution computation: its stated efficiency comes from how HarsanyiNet represents interactions and redistributes them when making a prediction.
summary.tldr: HarsanyiNet is designed to compute predictions and exact input Shapley values together in one forward pass.

title: HarsanyiNet: Computing Accurate Shapley Values in a Single Forward Propagation

abstract: Addressing imbalanced or long-tailed data is a major challenge in visual recognition tasks due to disparities between training and testing distributions and issues with data noise. We propose the Wrapped Cauchy Distributed Angular Softmax (WCDAS), a novel softmax function that incorporates data-wise Gaussian-based kernels into the angular correlation between feature representations and classifier weights, effectively mitigating noise and sparse sampling concerns. The class-wise distribution of angular representation becomes a sum of these kernels. Our theoretical analysis reveals that the wrapped Cauchy distribution excels the Gaussian distribution in approximating mixed distributions. Additionally, WCDAS uses trainable concentration parameters to dynamically adjust the compactness and margin of each class. Empirical results confirm label-aware behavior in these parameters and demonstrate WCDAS’s superiority over other state-of-the-art softmax-based methods in handling long-tailed visual recognition across multiple benchmark datasets. The code is public available.

paragraphs: Long-tailed visual recognition involves classes with very different amounts of training data. Sparse observations, noise, and differences between training and testing distributions make this setting challenging. The paper proposes Wrapped Cauchy Distributed Angular Softmax, or WCDAS, to improve how a classifier models class information in its output function.

WCDAS incorporates sample-specific Gaussian-based kernels into the angular relationship between feature representations and classifier weights. Each class’s angular distribution becomes a mixture of these kernels. The theoretical analysis supports a wrapped Cauchy distribution over a Gaussian distribution for approximating the mixed distributions considered. Trainable concentration parameters also adjust each class’s compactness and margin dynamically.

Empirical results show that these concentration parameters behave in a label-aware way. Across multiple long-tailed visual recognition benchmarks, WCDAS outperforms the state-of-the-art softmax-based alternatives evaluated. The contribution combines a distributional model of angular features with class-specific adaptation, addressing the uneven and noisy evidence available across classes within the classifier’s scoring mechanism.
summary.tldr: WCDAS models angular class distributions with adaptive concentration parameters to improve visual recognition on long-tailed datasets.

title: Wrapped Cauchy Distributed Angular Softmax for Long-Tailed Visual Recognition

abstract: Selecting exploratory actions that generate a rich stream of experience for better learning is a fundamental challenge in reinforcement learning (RL). An approach to tackle this problem consists in selecting actions according to specific policies for an extended period of time, also known as options. A recent line of work to derive such exploratory options builds upon the eigenfunctions of the graph Laplacian. Importantly, until now these methods have been mostly limited to tabular domains where (1) the graph Laplacian matrix was either given or could be fully estimated, (2) performing eigendecomposition on this matrix was computationally tractable, and (3) value functions could be learned exactly. Additionally, these methods required a separate option discovery phase. These assumptions are fundamentally not scalable. In this paper we address these limitations and show how recent results for directly approximating the eigenfunctions of the Laplacian can be leveraged to truly scale up options-based exploration. To do so, we introduce a fully online deep RL algorithm for discovering Laplacian-based options and evaluate our approach on a variety of pixel-based tasks. We compare to several state-of-the-art exploration methods and show that our approach is effective, general, and especially promising in non-stationary settings.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents need exploration that produces useful experience. One approach uses options: policies followed for an extended period rather than selecting each exploratory action independently. This paper develops a scalable way to discover options from the eigenfunctions of a graph Laplacian, mathematical objects used by earlier methods to organize exploration.

Previous Laplacian-based approaches were mostly restricted to tabular environments. They depended on having or fully estimating the Laplacian matrix, being able to compute its eigendecomposition, and learning value functions exactly. They also required a separate phase for discovering options. Together, these requirements made it difficult to apply the approach to larger problems with complex observations.

The authors use results for directly approximating Laplacian eigenfunctions to build a fully online deep reinforcement-learning algorithm. Option discovery can therefore occur during ongoing learning without a separate discovery phase. Evaluations on multiple tasks with pixel observations compare the method against leading exploration approaches. The results support its effectiveness and generality, with particularly promising findings in settings that change over time.
summary.tldr: An online deep reinforcement-learning method scales Laplacian-based exploratory options to pixel-based tasks, with promising results in changing environments.

title: Deep Laplacian-based Options for Temporally-Extended Exploration

abstract: Labels are typically sparse in real-world time series due to the high annotation cost. Recently, consistency regularization techniques have been used to generate artificial labels from unlabeled augmented instances. To fully exploit the sequential characteristic of time series in consistency regularization, we propose a novel method of data augmentation called context-attached augmentation , which adds preceding and succeeding instances to a target instance to form its augmented instance. Unlike the existing augmentation techniques that modify a target instance by directly perturbing its attributes, the context-attached augmentation generates instances augmented with varying contexts while maintaining the target instance. Based on our augmentation method, we propose a context consistency regularization framework, which first adds different contexts to a target instance sampled from a given time series and then shares unitary reliability-based cross-window labels across the augmented instances to maintain consistency. We demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms the existing state-of-the-art consistency regularization frameworks through comprehensive experiments on real-world time-series datasets.

paragraphs: Time-series labels are often scarce because annotation is expensive. Consistency regularization helps use unlabeled data by encouraging related versions of an example to receive compatible predictions. This paper develops a version that explicitly uses the sequential structure of the data, making the surrounding observations part of how training examples are constructed.

The proposed context-attached augmentation keeps the target instance intact and attaches preceding and succeeding instances. Different surrounding contexts create different augmented versions of the same target. The framework then shares common labels across these windows using a reliability-based procedure, encouraging consistency when the target appears with different neighboring observations.

This approach changes what varies during augmentation: the context changes while the target itself remains fixed. That gives the learning procedure a way to exploit neighboring information without directly perturbing the target's attributes. Experiments on real-world time-series datasets show that the framework outperforms the existing state-of-the-art consistency regularization methods evaluated, supporting the usefulness of this contextual approach to sparse labels.
summary.tldr: Varying the context around an unchanged time-series instance improves consistency-based learning when labels are sparse.

title: Context Consistency Regularization for Label Sparsity in Time Series

abstract: Predictor-based methods have substantially enhanced Neural Architecture Search (NAS) optimization. The efficacy of these predictors is largely influenced by the method of encoding neural network architectures. While traditional encodings used an adjacency matrix describing the graph structure of a neural network, novel encodings embrace a variety of approaches from unsupervised pretraining of latent representations to vectors of zero-cost proxies. In this paper, we categorize and investigate neural encodings from three main types: structural, learned, and score-based. Furthermore, we extend these encodings and introduce unified encodings, that extend NAS predictors to multiple search spaces. Our analysis draws from experiments conducted on over 1.5 million neural network architectures on NAS spaces such as NASBench-101 (NB101), NB201, NB301, Network Design Spaces (NDS), and TransNASBench-101. Building on our study, we present our predictor FLAN: Flow Attention for NAS. FLAN integrates critical insights on predictor design, transfer learning, and unified encodings to enable more than an order of magnitude cost reduction for training NAS accuracy predictors. Our implementation and encodings for all neural networks are open-sourced at https://github.com/abdelfattah-lab/flan_nas.

paragraphs: Prediction-based neural architecture search depends on models that estimate how well candidate networks will perform. The representation given to those predictors strongly influences their usefulness. This paper examines that representation choice, moving beyond the traditional adjacency matrix that describes a network’s graph connections.

The authors organize encodings into three categories: structural descriptions, learned representations, and score-based vectors. They also introduce unified encodings that allow predictors to operate across multiple architecture search spaces. Their investigation covers more than 1.5 million architectures from several established spaces, providing a broad basis for studying how encoding and predictor design work together.

The resulting predictor, Flow Attention for NAS, or FLAN, combines lessons about architecture representations, transfer learning, and unified encodings. The authors report that it reduces the cost of training architecture accuracy predictors by more than an order of magnitude. This finding concerns the predictor-training stage of architecture search: better representations and reuse across spaces can make that supporting component substantially less expensive.
summary.tldr: The paper studies architecture encodings and introduces FLAN, reducing NAS accuracy-predictor training costs by more than an order of magnitude.

title: Encodings for Prediction-based Neural Architecture Search

abstract: We propose a standardized version of fairness measures for continuous scores with a reasonable interpretation based on the Wasserstein distance. Our measures are easily computable and well suited for quantifying and interpreting the strength of group disparities as well as for comparing biases across different models, datasets, or time points. We derive a link between the different families of existing fairness measures for scores and show that the proposed standardized fairness measures outperform ROC-based fairness measures because they are more explicit and can quantify significant biases that ROC-based fairness measures miss.

paragraphs: Fairness assessment for continuous risk scores needs to describe the size of disparities between groups, not just identify that some disparity exists. This paper proposes standardized fairness measures with an interpretation based on Wasserstein distance. The emphasis is on making differences in score distributions both computable and understandable.

Standardization is central to the intended use. The authors design the measures to support comparisons across models, datasets, and time points, so that an assessment can address how the strength of a disparity differs between settings. They also derive a connection between existing families of score-based fairness measures, placing the proposed quantities within a broader mathematical account of how these assessments relate.

The authors report that their measures outperform ROC-based fairness measures in explicitness and in detecting significant biases that the ROC-based measures miss. The claimed improvement concerns the ability to quantify and interpret group disparities in continuous scores. This makes the work a contribution to fairness measurement: it provides a clearer way to characterize observed differences and compare their magnitude across evaluated systems.
summary.tldr: Standardized Wasserstein-based fairness measures quantify group disparities in continuous scores, including biases missed by ROC-based measures.

title: Standardized Interpretable Fairness Measures for Continuous Risk Scores

abstract: An increasingly popular machine learning paradigm is to pretrain a neural network (NN) on many tasks offline, then adapt it to downstream tasks, often by re-training only the last linear layer of the network. This approach yields strong downstream performance in a variety of contexts, demonstrating that multitask pretraining leads to effective feature learning. Although several recent theoretical studies have shown that shallow NNs learn meaningful features when either (i) they are trained on a single task or (ii) they are linear, very little is known about the closer-to-practice case of nonlinear NNs trained on multiple tasks. In this work, we present the first results proving that feature learning occurs during training with a nonlinear model on multiple tasks. Our key insight is that multi-task pretraining induces a pseudo-contrastive loss that favors representations that align points that typically have the same label across tasks. Using this observation, we show that when the tasks are binary classification tasks with labels depending on the projection of the data onto an $r$-dimensional subspace within the $d\gg r$-dimensional input space, a simple gradient-based multitask learning algorithm on a two-layer ReLU NN recovers this projection, allowing for generalization to downstream tasks with sample and neuron complexity independent of $d$. In contrast, we show that with high probability over the draw of a single task, training on this single task cannot guarantee to learn all $r$ ground-truth features.

paragraphs: Pretraining on multiple tasks often produces features that support later adaptation by changing only a final linear layer. This paper provides a theoretical explanation for feature learning in nonlinear networks trained across tasks. It studies two-layer ReLU networks, extending beyond prior theory focused on single-task training or linear models.

The key insight is that multitask pretraining induces a pseudo-contrastive loss: it encourages representations to align points that tend to share labels across tasks. The analysis assumes binary classification tasks whose labels depend on an r-dimensional projection of data from a much larger d-dimensional input space. Under this setting, a simple gradient-based algorithm recovers the relevant projection.

The recovered representation supports downstream generalization with sample and neuron complexity independent of the ambient dimension d. In contrast, with high probability over a single task’s draw, training only on that task cannot guarantee recovery of all r underlying features. The result explains how task diversity can reveal shared structure that a single task may leave insufficiently identified.
summary.tldr: Under a shared low-dimensional task structure, multitask training provably recovers features that support dimension-independent downstream learning.

title: Provable Multi-Task Representation Learning by Two-Layer ReLU Neural Networks

abstract: High-probability analysis of stochastic first-order optimization methods under mild assumptions on the noise has been gaining a lot of attention in recent years. Typically, gradient clipping is one of the key algorithmic ingredients to derive good high-probability guarantees when the noise is heavy-tailed. However, if implemented naively, clipping can spoil the convergence of the popular methods for composite and distributed optimization (Prox-SGD/Parallel SGD) even in the absence of any noise. Due to this reason, many works on high-probability analysis consider only unconstrained non-distributed problems, and the existing results for composite/distributed problems do not include some important special cases (like strongly convex problems) and are not optimal. To address this issue, we propose new stochastic methods for composite and distributed optimization based on the clipping of stochastic gradient differences and prove tight high-probability convergence results (including nearly optimal ones) for the new methods. In addition, we also develop new methods for composite and distributed variational inequalities and analyze the high-probability convergence of these methods.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization methods use noisy gradient information, and heavy-tailed noise makes strong reliability guarantees difficult. Gradient clipping is a common ingredient in high-probability analyses because it limits extreme updates. This paper identifies a complication: naive clipping can prevent convergence in composite or distributed optimization, even when there is no noise.

The authors propose methods that clip stochastic gradient differences. They analyze these methods for composite and distributed minimization and establish tight high-probability convergence results, including nearly optimal guarantees. The work addresses gaps in previous analyses, which often focused on unconstrained, nondistributed settings or omitted important cases such as strongly convex problems.

The paper also develops and analyzes corresponding methods for composite and distributed variational inequalities. Its contribution is both algorithmic and theoretical: the placement of clipping changes, and the resulting procedures receive guarantees suited to heavy-tailed noise. The central lesson is that controlling unusually large stochastic updates must be done in a way that preserves the optimization method's underlying convergence behavior.
summary.tldr: Clipping stochastic gradient differences enables tight high-probability guarantees for composite and distributed optimization with heavy-tailed noise.

title: High-Probability Convergence for Composite and Distributed Stochastic Minimization and Variational Inequalities with Heavy-Tailed Noise

abstract: Trustworthy ML systems should not only return accurate predictions, but also a reliable representation of their uncertainty. Bayesian methods are commonly used to quantify both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty, but alternative approaches, such as evidential deep learning methods, have become popular in recent years. The latter group of methods in essence extends empirical risk minimization (ERM) for predicting second-order probability distributions over outcomes, from which measures of epistemic (and aleatoric) uncertainty can be extracted. This paper presents novel theoretical insights of evidential deep learning, highlighting the difficulties in optimizing second-order loss functions and interpreting the resulting epistemic uncertainty measures. With a systematic setup that covers a wide range of approaches for classification, regression and counts, it provides novel insights into issues of identifiability and convergence in second-order loss minimization, and the relative (rather than absolute) nature of epistemic uncertainty measures.

paragraphs: A useful uncertainty estimate should distinguish unpredictable outcomes from uncertainty caused by limited model knowledge. Evidential deep learning attempts to represent these distinctions by predicting second-order distributions: probability distributions over possible predictive distributions. This paper examines whether the resulting quantities can be interpreted faithfully as uncertainty about what a model knows.

The authors analyze the learning objectives used to fit these richer distributions. Their framework covers classification, regression, and count prediction, allowing them to investigate issues shared across a wide range of approaches. Two central concerns are identifiability, or whether the learning problem determines the intended uncertainty representation, and convergence, or what minimizing the objective actually leads toward.

The analysis also highlights that the resulting measures of epistemic uncertainty have a relative rather than absolute character. This matters because a numerical uncertainty output can appear more definitive than its training objective justifies. The paper's contribution is a theoretical account of difficulties in optimization and interpretation, helping clarify what these methods' uncertainty estimates can mean rather than treating the presence of a second-order distribution as sufficient assurance.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies theoretical difficulties in learning and interpreting epistemic uncertainty through evidential deep learning.

title: Is Epistemic Uncertainty Faithfully Represented by Evidential Deep Learning Methods?

abstract: In many predictive contexts (e.g., credit lending), true outcomes are only observed for samples that were positively classified in the past. These past observations, in turn, form training datasets for classifiers that make future predictions. However, such training datasets lack information about the outcomes of samples that were (incorrectly) negatively classified in the past and can lead to erroneous classifiers. We present an approach that trains a classifier using available data and comes with a family of exploration strategies to collect outcome data about subpopulations that otherwise would have been ignored. For any exploration strategy, the approach comes with guarantees that (1) all sub-populations are explored, (2) the fraction of false positives is bounded, and (3) the trained classifier converges to a "desired" classifier. The right exploration strategy is context-dependent; it can be chosen to improve learning guarantees and encode context-specific group fairness properties. Evaluation on real-world datasets shows that this approach consistently boosts the quality of collected outcome data and improves the fraction of true positives for all groups, with only a small reduction in predictive utility.

paragraphs: In some classification settings, a decision determines whether its true outcome will ever be observed. Credit lending is one example: past positive decisions supply outcome data, while rejected cases can remain unobserved. A classifier trained on those records can therefore inherit gaps created by earlier decisions, including mistaken negative classifications.

This paper combines classifier training with a family of exploration strategies that collect outcomes from otherwise neglected subpopulations. For every exploration strategy within the approach, the authors provide guarantees that all subpopulations are explored, the fraction of false positives is bounded, and the learned classifier converges to a desired classifier. Exploration thus becomes part of the learning process rather than a separate data collection concern.

The choice of strategy remains context-dependent and can encode group fairness properties or improve learning guarantees. On the evaluated real-world datasets, the approach improves collected outcome data and increases the fraction of true positives for every group, with a small reduction in predictive utility. The findings connect fairer learning opportunities with deliberate decisions about which missing outcomes to observe.
summary.tldr: Exploration strategies collect outcomes from overlooked subpopulations while providing learning guarantees and supporting context-specific group fairness.

title: Fair Classification with Partial Feedback: An Exploration-Based Data Collection Approach

abstract: Assessing response quality to instructions in language models is vital but challenging due to the complexity of human language across different contexts. This complexity often results in ambiguous or inconsistent interpretations, making accurate assessment difficult. To address this issue, we propose a novel Uncertainty-aware Reward Model (URM) that introduces a robust uncertainty estimation for the quality of paired responses based on Bayesian approximation. Trained with preference datasets, our uncertainty-enabled proxy not only scores rewards for responses but also evaluates their inherent uncertainty. Empirical results demonstrate significant benefits of incorporating the proposed proxy into language model training. Our method boosts the instruction following capability of language models by refining data curation for training and improving policy optimization objectives, thereby surpassing existing methods by a large margin on benchmarks such as Vicuna and MT-bench. These findings highlight that our proposed approach substantially advances language model training and paves a new way of harnessing uncertainty within language models.

paragraphs: Judging whether a language model has followed an instruction well can be difficult because language admits ambiguous or inconsistent interpretations across contexts. A quality score alone does not express how uncertain that judgment is. This paper introduces an Uncertainty-aware Reward Model, or URM, to represent both aspects when comparing responses.

URM is trained on preference datasets and uses a Bayesian approximation to estimate uncertainty about the quality of paired responses. The resulting proxy produces reward scores together with uncertainty estimates. The authors incorporate this information into language model training in two ways: refining which data are curated for training and improving the objectives used for policy optimization.

The experiments report substantial improvements in instruction following, with large margins over existing methods on benchmarks including Vicuna and MT-bench. These results support using uncertainty in the training process rather than treating every quality assessment as equally dependable. The contribution connects an uncertainty-aware evaluator to concrete changes in data curation and optimization, with measured gains in the evaluated models.
summary.tldr: An uncertainty-aware reward model improves instruction following by informing training-data curation and policy optimization.

title: Improving Instruction Following in Language Models through Proxy-Based Uncertainty Estimation

abstract: Multi-class unsupervised anomaly detection aims to create a unified model for identifying anomalies in objects from multiple classes when only normal data is available. In such a challenging setting, widely used reconstruction-based networks persistently grapple with the "identical shortcut" problem, wherein the infiltration of abnormal information from the condition biases the output towards an anomalous distribution. In response to this critical challenge, we introduce a Vague Prototype-Oriented Diffusion Model (VPDM) that extracts only fundamental information from the condition to prevent the occurrence of the "identical shortcut" problem from the input layer. This model leverages prototypes that contain only vague information about the target as the initial condition. Subsequently, a novel conditional diffusion model is introduced to incrementally enhance details based on vague conditions. Finally, a Vague Prototype-Oriented Optimal Transport (VPOT) method is proposed to provide more accurate information about conditions. All these components are seamlessly integrated into a unified optimization objective. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated across diverse datasets, including the MVTec, VisA, and MPDD benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art results.

The findings support controlling what information is available to the reconstruction process as a way to address the shortcut. The design combines deliberately vague initial guidance with gradual refinement, seeking to preserve useful object information without allowing abnormal details in the condition to dictate the reconstructed output.
summary.tldr: VPDM uses vague prototypes and conditional diffusion to reduce anomaly copying in reconstruction-based multi-class anomaly detection.

title: Vague Prototype-Oriented Diffusion Model for Multi-Class Anomaly Detection

abstract: The current state-of-the-art No-Reference Image Quality Assessment (NR-IQA) methods typically rely on feature extraction from upstream semantic backbone networks, assuming that all extracted features are relevant. However, we make a key observation that not all features are beneficial, and some may even be harmful, necessitating careful selection. Empirically, we find that many image pairs with small feature spatial distances can have vastly different quality scores, indicating that the extracted features may contain quality-irrelevant noise. To address this issue, we propose a Quality-Aware Feature Matching IQA Metric (QFM-IQM) that employs an adversarial perspective to remove harmful semantic noise features from the upstream task. Specifically, QFM-IQM enhances the semantic noise distinguish capabilities by matching image pairs with similar quality scores but varying semantic features as adversarial semantic noise and adaptively adjusting the upstream task’s features by reducing sensitivity to adversarial noise perturbation. Furthermore, we utilize a distillation framework to expand the dataset and improve the model’s generalization ability. Extensive experiments conducted on eight standard IQA datasets have demonstrated the effectiveness of our proposed QFM-IQM.

paragraphs: Estimating image quality without a reference image often begins with features from a network trained to recognize semantic content. This paper questions whether every such feature helps judge quality. The authors observe that images can be close in the extracted feature space yet have very different quality scores, suggesting that some features obscure the distinctions the quality predictor needs.

Their Quality-Aware Feature Matching IQA Metric uses pairs of images with similar quality but different semantic features. These differences serve as adversarial semantic noise: variation that the quality assessment should resist. The method adaptively adjusts the upstream features by reducing sensitivity to those perturbations, aiming to remove harmful semantic information while retaining useful quality information.

A distillation framework expands the dataset and supports better generalization. Experiments across eight standard image quality datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The central implication is that features useful for recognizing image content need careful adaptation for quality assessment; explicitly controlling sensitivity to semantic differences provides a way to make that adaptation.
summary.tldr: Quality-aware feature matching improves image quality assessment by reducing sensitivity to semantic differences that do not reflect quality.

title: Adaptive Feature Selection for No-Reference Image Quality Assessment by Mitigating Semantic Noise Sensitivity

abstract: Data valuation quantifies the contribution of each data point to the performance of a machine learning model. Existing works typically define the value of data by its improvement of the validation performance of the trained model. However, this approach can be impractical to apply in collaborative machine learning and data marketplace since it is difficult for the parties/buyers to agree on a common validation dataset or determine the exact validation distribution a priori. To address this, we propose a distributionally robust data valuation approach to perform data valuation without known/fixed validation distributions. Our approach defines the value of data by its improvement of the distributionally robust generalization error (DRGE), thus providing a worst-case performance guarantee without a known/fixed validation distribution. However, since computing DRGE directly is infeasible, we propose using model deviation as a proxy for the marginal improvement of DRGE (for kernel regression and neural networks) to compute data values. Furthermore, we identify a notion of uniqueness where low uniqueness characterizes low-value data. We empirically demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing data valuation approaches in data selection and data removal tasks on real-world datasets (e.g., housing price prediction, diabetes hospitalization prediction).

paragraphs: Data valuation assigns importance to individual training examples based on their contribution to model performance. A common approach measures improvement on a validation dataset. That becomes awkward in collaborative learning or data marketplaces, where participants may disagree on a validation set or may not know the eventual evaluation distribution in advance.

This paper instead defines value through improvement in distributionally robust generalization error, which supports a worst-case performance guarantee without a known or fixed validation distribution. Directly computing this error is infeasible, so the authors use model deviation as a proxy for its marginal improvement. They develop this approach for kernel regression and neural networks.

The central shift is from valuing examples against one agreed evaluation distribution to valuing their contribution under distributional uncertainty, with a computable proxy making that objective usable.
summary.tldr: The paper values training examples through a computable proxy for robust generalization improvement without requiring a fixed validation distribution.

title: Distributionally Robust Data Valuation

abstract: Unsupervised representation learning has become an important ingredient of today’s deep learning systems. However, only a few methods exist that explain a learned vector embedding in the sense of providing information about which parts of an input are the most important for its representation. These methods generate the explanation for a given input after the model has been evaluated and tend to produce either inaccurate explanations or are slow, which limits their practical use. To address these limitations, we introduce the Neural Explanation Masks (NEM) framework, which turns a fixed representation model into a self-explaining model by augmenting it with a masking network. This network provides occlusion-based explanations in parallel to computing the representations during inference. We present an instance of this framework, the NEM-U (NEM using U-net structure) architecture, which leverages similarities between segmentation and occlusion-based masks. Our experiments show that NEM-U generates explanations faster and with lower complexity compared to the current state-of-the-art while maintaining high accuracy as measured by locality.

paragraphs: Unsupervised representation models turn inputs into vector embeddings, but those vectors do not directly show which input regions matter most. Existing explanation methods often operate after the representation model has run. The paper identifies a practical tension in these methods: their explanations can be inaccurate, or producing them can take too much time.

Neural Explanation Masks address this by adding a masking network to a fixed representation model. During inference, the added network produces an occlusion-based explanation alongside the representation computation. The explanation therefore becomes part of the augmented model’s inference process, identifying important input regions through masks.

The authors instantiate this framework as NEM-U, using a U-net structure and the connection between segmentation and explanation masks. Their experiments show faster explanation generation and lower complexity than current state-of-the-art methods while retaining high accuracy according to locality. The result supports an approach in which a dedicated learned masking network makes explanations more practical to obtain whenever the representation model is evaluated.
summary.tldr: NEM-U adds a masking network that explains embeddings during inference, producing faster, lower-complexity explanations while maintaining high locality-based accuracy.

title: Finding NEM-U: Explaining unsupervised representation learning through neural network generated explanation masks

abstract: The incredible success of transformers on sequence modeling tasks can be largely attributed to the self-attention mechanism, which allows information to be transferred between different parts of a sequence. Self-attention allows transformers to encode causal structure which makes them particularly suitable for sequence modeling. However, the process by which transformers learn such causal structure via gradient-based training algorithms remains poorly understood. To better understand this process, we introduce an in-context learning task that requires learning latent causal structure. We prove that gradient descent on a simplified two-layer transformer learns to solve this task by encoding the latent causal graph in the first attention layer. The key insight of our proof is that the gradient of the attention matrix encodes the mutual information between tokens. As a consequence of the data processing inequality, the largest entries of this gradient correspond to edges in the latent causal graph. As a special case, when the sequences are generated from in-context Markov chains, we prove that transformers learn an induction head (Olsson et al., 2022). We confirm our theoretical findings by showing that transformers trained on our in-context learning task are able to recover a wide variety of causal structures.
