paragraphs: Determining whether examples were used to train a language model matters for auditing and evaluation. The paper argues that judging examples individually is insufficient when the goal is statistically reliable evidence about an identified collection. PTDI therefore treats training-data identification as a set-level inference problem with explicit control over false identifications.

The method requires a collection of data known to be unseen during training. It uses this reference set to calculate conformal p-values for candidate examples. A Jackknife-corrected Beta boundary estimator then estimates the proportion of training examples in the candidate set, allowing the p-values to be scaled before applying the Benjamini–Hochberg selection procedure.

The resulting distribution-free approach provides provable, strict control of the false identification rate for the selected subset. This is a guarantee about errors in the identified set, rather than certainty about every individual example. Experiments across models and datasets report higher power than prior methods while retaining the stated error control, supporting more effective identification within a statistically controlled procedure.
summary.tldr: PTDI identifies sets of likely training examples with provable false identification rate control using known unseen data.

title: Provable Training Data Identification for Large Language Models

abstract: Open-world object detection (OWOD) requires incrementally detecting known categories while reliably identifying unknown objects. Existing methods primarily focus on improving unknown recall, yet overlook interpretability, often leading to known–unknown confusion and reduced prediction reliability. This paper aims to make the entire OWOD framework interpretable, enabling the detector to truly “knowing the unknown.” To this end, we propose a concept-driven InterPretable OWOD framework(IPOW) by introducing a Concept Decomposition Model (CDM) for OWOD, which explicitly decomposes the coupled RoI features in Faster R-CNN into discriminative, shared, and background concepts. Discriminative concepts identify the most discriminative features to enlarge the distances between known categories, while shared and background concepts, due to their strong generalization ability, can be readily transferred to detect unknown categories. Leveraging the interpretable framework, we identify that known–unknown confusion arises when unknown objects fall into the discriminative space of known classes. To address this, we propose Concept-Guided Rectification (CGR) to further resolve such confusion. Extensive experiments show that IPOW significantly improves unknown recall while mitigating confusion, and provides concept-level interpretability for both known and unknown predictions.

paragraphs: Open-world object detection must recognize known categories while also identifying objects outside those categories. This paper argues that improving unknown-object recall alone leaves an important problem unresolved: a detector can still confuse known and unknown objects without exposing why. IPOW introduces an interpretable representation intended to improve both recognition and the explanation of predictions.

Its Concept Decomposition Model splits Faster R-CNN region features into discriminative, shared, and background concepts. Discriminative concepts help separate known classes. Shared and background concepts provide information that can transfer to unknown categories. This division gives the detector distinct representational components whose roles can be examined for both known and unknown predictions.

Using that decomposition, the authors identify confusion when unknown objects enter the discriminative feature space associated with known classes. They introduce Concept-Guided Rectification to address this overlap. Experiments report significantly improved unknown recall alongside reduced confusion. The contribution connects interpretability to a concrete correction mechanism: exposing the source of a mistaken classification helps guide how the detector should be adjusted.
summary.tldr: IPOW decomposes object features into interpretable concepts to improve unknown-object detection and reduce confusion with known classes.

title: Knowing the Unknown: Interpretable Open-World Object Detection via Concept Decomposition Model

abstract: Lifelong Model Editing aims to continuously update evolving facts in Large Language Models while preserving unrelated knowledge and general capabilities, yet it remains plagued by catastrophic forgetting and model collapse. Empirically, we find that recent editors resilient over long horizons share the same core strategy: Lifelong Normalization (LN), which normalizes value gradients using running statistics. Removing LN causes immediate performance collapse, and we observe a counter-intuitive positive cumulative effect where early edits can promote the success of future edits. Yet the mechanism of LN remains a "black box", leaving its precise role in lifelong stability poorly understood. In this work, we provide the first theoretical account of LN in the lifelong regime. Our analysis reveals a self-reinforcing stability loop and proves that, when combined with ridge-regularized regression, LN yields parameter updates with asymptotic orthogonality and bounded norms, directly mitigating forgetting and systemic collapse. Based on these insights, we derive StableEdit, which strengthens this stability loop via an explicit warm-up stage and full whitening, improving long-horizon stability at minimal overhead. Extensive experiments validate our theory and demonstrate competitive performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/MINE-USTC/StableEdit.

The paper identifies Lifelong Normalization as a shared mechanism in recent editors that remain stable over long sequences. This mechanism normalizes value gradients using running statistics. The contribution explains why accumulated editing history can become a source of stability under this mechanism, rather than treating every additional edit solely as another opportunity for damage.
summary.tldr: The paper explains how Lifelong Normalization stabilizes repeated model edits and uses that analysis to develop StableEdit.

title: More Edits, More Stable: Understanding the Lifelong Normalization in Sequential Model Editing

abstract: Phenotypic screening experiments produce many microscope images of cells under diverse perturbations, with biologically significant responses often subtle or difficult to identify visually. A central challenge is to extract image representations that distinguish activity from controls and group phenotypically similar perturbations. In this work we propose new adaptations of contrastive loss functions that incorporate experimental metadata as learned class vectors, and a geometrically inspired variant, called SPC, where class vectors are confined to the unit sphere and updated only by attractive terms (allowing more overlap of phenotypically similar classes). The approach is tested on two popular benchmarking datasets, BBBC021 and RxRx3-core; and we also evaluate performance on uncurated screens of HaCaT cells to gauge effectiveness in a realistic use-case scenario. We find we outperform prior methods across the three datasets and on a wide array of metrics measuring phenotype grouping, biological recall, drug-target interaction and mechanism-of-action inference. We also show we maintain this improved performance compared to models over 10x larger in parameter count, and that SPC can be used as an effective fine-tuning technique. The method is easy to implement and is well suited to settings with limited data or compute resources.

paragraphs: Phenotypic screening uses microscope images to examine how cells respond to different perturbations. Useful representations must distinguish meaningful changes from controls while grouping perturbations that produce similar biological effects. That is difficult when the relevant visual differences are subtle and experimental classes can have overlapping appearances.

The paper adapts contrastive training by representing experimental metadata with learned class vectors. Its SPC variant constrains these vectors to a unit sphere and updates them using only attractive terms. This asymmetric treatment allows classes with similar phenotypes to overlap more, rather than requiring their representations to remain strongly separated.

Evaluations cover BBBC021, RxRx3-core, and uncurated HaCaT-cell screens. The method outperforms prior approaches across measures of phenotype grouping, biological recall, drug-target interactions, and mechanism-of-action inference. It also retains its advantage against models with more than ten times as many parameters, and SPC works effectively for fine-tuning. Together, these results suggest that shaping the training objective around biological similarity can deliver useful representations without requiring very large models, especially where data or computation is limited.
summary.tldr: Asymmetric contrastive training improves cellular-image representations by allowing biologically similar experimental classes to overlap.

title: Asymmetric Contrastive Objectives for Efficient Phenotypic Screening

abstract: While LLM-based agents excel at individual tasks, effective collaboration with realistic human partners remains challenging. Most of the existing conversation-level collaborative studies lack grounded interaction and behavioral execution, motivating the need for cooperative game environments that enable contextualized and immersive collaboration. To this end, this paper proposes CollabBench, a benchmark for evaluating and training collaborative agents in cooperative games. CollabBench features a Diverse Player Profile Simulation pipeline to model varied players behaviors, and a Collaborative Agentic Training paradigm that unifies reasoning, communication, and action via agentic rollouts, optimized with a hybrid reward balancing task efficiency and affective adaptation. We further extend classic environments to CWAH-MultiPlayer and Cook-MultiPlayer for systematic evaluation under diverse personalities. Experiments with efficiency and affective metrics show that our trained models outperform base models, achieving 19.5% higher efficiency and 24.4% improved affective performance. Further analysis reveals key collaborative limitations of existing models and offers insights for future collaborative training.

paragraphs: Being good at an individual task does not ensure that a language-model agent will cooperate effectively with a partner. Collaboration requires communication to influence actions in a shared situation, while accommodating different partner behaviors. CollabBench studies these demands through cooperative games, where conversational choices are tied to behavior and task execution.

The framework includes a simulation pipeline for generating diverse player profiles and a training approach that combines reasoning, communication, and action within agent interaction sequences. These results show improvements within the benchmark’s cooperative settings and demonstrate why measuring task completion alongside adaptation to partners offers a fuller account of collaboration than conversation-only evaluation.
summary.tldr: CollabBench evaluates and trains cooperation with diverse simulated partners, improving both task efficiency and affective performance.

title: CollabBench: Benchmarking and Unleashing Collaborative Ability of LLMs with Diverse Players via Proactive Engagement

abstract: Neighborhood search operators are critical to the performance of Multi-Objective Evolutionary Algorithms (MOEAs) and rely heavily on expert design. Although recent LLM-based Automated Heuristic Design (AHD) methods have made notable progress, they primarily optimize individual heuristics or components independently, lacking explicit exploration and exploitation of dynamic coupling relationships between operators. In this paper, multi-operator optimization in MOEAs is formulated as a Markov decision process, enabling the improvement of interdependent operators through sequential decision-making. To address this, we propose the Evolution of Operator Combination (E2OC) framework for MOEAs, which achieves the co-evolution of design strategies and executable codes. E2OC employs Monte Carlo Tree Search to progressively search combinations of operator design strategies and adopts an operator rotation mechanism to identify effective operator configurations while supporting the integration of mainstream AHD methods as the underlying designer. Experimental results across AHD tasks with varying objectives and problem scales show that E2OC consistently outperforms state-of-the-art AHD and other multi-heuristic co-design frameworks, demonstrating strong generalization and sustained optimization capability.

To address this, we propose the Evolution of Operator Combination (E2OC) framework for MOEAs, which achieves the co-evolution of design strategies and executable codes. paragraphs: Multi-objective evolutionary algorithms rely on search operators that propose changes to candidate solutions. These operators are often designed by experts, although language models increasingly help automate their construction. This paper argues that optimizing each operator separately misses an important source of performance: the changing relationships between operators used within the same search.

E2OC treats multi-operator optimization as a Markov decision process, framing design as a sequence of choices whose effects depend on the current configuration. It evolves both design strategies and executable code. Monte Carlo Tree Search explores combinations of operator-design strategies, while an operator rotation mechanism helps identify effective configurations. The framework can incorporate established automated heuristic-design methods as the underlying designer.

Experiments span heuristic-design tasks with different objectives and problem scales. E2OC consistently outperforms leading automated-design methods and other frameworks for jointly designing multiple heuristics. The reported generalization and sustained optimization results support designing operators as an interacting collection, with attention to how their combinations perform over successive decisions.
summary.tldr: E2OC improves automated heuristic design by jointly evolving interacting search operators through sequential exploration of their combinations.

title: Evolving Interdependent Operators with Large Language Models for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization

abstract: Language models achieve impressive performance on a variety of knowledge, language, and reasoning tasks due to the scale and diversity of pretraining data available. The standard training recipe is a two-stage paradigm: pretraining first on the full corpus of data followed by specialization on a subset of high quality, specialized data from the full corpus. In the multi-domain setting, this involves continued pretraining of multiple models on each specialized domain, referred to as split model training. We propose a method for pretraining multiple models independently over a general pretraining corpus, and determining the optimal compute allocation between pretraining and continued pretraining using scaling laws. Our approach accurately predicts the loss of a model of size $N$ with $D$ pretraining and $D’$ specialization tokens, and extrapolates to larger model sizes and number of tokens. Applied to language model training, our approach improves performance consistently across common sense knowledge and reasoning benchmarks across different model sizes and compute budgets.

paragraphs: Language models commonly learn from a broad corpus before continuing training on specialized data. The paper develops a scaling-law approach to guide that division.

The proposed method considers multiple models pretrained independently on a general corpus and then trained further for specialized domains. It predicts model loss using three quantities: model size, the number of general pretraining tokens, and the number of specialization tokens. These predictions provide a basis for selecting the compute allocation between the two training stages.

The authors report that the resulting loss model extrapolates to larger models and larger token budgets. Applied to language-model training, the allocation approach consistently improves common-sense knowledge and reasoning benchmark performance across the tested model sizes and compute budgets. The practical contribution is a predictive way to plan specialization, linking training-stage budgets to expected performance instead of treating the split as a fixed recipe.
summary.tldr: Scaling laws predict specialized-model loss and guide compute allocation between general pretraining and domain-specific continued training.

title: Optimal Splitting of Language Models from Mixtures to Specialized Domains

abstract: While Prover-Verifier Games (PVGs) offer a promising path toward verifiability in nonlinear classification models, they have not yet been applied to complex inputs such as high-dimensional images. Conversely, expressive concept encodings effectively allow to translate such data into interpretable concepts but are often utilised in the context of low-capacity linear predictors. In this work, we push towards real-world verifiability by combining the strengths of both approaches. We introduce Neural Concept Verifier (NCV), a unified framework combining PVGs for formal verifiability with concept encodings to handle complex, high-dimensional inputs in an interpretable way. NCV achieves this by utilizing recent minimally supervised concept discovery models to extract structured concept encodings from raw inputs. A prover then selects a subset of these encodings, which a verifier, implemented as a nonlinear predictor, uses exclusively for decision-making. Our evaluations show that NCV outperforms classic concept-based models and pixel-based PVG classifier baselines on high-dimensional, logically complex datasets and helps mitigate shortcut behavior. Overall, we demonstrate NCV as a promising step toward concept-level, verifiable AI.

Neural Concept Verifier combines these approaches to support more expressive decisions over structured concepts.

The framework first uses minimally supervised concept discovery models to extract encodings from raw inputs. A prover selects a subset of those encodings, and a nonlinear verifier bases its decision exclusively on that subset. This makes the selected concept information the verifier’s entire input, connecting the decision process to the evidence supplied through the prover–verifier structure.

The evaluations also show that it helps mitigate shortcut behavior. The contribution is a unified framework that brings concept discovery into a formal-verifiability approach, with empirical results supporting its usefulness for more complex inputs. The authors present it as a step toward concept-level verifiable AI.
summary.tldr: Neural Concept Verifier combines discovered concepts with prover–verifier games to improve classification and reduce shortcut behavior on complex inputs.

title: Neural Concept Verifier: Scaling Prover-Verifier Games via Concept Encodings

abstract: While traditional network analysis focuses on single-layer networks, real-world systems often form multilayer networks with multiple relationship types. However, existing methods typically fail to capture complex inter-layer dependencies by treating layers independently or aggregating them. To address this, we propose T-GINEE (Tensor-Based Generalized Multilayer-graph Estimating Equation), a statistical regularization framework combining tensor-based generalized estimating equations with task-specific loss to model cross-network correlations explicitly. Key innovations include: (1) CP tensor decomposition capturing structural dependencies via shared latent factors; (2) a generalized estimating equation framework modeling inter-layer correlations through working covariance matrices; and (3) a flexible link function accommodating characteristics like sparsity. Our theoretical analysis establishes consistency and asymptotic normality under mild conditions. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets validate T-GINEE’s effectiveness for multilayer network analysis. Our code is available in the supplementary materials to ensure reproducibility.

paragraphs: Many networks contain several kinds of relationships, represented as separate layers. Treating each layer independently can miss dependencies between them, while combining them into one graph can also lose that structure. T-GINEE introduces a statistical regularization framework that explicitly represents cross-layer correlations alongside the loss for the task being solved.

The method uses CP tensor decomposition to express structural dependencies through shared latent factors. Generalized estimating equations incorporate inter-layer relationships through working covariance matrices, and a flexible link function accommodates properties such as sparsity. These components give the framework separate ways to capture shared structure, model statistical dependence, and adapt to characteristics of the observed network.

Under conditions described as mild, the theoretical analysis establishes consistency and asymptotic normality. Those are conditional large-sample guarantees about estimation behavior. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets also support the method’s effectiveness. Together, the results motivate explicitly modeling correlations between relationship layers when learning representations of multilayer networks.
summary.tldr: T-GINEE combines tensor decomposition and statistical estimating equations to learn multilayer graph representations with explicit cross-layer correlations.

title: T-GINEE: A Tensor-Based Multilayer Graph Representation Learning

abstract: The increasingly realistic and diverse generative data has led some deepfake detection methods to shift towards learning robust real content, e.g., via reconstruction-based tasks. However, most existing approaches rely primarily on prevalent continuous modeling (e.g., GMMs, VAEs, Diffusion Models) to construct a continuous latent manifold of real data, with the aim of improving the generalization capability, while overlooking a critical issue, i.e., such continuity may facilitate the interpolation of forgery artifacts, consequently causing ambiguity in detection. To alleviate this problem, we integrate discrete modeling into the feature space of the CLIP vision encoder, striking a balance between continuous manifold modeling and discrete representation. By incorporating a learnable vector quantized codebook, the real latent manifold is discretized, imposing a more stringent information bottleneck that reduces the likelihood of embedding generative artifacts. In order to further enhance the generalization of discrete modeling, we propose an adaptive tangent space projection mechanism that yields a continuous relaxation of the discrete real distribution within a controllable range. With these components, our method constructs a real distribution that is both tightly constrained and broadly generalizable, enhancing robustness to unseen forgeries. Extensive experiments on diverse datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Some deepfake detectors learn what real content looks like so they can recognize unfamiliar forgeries. This paper identifies a possible weakness in representing real content as a continuous space: smooth interpolation may also accommodate artifacts produced by generative models. That can blur the distinction the detector is meant to preserve.

The proposed method introduces a learned vector-quantized codebook into the feature space of a CLIP vision encoder. The codebook represents real content through discrete alternatives, creating a tighter information bottleneck. The intended effect is to reduce the likelihood that generative artifacts fit comfortably inside the learned representation of real data.

Strict discreteness also needs flexibility to generalize. The authors therefore add an adaptive tangent-space projection that permits a controlled continuous relaxation around the discrete representation. Together, the components aim to constrain the real-data distribution while allowing useful variation. Experiments across diverse datasets support the method’s effectiveness and robustness to unseen forgeries; the mechanism reduces an identified risk rather than guaranteeing that every forgery will be excluded.
summary.tldr: The method combines discrete real-image representations with controlled continuous flexibility to improve detection of unseen deepfakes.

title: Breaking Manifold Continuity: Vector Quantized Modeling for Real-Centric Deepfake Detection

abstract: Multimodal unlearning aims to eliminate specific data from pretrained multimodal models, which offers significant advantages in data privacy and model efficiency. Current methods struggle to achieve the desired properties of effectiveness, reliability and locality, due to the complex interdependency of unimodal and multimodal knowledge. By introducing a causal perspective, we propose multimodal unlearning with decoupled knowledge components. To promote fine-grained understanding of multimodal context, we introduce Multimodal Variational Inference (MVI) to infer modal-specific and -consistent factors with incomplete sample observation. With foundation of decoupled knowledge, we propose contrastive semantic editing to regulate multimodal unlearning towards refined forgetting. Experiments on privacy- and copyright-sensitive scenarios validate effectiveness of our method across multiple scenarios, ensuring the unlearned model maintains high reliability and locality.

paragraphs: Removing selected information from a pretrained multimodal model is difficult because knowledge within each modality interacts with knowledge shared across modalities. A change intended to forget particular data can therefore affect other knowledge. This paper seeks more effective and reliable forgetting while keeping its effects localized to the intended information.

The authors introduce a causal perspective that separates knowledge into components. Their Multimodal Variational Inference method infers factors specific to individual modalities and factors consistent across them, even with incomplete sample observations. This provides a finer representation of what a multimodal example contains than treating the whole example as a single forgetting target.

The method then applies contrastive semantic editing to regulate forgetting using those separated components. Experiments in privacy-sensitive and copyright-sensitive scenarios report effective unlearning while maintaining high reliability and locality. The stated contribution is a more targeted way to manage interconnected multimodal knowledge, with the reported evidence supporting preservation of unrelated information alongside the desired forgetting.
summary.tldr: Separating modality-specific and shared knowledge enables more targeted multimodal unlearning with reported gains in reliability and locality.

title: Beyond Sample-Level Forgetting: Improving Reliability in Multimodal Unlearning

abstract: Despite the success of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), existing reward modeling methods largely rely on explicit feedback, which is costly to collect and difficult to scale. This work studies implicit reward modeling, learning reward models from implicit user feedback, such as clicks, copies and skips. While scalable and cost-effective, implicit feedback poses two key challenges: (1) It lacks definitive negative samples, which makes standard positive-negative classification methods inapplicable; (2) It suffers from selection bias, where responses have heterogeneous propensities to elicit feedback, which further obscures definitive negative samples. To address these challenges, we propose ImplicitRM, which learns unbiased reward models from implicit feedback. It stratifies training samples into four latent groups using a stratification model and derives a likelihood-maximization objective that is theoretically unbiased, thereby addressing both challenges. Experiments across diverse LLM backbones and benchmark datasets validate that ImplicitRM learns accurate reward models from implicit feedback and improves performance on downstream RLHF tasks.

paragraphs: Clicks, copies, and skips offer abundant feedback about language-model responses without requiring explicit ratings. However, learning preferences from those actions is difficult: the absence of a positive action does not establish a negative judgment. Responses also differ in their likelihood of attracting feedback, creating selection bias in the observations.

ImplicitRM addresses both issues through a model that stratifies training samples into four latent groups. Using that structure, the authors derive a likelihood-maximization objective described as theoretically unbiased. The method therefore accounts for hidden distinctions in the feedback-generating process instead of applying ordinary positive-negative classification directly to observed interactions.

Experiments across multiple language-model backbones and benchmark datasets show accurate reward modeling from implicit feedback and improved downstream reinforcement learning from human feedback. The findings support using naturally occurring user actions as a scalable training signal when their ambiguity and selection effects are modeled explicitly. The theoretical unbiasedness claim concerns the proposed objective, while the experiments establish its reported practical usefulness.
summary.tldr: ImplicitRM models hidden feedback groups to address missing negatives and selection bias when learning rewards from user interactions.

title: Unbiased Reward Modeling from Implicit Feedback for LLM Alignment

abstract: Chain of thought (CoT) elicits reasoning in large language models by explicitly generating intermediate tokens. In contrast, latent thought reasoning operates directly in the continuous latent space, enabling computation beyond discrete linguistic representations. While both approaches exploit iterative computation, their comparative capabilities remain underexplored. In this work, we present a formal analysis showing that latent thought admits efficient parallel computation, in contrast to the inherently sequential nature of CoT. Conversely, CoT enables approximate counting through stochastic decoding. These separations suggest the tasks for which depth-driven recursion is more suitable, thereby offering practical guidance for choosing between reasoning paradigms.

paragraphs: Chain of thought makes intermediate reasoning explicit by generating tokens. Latent thought instead carries out intermediate computation in a continuous internal representation. Both approaches give a model additional rounds of computation, but the paper asks whether their different representations create meaningful differences in what that computation can efficiently accomplish.

The authors provide a formal comparison showing that latent thought permits efficient parallel computation, whereas chain-of-thought generation is inherently sequential. This separates the capabilities of the two approaches rather than treating them as interchangeable ways to extend reasoning. The analysis also identifies a capability in the other direction: chain of thought can perform approximate counting through stochastic decoding, connecting its computational behavior to the randomness of generated tokens.

These results offer guidance about matching a reasoning approach to a task's computational structure. In particular, they help distinguish settings suited to parallel computation from those where depth-driven recursion is more appropriate. The contribution is a theoretical account of complementary capabilities, providing a basis for choosing between explicit token-based reasoning and computation within latent representations.
summary.tldr: A formal analysis distinguishes latent thought's efficient parallel computation from chain of thought's sequential reasoning and stochastic approximate counting.

title: A Formal Comparison Between Chain of Thought and Latent Thought

abstract: Federated Adversarial Learning (FAL) enhances model robustness by integrating adversarial training into the federated learning framework. Despite recent advances proposing efficient FAL algorithms, existing work has mainly focused on convergence properties, with limited understanding of their generalization capabilities. To address this, we present the unified theoretical framework for analyzing FAL generalization through the lens of algorithmic stability. We first analyze general FAL algorithms based on stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and derive perturbation-dependent generalization bounds, which reveal that stronger adversarial attacks can lead to degraded generalization. To mitigate the impact of adversarial perturbations, we leverage Moreau envelope optimization and establish a perturbation-independent bound, demonstrating its efficacy in simultaneously enhancing both robustness and generalization. Finally, we extend our analysis to the practical black-box setting, demonstrating that zeroth-order optimization techniques can effectively maintain both robustness and generalization even without local gradient access.

paragraphs: Federated adversarial learning combines distributed training with robustness to perturbed inputs. Existing theory has emphasized whether optimization converges, leaving less understanding of performance on unseen data. This paper uses algorithmic stability to study generalization across a broad family of such methods.

For SGD-based algorithms, the authors derive bounds that depend on adversarial perturbation strength, showing how stronger attacks can worsen the generalization guarantee. They then use Moreau-envelope optimization to obtain a perturbation-independent bound. This provides a theoretically motivated way to manage robustness and generalization together.

The analysis extends to black-box settings through zeroth-order optimization, where clients need not expose local gradients. The contribution is a unified generalization perspective that spans ordinary gradient access and a more restricted practical setting. It clarifies why convergence or resistance to stronger training attacks alone does not fully characterize the quality of a federated adversarial learner.
summary.tldr: Stability analysis explains perturbation-dependent generalization in federated adversarial learning and motivates smoother, black-box-compatible alternatives.

title: Towards Understanding Generalization of Federated Adversarial Learning: Perspective of Algorithmic Stability

abstract: Reconstructing atomistic crystal structures from a single noisy STEM projection is an ill-posed inverse problem: multiple lattices can explain similar contrast, and purely feed-forward models cannot verify physical validity. We present AutoMat, a failure-aware agentic controller that performs inference-time hypothesis search with closed-loop verification to convert Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy (STEM) images into simulation-ready crystal structures and downstream properties. AutoMat composes perception and physics modules—pattern-adaptive denoising, physics-guided template retrieval as a state-dependent auxiliary branch, symmetry-constrained atomic reconstruction, and MLIP-based relaxation/validation—and triggers rollback-and-retry when verification fails. For systematic evaluation, we introduce STEM2Mat-Bench, a benchmark dataset containing 450+ annotated samples. Performance is assessed using lattice root-mean-square deviation (RMSD), formation energy mean absolute error (MAE), and structure matching accuracy. Results demonstrate that AutoMat outperforms existing approaches including SOTA models, specialized domain tools, and closed-source multimodal large models. This work establishes a direct pathway from microscopic characterization to atomic-scale modeling, addressing a fundamental challenge in materials science.

paragraphs: A single noisy electron-microscopy projection does not uniquely determine a crystal’s atomic structure: different lattices can produce similar image contrast. AutoMat approaches reconstruction as a search over hypotheses that must undergo physical verification. Its controller connects image interpretation to the production of crystal structures suitable for simulation and downstream property calculations.

The system combines pattern-adaptive denoising, symmetry-constrained atomic reconstruction, and relaxation and validation using machine-learning interatomic potentials. Physics-guided template retrieval serves as an auxiliary branch whose use depends on the current state. When verification fails, the controller can roll back and retry, allowing physical feedback to influence the reconstruction process during inference.

The authors introduce STEM2Mat-Bench, containing more than 450 annotated samples, and assess lattice deviation, formation-energy error, and structure-matching accuracy. They report better performance than existing models, specialized tools, and closed-source multimodal models. The findings support a workflow in which reconstruction and physical checking work together to address ambiguity in microscopy, rather than treating the initial image interpretation as a finished structure.
summary.tldr: AutoMat searches and physically verifies crystal reconstructions from noisy microscopy images, retrying failed hypotheses to produce simulation-ready structures.

title: AutoMat: Physics-Guided Agentic Reasoning for Solving Ill-Posed Inverse Microscopy Problems

abstract: Multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) is a fundamental framework for real-world decision-making problems involving multiple conflicting criteria. Existing multi-policy (MP) methods typically rely on online evolutionary frameworks that maintain large policy populations, leading to high sample complexity and excessive agent–environment interactions. To mitigate these limitations, we present Multi-policy Pareto Front Tracking (MPFT), a framework without a self-evolving population. It leverages an efficient Pareto-tracking mechanism initialized with single-objective extreme policies to trace the Pareto front, and further densifies sparse regions to achieve an accurate approximation of the full Pareto front. MPFT can be seamlessly integrated with advanced offline MORL algorithms, thereby substantially improving sample efficiency. We evaluate MPFT on six robotic control tasks with up to three objectives and three high-dimensional tasks with more than three objectives. Experimental results show that MPFT outperforms state-ofthe-art baselines in terms of hypervolume and expected utility. It also significantly reduces agent–environment interactions. These results further demonstrate that MPFT serves as a general purpose framework that can seamlessly integrate both online and offline MORL algorithms.

paragraphs: Multi-objective reinforcement learning seeks policies that offer useful tradeoffs among conflicting criteria. Many methods maintain large populations of policies and evolve them through repeated interaction with an environment. That process can require many samples. Multi-policy Pareto Front Tracking, or MPFT, instead constructs an approximation of the tradeoff frontier without maintaining a self-evolving population.

MPFT starts from extreme policies optimized for individual objectives. It then tracks the Pareto front and adds coverage in sparse regions to improve the approximation. This approach makes tracing and filling the frontier the organizing mechanism for finding multiple policies. It can also integrate with offline multi-objective learning algorithms, supporting better sample efficiency.

The authors evaluate six robotic control tasks with up to three objectives and three high-dimensional tasks with more than three objectives. MPFT outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on hypervolume and expected utility while substantially reducing environment interactions. The results support its use as a framework that can incorporate both online and offline learning methods.
summary.tldr: MPFT traces and fills the Pareto front without an evolving policy population, improving tradeoff quality while reducing environment interactions.

title: Population-Free Pareto Tracking for Sample-Efficient Multi-Policy MORL

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as autonomous agents in complex, long-horizon applications, where effective memory is critical for sustained performance. Yet existing memory benchmarks are largely dialogue-centric, while real agent memory consists of continuous agent-environment interaction trajectories composed of states, actions, observations, and tool outputs. To address this gap, we introduce AMA-Bench (Agent Memory with Any length), a benchmark for evaluating long-horizon memory in realistic agentic settings. AMA-Bench combines real-world agent trajectories from representative applications with expert-curated QA, as well as synthetic trajectories that scale to arbitrary horizons with rule-based QA. Our study shows that existing memory systems underperform because they fail to capture causal and objective information and rely heavily on lossy similarity-based retrieval. We further propose AMA-Agent, a memory system based on causality-graph construction and tool-augmented retrieval. AMA-Agent achieves 57.22% accuracy on AMA-Bench, outperforming the strongest baseline by 11.16%. Resources are available at: https://ama-bench.github.io/.

paragraphs: An autonomous agent's memory must retain more than a conversation. Over a long task, the agent encounters states, takes actions, receives observations, and reads tool outputs. AMA-Bench evaluates memory using these interaction histories, addressing a mismatch between dialogue-focused benchmarks and the information agents actually need to preserve.

The benchmark combines two sources of evidence. Real application trajectories come with questions curated by experts, while synthetic trajectories can extend to arbitrary lengths and support questions generated from rules. This combination allows evaluation on realistic histories as well as controlled histories whose length can be increased.

The authors find that existing memory systems struggle to preserve causal and objective information and depend heavily on similarity retrieval that loses relevant content. Their proposed AMA-Agent constructs causality graphs and retrieves information with tool support. It achieves 57.22% accuracy, reported as outperforming the strongest baseline by 11.16%. The result supports organizing memory around relationships within an agent's experience, beyond retrieving fragments that merely resemble a question.
summary.tldr: AMA-Bench tests memory over extended agent interactions, and AMA-Agent improves results using causality graphs and tool-assisted retrieval.

title: AMA-Bench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Memory for Agentic Applications

abstract: Learning humanoid control from video provides a scalable alternative to the scarcity of high-fidelity robot data. Existing methods, however, often rely on curated datasets and treat video as passive kinematic priors. They fail to capture dynamic humanoid interactions with the environment, which are essential for robust control in complex physical environments. To address this, we propose TR*ansferable Interaction P*rimitives (TRIP), a framework designed to extract and ground interactions from unlabeled game videos for locomotion control. To bridge the reality gap, we introduce a shared context latent space that aligns implicit video-domain features with functional target-domain observations, enabling the seamless transfer of video-mined strategies to reinforcement learning policies. abstract: Open-source AI is scaling rapidly, and model hubs now host millions of artifacts. Each foundation model can spawn large numbers of fine-tunes, adapters, quantizations, merges, and forks. We take the position that compute efficiency alone is insufficient for sustainability in open-source AI. Lower per-run costs can accelerate experimentation and deployment, increasing aggregate footprint unless impacts are measurable and comparable across derivative lineages. However, the energy use, water consumption, and emissions of these derivative lineages are rarely measured or disclosed in a consistent, comparable way, leaving aggregate ecosystem impact largely invisible. We argue that sustainable open-source AI requires a coordination infrastructure that tracks impacts across model lineages, not only base models. We propose Data and Impact Accounting (DIA), a lightweight, non-restrictive transparency layer that (i) standardizes carbon-and-water reporting metadata, (ii) integrates low-friction measurement into common training and inference pipelines, and (iii) aggregates reports via public dashboards to summarize cumulative impacts across releases and derivatives. DIA makes derivative costs visible and supports ecosystem-level accountability while preserving openness. Project Page: https://vectorinstitute.github.io/ai-impact-accounting

paragraphs: A foundation model can generate many descendants through fine-tuning, adapters, quantization, merging, and forks. This paper argues that the environmental impact of open-source AI must be tracked across those related releases. Measuring a base model alone leaves the accumulated energy use, water consumption, and emissions of its derivatives largely out of view.

The authors also explain why cheaper individual runs do not necessarily make the ecosystem sustainable. Lower costs can encourage more experimentation and deployment, potentially increasing total impact. They propose Data and Impact Accounting, a lightweight transparency layer that standardizes carbon and water reporting metadata, adds measurement to common training and inference workflows, and combines reports in public dashboards.

The proposal is intended to make cumulative impacts comparable across model families while preserving openness. Its emphasis is coordination: measurements need consistent formats and aggregation to reveal costs distributed across many developers and releases. The paper presents this accounting infrastructure as a requirement for ecosystem-level responsibility, rather than treating computational efficiency per run as sufficient evidence of sustainability.
summary.tldr: Data and Impact Accounting would track cumulative environmental costs across open-source models and their derivatives.

abstract: A geometric and non parametric procedure for testing if two finite set of points are linearly separable is proposed. The Linear Separability Test is equivalent to a test that determines if a strictly positive point h > 0 exists in the range of a matrix A (related to the points in the two finite sets). The algorithm proposed in the paper iteratively checks if a strictly positive point exists in a subspace by projecting a strictly positive vector with equal co-ordinates (p), on the subspace. At the end of each iteration, the subspace is reduced to a lower dimensional subspace. The test is completed within r ≤ min(n, d + 1) steps, for both linearly separable and non separable problems (r is the rank of A, n is the number of points and d is the dimension of the space containing the points). The worst case time complexity of the algorithm is O(nr³) and space complexity of the algorithm is O(nd). A small review of some of the prominent algorithms and their time complexities is included. The worst case computational complexity of our algorithm is lower than the worst case computational complexity of Simplex, Perceptron, Support Vector Machine and Convex Hull Algorithms, if d < n^(2/3).

paragraphs: The paper asks whether two finite collections of points can be separated by a linear boundary. It proposes a geometric, nonparametric test that turns this question into a different one: does the range of a matrix constructed from the points contain a vector whose coordinates are all strictly positive?

The algorithm investigates this positivity question through projections. It starts with a positive vector whose coordinates are equal and projects it onto the relevant subspace. After each iteration, it reduces the search to a lower-dimensional subspace. This shrinking construction gives a finite completion guarantee for both separable and nonseparable inputs.

The test finishes within r steps, where r is the matrix rank and is at most the smaller of n and d + 1. Its worst-case time cost is O(nr³), with O(nd) storage. The stated complexity advantage over Simplex, Perceptron, SVM, and convex-hull algorithms is conditional: it holds when d < n^(2/3). This is a worst-case comparison, rather than an assertion about every individual run.
summary.tldr: A projection-based test decides linear separability in a bounded number of steps, with a stated worst-case complexity advantage under a dimensionality condition.

title: A fast linear separability test by projection of positive points on subspaces

abstract: Multiple kernel learning algorithms are proposed to combine kernels in order to obtain a better similarity measure or to integrate feature representations coming from different data sources. Most of the previous research on such methods is focused on the computational efficiency issue. However, it is still not feasible to combine many kernels using existing Bayesian approaches due to their high time complexity. We propose a fully conjugate Bayesian formulation and derive a deterministic variational approximation, which allows us to combine hundreds or thousands of kernels very efficiently. We briefly explain how the proposed method can be extended for multiclass learning and semi-supervised learning. Experiments with large numbers of kernels on benchmark data sets show that our inference method is quite fast, requiring less than a minute. On one bioinformatics and three image recognition data sets, our method outperforms previously reported results with better generalization performance.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning combines different measures of similarity, potentially bringing together feature representations from several data sources. Bayesian approaches offer a framework for learning these combinations, but their computational demands have made large collections of kernels difficult to handle. This paper targets that obstacle directly.

The authors construct a fully conjugate Bayesian formulation and derive a deterministic variational approximation for inference. The formulation is designed so that the probabilistic components work together in a computationally manageable way. This enables efficient combinations of hundreds or thousands of kernels. The paper also outlines extensions to multiclass learning and learning with both labeled and unlabeled data.

Experiments involving large kernel collections report inference times below one minute on the benchmark datasets considered. On one bioinformatics dataset and three image-recognition datasets, the method also improves generalization over previously reported results. Together, these findings support the approach as a way to make large Bayesian kernel combinations practical while retaining useful predictive performance in the tested applications.
summary.tldr: A conjugate Bayesian formulation and variational inference make learning combinations of hundreds or thousands of kernels computationally practical.

title: Bayesian Efficient Multiple Kernel Learning

abstract: With the advent of kernel methods, automating the task of specifying a suitable kernel has become increasingly important. In this context, the Multiple Kernel Learning (MKL) problem of finding a combination of pre-specified base kernels that is suitable for the task at hand has received significant attention from researchers. In this paper we show that Multiple Kernel Learning can be framed as a standard binary classification problem with additional constraints that ensure the positive definiteness of the learned kernel. Framing MKL in this way has the distinct advantage that it makes it easy to leverage the extensive research in binary classification to develop better performing and more scalable MKL algorithms that are conceptually simpler, and, arguably, more accessible to practitioners. Experiments on nine data sets from different domains show that, despite their simplicity, the proposed techniques can significantly outperform current leading MKL approaches.

paragraphs: Kernel methods depend on a way of measuring similarity that suits the prediction task. Multiple kernel learning addresses this choice by combining a collection of predefined kernels. The paper asks whether learning this combination can be expressed through a familiar learning problem, making kernel selection easier to develop and apply.

The authors show that multiple kernel learning can be formulated as binary classification with extra constraints. These constraints ensure that the resulting similarity function has the positive definiteness required of the learned kernel. The reformulation connects kernel construction to the extensive collection of methods already available for binary classification, providing a route to simpler and more scalable algorithms.

Experiments across nine datasets from different domains show that the proposed techniques can significantly outperform leading multiple kernel learning approaches. The finding supports the practical value of the reformulation: conceptual simplicity can coexist with strong predictive performance. Its broader contribution is a framework for adapting classification research to kernel learning while explicitly preserving the mathematical requirements of the kernel.
summary.tldr: The paper recasts multiple kernel learning as constrained binary classification, enabling simple methods that can outperform leading alternatives.
